children.translated_text: Nyāyakusumāñjali (A Handful of Flowers of Logic).
First Chapter (Prathamastabakaḥ).
[Ku.1.101] Spreading in the direction of the good, its festivity bound to the awakening of the fragrance of the virtuous,
not wilting when crushed, a ground of honey flowing with the nectar of immortality —
this [offering] placed at the pair of feet of the Lord, like a bee buzzing [around them],
may this pure, unobstructed handful of flowers of logic (<s>Nyāyaprasūnāñjali</s>) delight my mind!  [verse 1]
The wise declare that the path to heaven (<s>svarga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)
is the worship of Him — [therefore] the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>) is herein examined.  [verse 2]

children.text: [ku.1.102] iha yadyapi yaṃ kamapi puruṣārthamarthayamānāḥ- śuddhabuddhasvabhāva ityaupaniṣadāḥ, ādividvān siddha iti kāpilāḥ, kleśakarmavipākā'śayairaparāmṛṣṭo nirmāṇakāyamadhiṣṭhāya sampradāyapradyota(3)(varta)ko 'nugrāhakaśceti pātañjalāḥ, lokavedaviruddhairapi nirlepaḥ svatantraśceti mahāpāśupatāḥ, śiva iti śaivāḥ, puruṣottama iti vaiṣṇavāḥ, pitāmaha iti paurāṇikāḥ, yajñapuruṣa iti yājñikāḥ, (4)sarvatra iti saugatāḥ, nivāraṇa iti digambarāḥ, upāsyatvena deśita (nodita) iti mīmāṃsakāḥ, lokavyavahārasiddha iti cārvākāḥ,(5) yāvaduktopapanna iti naiyāyikāḥ, kiṃ bahunā- kāravo 'pi yaṃ viśvakarmeti upāsate, tasminneva jātigotrapravaracaraṇakuladharmādivadāsaṃsāraṃ prasiddhānubhā(bha)ve bhagavati bhave sandeha eva kutaḥ? kiṃ nirūpaṇīyam?- [ku.1.103] tathāpi- nyāyacarceyamīśasya mananavyapadeśabhāk /
children.translated_text: [Ku.1.102] Here, although [various schools] seeking whatever human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) [describe Him differently] — the <s>Aupaniṣadas</s> (Vedāntins) [say He is] 'of pure and awakened nature'; the <s>Kāpilas</s> (Sāṅkhyas) [say He is] 'the primordial knower, the perfected one'; the <s>Pātañjalas</s> (Yogins) [say He is] 'untouched by afflictions, actions, results, and latent impressions, the illuminator (sustainer) of tradition, the gracious one presiding over a created body'; the <s>Mahāpāśupatas</s> [say He is] 'unstained even by [acts] contrary to world and Veda, self-dependent'; the <s>Śaivas</s> [say He is] '<s>Śiva</s>'; the <s>Vaiṣṇavas</s> [say He is] '<s>Puruṣottama</s>' (Supreme Person); the <s>Paurāṇikas</s> [say He is] '<s>Pitāmaha</s>' (Grandfather); the <s>Yājñikas</s> (ritualists) [say He is] '<s>Yajñapuruṣa</s>' (Sacrifice-Person); the <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) [say He is] 'the omnipresent one'; the <s>Digambaras</s> (Jains) [say He is] 'the remover [of karma]'; the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> [say He is] 'taught (enjoined) as an object of worship'; the <s>Cārvākas</s> (materialists) [say He is] 'established through worldly convention'; the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> (logicians) [say He is] 'as established by the stated proofs'; why say more — even craftsmen worship Him as <s>Viśvakarman</s>. Regarding that very Lord <s>Bhava</s>, well-known in experience as [enduring] throughout transmigration — like caste, lineage, family line, school, and family customs — where is any doubt? What is there to examine? — [Ku.1.103] Nevertheless: This logical inquiry concerning the Lord, bearing the designation of reflection (<s>manana</s>),
is itself worship (<s>upāsanā</s>), arising after hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>).  [verse 3]

children.text: śruto hi bhagavān bahuśaḥ śrutismṛtītihāsapurāṇeṣvidānīṃ mantavyo bhavatiḥ, "śrotavyo mantavya" iti śruteḥ; "āgamenānumānena dhyānābhyāsarasena ca /
children.translated_text: For the Lord has been heard of many times in the <s>Śrutis</s>, <s>Smṛtis</s>, <s>Itihāsas</s>, and <s>Purāṇas</s>; now He is to be reflected upon, since the <s>Śruti</s> says: 'He is to be heard, He is to be reflected upon.' And: 'By scripture, by inference, and by the relish of meditative practice,
devising wisdom in three ways, one attains the highest <s>yoga</s>.'
Thus says the <s>Smṛti</s> also.

children.text: [ku.1.104] tadiha saṅkṣepataḥ pañcatayī vipratipattiḥ- alaukikasya paralokasādhanasyābhāvāt ; anyathāpi paralokasādhanānuṣṭhānasambhavāt ; tadabhāvā'vedakapramāṇasadbhāvāt ; sattve 'pi tasyāpramāṇatvāt ; tatsādhakapramāṇābhāvācceti //
children.translated_text: [Ku.1.104] Here, in summary, there is a fivefold controversy: (1) because there is no non-mundane means to the other world; (2) because the performance of means to the other world is possible otherwise [i.e., without God]; (3) because there exists a valid means of knowledge that [proves] the absence of that [God]; (4) because even if it [such a pramāṇa] exists, it is not a valid means of knowledge; and (5) because there is no valid means of knowledge that could prove Him.
[Ku.1.105] Of these, the first alternative [is refuted] — because: From dependence [on something unseen], from beginninglessness, from diversity, from universal operation,
from the restriction to each individual self, and from [the nature of] enjoyment — there exists a non-mundane cause.  [verse 4]

children.text: [ku.1.106] na hyayaṃ saṃsāraḥ (8) aneka(naika)vidha(vidho)dukhamayo nirapekṣo bhavitumarhati /
children.translated_text: [Ku.1.106] For this <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), consisting of manifold sufferings, cannot be without dependence [on a cause].

children.text: tadā hi- syādeva, na syādeva vā- na tu kadācit syāt //
children.translated_text: For then — it would always exist, or never exist at all — but it would not be occasional.

children.text: akasmādeva bhavatīti cenna- hetubhūtiniṣedho na svānupākhyavidhirna ca /
children.translated_text: If [one says] 'it arises without any cause at all' — no: the denial of a cause is not a positive prescription of self-description, nor is it
a description of [its own] nature — because of the fixedness of the limit.  [verse 5]

children.text:
[ku.1.107] hetuniṣedhe bhavanasyānapekṣatvena (9) sarvadā bhavanam, aviśeṣāt /
bhavanapratiṣedhe, prāgiva paścādapyabhavanam, aviśeṣāt /
utpatteḥ pūrvaṃ svayamasataḥ svotpattāvaprabhutvena svasmāditi pakṣānupapatteḥ /
paurvāparya(10) niyamaśca kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ /
na caikaṃ pūrvamaparaṃ ca,tattvasya bhedādhiṣṭhānatvāt /
anupākhyasya hetutve prāgiti satvaprasaktau punaḥ sadātanatvāpatteḥ /
[ku.1.108] syādetat- na akasmāditi kāraṇaniṣedhamātraṃ vā bhavanapratiṣedho vā svātmahetukatvaṃ vā nirupākhyahetukatvaṃ vābhidhitsitam /
api tvanapekṣa eva kaścinniyatadeśa(11)svabhāvavanniyatakālasvabhāva iti brūmaḥ- (12)na, niravadhitve aniyatāvadhikatve vā kādācitkatvavyāghātāt /
na hyuttarakālasiddhitvamātraṃ kādācitkatm; kiṃ tu prāgasatve sati /
sāvadhītve tu sa eva prācyo heturityucyate /
[ku.1.109] astu prāgabhāva evāvadhiriti cenna, anyeṣāmapi tatkāle satvāt anyathā tasyaiva nirūpaṇānupapatteḥ /
tathā ca na tadekāvadhitvamaviśeṣāt /
itaranirapekṣasya prāgabhāvasyāvadhitve prāgapi tadavadheḥ(13) kāryasya sattvaprasaṅgāt /
[ku.1.110] santu ye kecidavadhayaḥ, na tu te 'pekṣyanta iti svabhāvārtha iti cet-"nāpekṣyanta" iti kor'thaḥ? kiṃ na niyatāḥ, āhosvinniyatā apyanupakārakāḥ? prathame dhūmo dahanavat gardabhamapyavadhīkuryāt, niyāmakābhāvāt /
dvitīye tu kimupakārāntareṇa, niyamasyaivāpekṣārthatvāt, tasyaiva ca kāraṇātmatvāt, īdṛśasya ca svabhāvavādasyeṣṭatvāt /
[ku.1.111] ṭhanityasvabhāvaniyamavadetat /
na hyākāśasya tattvamākasmikamiti sarvasya kiṃ na syāditi vaktumucitam" iti cenna, sarvasya bhavataḥ svabhāvatvānupapatteḥ /
na hyekamanekasvabhāvaṃ (vo)(14)nāma, vyāghātāt /
nanvevamihāpi sarvadā bhavataḥ kādācitkatvasvabhāvavyāghāta iti tulyaḥ parihāraḥ- na tulyaḥ- niravadhitve aniyatāvadhitve vā kādācitkatvavyāghātāt niyatāvadhitve hetuvādābhyupagamāt /
[ku.1.112] syādetat- uttarasya pūrvaḥ, pūrvasyottaro madhyamasyobhayamavadhirastu; darśanasya durapahnavatvāt /
tvayāpyetadabhyupagantavyam /

children.translated_text: For even in non-existence, as in existence, there is no being-limited-by-both.
The same would apply to existences where one or the other terminus is not apprehended — it would not [follow], because of beginninglessness.
[Ku.1.113] This stream is not one having a beginning; nor does it possess a single power different [from its constituents].
One who strives for the truth must attend to [the methods of] agreement (<s>anvaya</s>) and difference (<s>vyatireka</s>).  [verse 6]

[Ku.1.107] If the cause is denied, then because of the non-dependence of origination, there would be origination at all times, since there is no distinguishing factor. If origination is denied, then just as before, there would be non-origination even afterwards, since there is no distinguishing factor. [Also,] because the position that the non-existent [thing], being powerless to produce its own origination, [originates] from itself prior to its origination is untenable. And the fixed sequence [of before and after] is [precisely] the cause-effect relation. Nor is one thing both prior and posterior, because [absolute] reality is the substratum of distinction. If the indescribable is the cause, then since there would follow the existence [of the effect] 'before' [i.e., always], it would again follow that it is eternal. [Ku.1.108] It may be objected: The [phrase] 'not without cause' is intended neither as a mere denial of a cause, nor as a denial of origination, nor as self-causation, nor as causation by something indescribable. Rather, we say that something, though not dependent [on anything else], has a fixed nature with respect to a particular time, just as it has with respect to a particular place and nature. — No, because if [the time] is limitless or has no fixed limit, the occasional nature [of things] would be contradicted. For mere belonging to a later time is not occasionality; rather, [it requires] prior non-existence. But when there is a limit, that very prior [condition] is called the cause. [Ku.1.109] If [one says] 'let prior non-existence itself be the limit' — no, because other things also exist at that time; otherwise, the very determination of that [prior non-existence] would be impossible. And thus it is not limited by that alone, since there is no distinguishing factor. If prior non-existence, independent of anything else, is the limit, then there would be the unwanted consequence that the effect exists even before that limit. [Ku.1.110] If [one says] 'let whatever [conditions] be the limits, but they are not depended upon — that is the meaning of intrinsic nature' — what does 'not depended upon' mean? Is it that they are not fixed, or that though fixed, they are non-contributory? In the first case, just as smoke [requires] fire, it would make even a donkey a limit, due to the absence of a determining factor. In the second case, what [need] is there for any other contribution, since restriction itself has the purpose of dependence, and that [restriction] itself constitutes causality, and since this kind of 'nature-doctrine' is [thereby already] accepted? [Ku.1.111] This is like [the argument about] the intrinsic nature of the fixedness of the eternals [such as space]. It is not proper to say 'the nature of space is causeless, so why shouldn't everything be?' — because the 'nature-ness' of everything is untenable for you. For one thing does not have multiple natures — that would be contradictory. [Objection:] But then the same applies here too — the nature of occasionality contradicts the nature of eternality — so the rejoinder is the same. — No, it is not the same: because if [the time] is limitless or has no fixed limit, occasionality is contradicted; whereas if there is a fixed limit, the doctrine of causation is [already] conceded. [Ku.1.112] It may be objected: Let the earlier be the limit of the later, the later the limit of the earlier, and both the limit of the middle — since direct experience is hard to deny. You too must concede this.

children.text:
[ku.1.114] prāgabhāvo hyuttarakālāvadhiranādiḥ, evaṃ bhāvo 'pi ghaṭādiḥ syāt /
anupalabhyamānaprākkoṭikaghaṭādiviṣayaṃ nedamaniṣṭamiti cenna- tāvanmātrāvadhisvabhāvatve tadaharvat pūrvedyurapi tamavadhīkṛtya taduttarasya satvaprasaṅgāt; apekṣaṇīyāntarābhavāt /
evaṃ pūrvapūrvamapi /
bhāve, tadeva sadātanatvāt /
tadaharevānena bhavitavyamiti asya svabhāva iti cenna-tasyāpyahnaḥ pūrvanyāyena pūrvamapi satvaprasaṅgāt /
tasmāttasyāpi tatpūrvakatvaṃ, evaṃ tatpūrvasyāpītyanāditvameva jyāyaḥ /
na tvapūrvānutpādeḥ kasyacidapūrvasya sambhava iti /
[ku.1.115] tathāpi vyaktyapekṣayā niyamo 'stu, na jātyapekṣayeti cenna, niyatajātīyasvabhāvatāvyāghātāt /
(15) yadi hi yataḥ kutaścidbhavanneva tajjātīyasvabhāvaḥsyāt, sarvasya sarvajātīyatvamekajātīyatvaṃ vā syāt /
evaṃ (yadi) tajjātīyena yataḥ kutaścidbhavitavyamiti asya svabhāvaḥ, tada'pi sarvasmātsarvajātīyamekajātīyaṃ vā syāt /
[ku.1.116] kathaṃ tarhi tṛṇāraṇimaṇibhyo bhavannāśuśukṣaṇirekajātīyaḥ? (16) ekaśaktimatvāditi cenna; yadi hi vijātīyeṣvapyekajātīya(17)kāryakaraṇaśaktiḥ samaveyāt, na kāryātkāraṇaviśeṣaḥ kvāpyanumīyeta; kāraṇavyāvṛtyā ca na tajjātīyasyaiva kāryasya vyāvṛttiravasīyeta /
tadabhāve 'pi tajjātīyaśaktimato 'nyasmādapi tadutpattisambhavāt /
yāvaddarśanaṃ vyavasthā bhaviṣyatīti cenna, nimittasyādarśanāt, dṛṣṭasya cānimittatvāt /
etena (18) sūkṣmajātīyā(sūkṣmādekajātīyatvā)diti nirastam, avahnerapi tatsaukṣmyāt dhūmotpattyāpatteḥ /
[ku.1.117] kāryajātibhedābhedayoḥ samavāyibhedābhedāveva tantram, na nimittāsamavāyinī iti cenna; tayorakāraṇatvaprasaṅgāt /
na hi sati bhāvamātraṃ tat; kiṃ tu satyeva bhāvaḥ /
na ca jātiniyame samavāyikāraṇamātraṃ nibandhanam, api tu sāmagrī /
anyathā dravyaguṇakarmaṇāmekopādānakatve vijātīyatvaṃ (19)na syāt /
na ca kāryadravyasyaiṣā rītiriti yuktam; ārabdhadugdhairevāvayavairdadhyārambhadarśanāt /
[ku.1.118] etenāpohavāde niyamo nirastaḥ;"kāryakāraṇabhāvadve"(20)tyādiviplavaprasaṅgāt /
tasmānniyatajātīyatāsvabhāva(21)bhaṅgena vyaktyapekṣayaiva niyama iti- [ku.1.119] (22)na; phūtkāreṇa tṛṇādereva, nirmanthanenāraṇereva pratiphalitataraṇikiraṇairmaṇereveti prakāraniyamavat tenaiva vyajyamānasya kāryajātibhedasya bhāvāt /
dṛśyate ca pāvakatvāviśeṣe 'pi pradīpaḥ prāsādodaravyāpakamālokamārabhate; na tathā jvālājālajaṭilo 'pi dārudahanaḥ , na tarāñcakārīṣaḥ /
yastu taṃ nākalayet, sa kāryasāmānyena kāraṇamātramanuminuyāditi kimanupannam /
[ku.1.120] evaṃ tarhi dhūmādāvapi kaścidanupalakṣaṇīyo viśeṣaḥ syāt, yasya dahanāpekṣeti, na dhūmādisāmānyādvahnisāmānyādisiddhiḥ /
etena vyatireko vyākhyātaḥ /
tathā ca kāryānupalabdhiliṅgabhaṅge svabhāvasyāpyasiddher(23)gatamanumāneneti cet-(24)na /
pratyakṣānupalambhagocaro jātibhedo na kāryaprayojaka iti vadato bauddhasya śirasyeṣa prahāraḥ /
asmākaṃ tu yatsāmānyākrāntayoryayoranvayavyatirekavattā, tayostathaiva hetuhetumadbhāvaniścayaḥ /
tathā cāvāntaraviśeṣasadbhāve 'pi na no virodhaḥ /
[ku.1.121] kiṃ punastārṇādau dahanasāmānyasya prayojakam; tṛṇādīnāṃ viśeṣa eva niyatatvāditi cet-(25) na /
tejomātrotpattau pavano nimittam; avayavasaṃyogo 'samavāyī; tejo 'vayavāḥsamavāyinaḥ /
iyameva sāmagrī gurutvavaddravyasahitā piṇḍitasya /
iyameva tejogatamudbhūtasparśamapekṣya dahanaṃ, tatrāpi jalaṃ prāpya divyaṃ, pārthivaṃ prāpya bhaumam, ubhayaṃ prāpyodaryamārabhata iti svayamūhanīyam /
[ku.1.122] tathāpyekamekajātīyameva vā kiñcitkāraṇamastu kṛtaṃ vicitreṇa /

children.translated_text: For even something that is not dissimilar [from its causes] is seen to produce many dissimilar effects.

children.text: yathā- pradīpa eka eva timirāpahārī vartivikārakārī rūpāntaravyavahārakārīti cenna- vaicitryāt kāryasya /
children.translated_text: For example, a single lamp dispels darkness, produces modification of the wick, and produces the experience of colors — [if this is the objection,] no, because of the diversity of the effect.

children.text: ekasya na kramaḥ kvāpi vaicitryaṃ ca samasya na /
children.translated_text: Of a single [cause], there is never in any case [simultaneous production]; and of a simultaneous [set], there is no diversity.
Nor is a difference of powers [possible] in what is undifferentiated; [for] one's own nature is insurmountable. (Verse 7)

[Ku 1.114] For prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>), which has the later time as its limit, is beginningless; likewise, a positive entity (<s>bhāva</s>) such as a pot would also [be beginningless]. If it be said that this is not an undesirable consequence, since the pot etc. whose prior limit is unapprehended [are such] — no, [we reply]: if [prior non-existence] had as its nature merely that limit, then just as [it exists] on that day, it would also exist on the previous day with that [limit] accepted, and so the existence of the subsequent [state] would follow; because there is an absence of a required intermediate [entity]. Likewise for each successive prior [moment]. In the case of a positive entity, that very [entity exists] because of its eternality. If it be said that 'it must exist on that very day — that is its nature' — no, because even for that day, by the previous reasoning, existence prior [to it] would follow. Therefore, that [prior non-existence] also has something prior to it; likewise for what is prior to that — and so beginninglessness is indeed preferable. But [it cannot be maintained] that something unprecedented arises, since nothing unprecedented is possible because of the non-origination of the unprecedented.
[Ku 1.115] Even so, let the regularity be with respect to individuals (<s>vyakti</s>), not with respect to universals (<s>jāti</s>) — no, because this would contradict the nature of belonging to a determinate universal. (15) For if something, arising from whatever [cause], had the nature of belonging to that universal, then everything would belong to every universal, or to one universal only. Similarly, if 'it must arise from whatever [cause] as belonging to that universal — that is its nature,' then again, everything from everything would belong to every universal, or to one only.
[Ku 1.116] Then how is fire, arising from grass, fire-sticks (<s>araṇi</s>), and gems, of one universal? (16) If it be said: because of possessing one power — no; for if the power to produce an effect of one universal inhered even in things of different universals, then no specific cause could ever be inferred from an effect; and from the exclusion of a cause, the exclusion of that very universal of effect could not be ascertained. Because even in the absence of that [cause], production of that [effect] from something else possessing the power of that universal would be possible. If it be said that regularity will be as far as observation [goes] — no, because the determining condition (<s>nimitta</s>) is not observed, and what is observed is not a determining condition. By this, [the view that] 'from something subtle, [there is] identity of universal' is refuted, since even from non-fire, production of smoke would follow because of the subtlety of that [fire].
[Ku 1.117] If it be said that the difference and non-difference of the universal of the effect depend solely on the difference and non-difference of the inherent cause (<s>samavāyin</s>), not on the efficient cause or non-inherent cause — no, because [otherwise] they would cease to be causes. For a mere positive entity, given [the inherent cause's] existence, is not that [cause]; rather, given existence itself, there is [the effect as a] positive entity. And the basis of the regularity of universals is not the inherent cause alone, but the aggregate of conditions (<s>sāmagrī</s>). Otherwise, since substance, quality, and action have one material cause, there would be no difference of universal [among them]. Nor is it correct [to say] that this is simply the way product-substances work; because we observe curds being produced by the very same parts that produced the milk.
[Ku 1.118] By this, regularity in the <s>apoha</s> (exclusion) theory is also refuted; because absurd consequences would follow [from the Buddhist theory beginning with] 'the two [aspects of] cause-effect relation.' Therefore, since the nature of belonging to a determinate universal would be destroyed, regularity would be with respect to individuals only — [Ku 1.119] (22) No; just as there is regularity of mode — fire from grass [is produced] by blowing, from fire-sticks by churning, from gems by reflected sunbeams — so too the difference of universal of the effect that is manifested by that very [mode] exists. And we observe that even though there is no difference in being fire, a lamp produces light pervading the interior of a palace, but a fire burning logs, though bristling with masses of flame, does not [do so], nor even more so does a fire of dried cow-dung. Whoever would not discern this would simply infer a mere cause from the general [nature of the] effect — what is wrong with that?
[Ku 1.120] In that case, even in smoke etc. there might be some imperceptible particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>) that depends on fire — so the establishment of fire-in-general from smoke-in-general etc. [would fail]. By this, the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) is also explained. And since, with the collapse of the mark [of inference] from non-apprehension of the effect and [inference based on] the essential nature, [everything] would have been [already] settled by inference — no, [we reply]: this is a blow on the head of the Buddhist who says that the difference of universal, which falls within the range of perception and non-apprehension, does not produce the effect. For us, however, the ascertainment of the cause-effect relation is precisely between those two that, as pervaded by the general, have positive and negative concomitance. And thus, even if intermediate particulars exist, there is no contradiction for us.
[Ku 1.121] What then is the producer of fire-in-general in grass etc.? If it be said: the particular [nature] of grass etc. itself, since it is invariable — (25) no. Wind is the efficient cause (<s>nimitta</s>) for the production of heat as such; conjunction of parts is the non-inherent [cause]; the parts of heat are the inherent causes. This very aggregate, together with the substance possessing gravity, [is the cause] of the compacted [fire]. This very [aggregate], with reference to the manifested heat of fire, [produces] burning; there, upon reaching water, [it becomes] celestial [fire]; upon reaching earth, terrestrial; upon reaching both, it produces gastric fire — this should be worked out by oneself.
[Ku 1.122] Even so, let there be one cause, or one of the same universal — what need of diverse [causes]?

children.text:
[ku.1.123] na tāvadekasmādanapekṣādanekam, akramāt kramavatkāryānupapatteḥ /
kramavattāvatkārya(ka)kāraṇasvabhāvatvāttasya, tat tathā; yaugapadyavaditi cet- (26)ayamapi ca kṣaṇabhaṅge parihāro na tu sahakārivāde /
pūrvapūrvānapekṣāyāṃ kramasyaiva vyāhateḥ /
kramaniyame tvanapekṣānupapatteḥ /
[ku.1.124] nāpyanekamavicitram /
(27)yadi hyanyūnamanatiriktaṃ vā dahanakāraṇamadahanasyāpi hetuḥ, nāsāvadahano dahano vā syāt; ubhayātmako
 vā syāt /
na caivam /
śaktibhedādayamadoṣa iti cenna- dharmibhedābhedābhyāṃ tasyānupapatteḥ /
asaṅkīrṇobhayajananasvabhāvatvādayamadoṣa iti cenna- /
na hi svādhīnamasyādahanatvam; api tu tajjanakasvabhāvādhīnam /
tathā ca tadāyattatvāddahanasyāpi tattvaṃ kena vāraṇīyam /
na hi tasmin janayitavye nāsau tatsvabhāvaḥ /
tasmādvicitratvāt kāryasya kāraṇenāpi vicitreṇa bhavitavyam /
na ca tat svabhāvatastathā /
tataḥ sahakārivaicitryānupraveśaḥ /

children.translated_text: But not even for a moment can it produce that [effect] without dependence on those [auxiliaries].

children.text: [ku.1.125] astu dṛṣṭameva sahakāricakram; kimapūrvakalpanayeti cenna- viśvavṛttitaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Ku 1.125] Let there be just the observed circle of auxiliary causes; what need of postulating something unprecedented? — No, because of the universal activity [of God].
The universal activity [of God] is not without fruit, nor does it have suffering as its sole fruit.
Nor is it [merely] having observed [worldly] gain as its fruit; nor is deception of this kind [possible]. (Verse 8)

[Ku 1.123] First, from a single [cause] without auxiliaries, multiple [effects do not arise], because a sequential effect cannot be produced from something without sequence. [If it be said that] the cause has the nature of producing sequential effects — then it is so [only because of auxiliaries]; [if it be said] it is like simultaneity — this solution also [works only] in the momentariness doctrine, not in the doctrine of auxiliary causes. Because if there is no dependence on each successive [auxiliary], sequence itself would be contradicted. But if sequence is regulated, non-dependence [on auxiliaries] would be impossible.
[Ku 1.124] Nor [can] multiple [causes without diversity produce diverse effects]. (27) For if a cause of fire that is neither deficient nor excessive were also a cause of non-fire, then that [effect] would be neither non-fire nor fire; or it would be both. But it is not so. If it be said there is no fault because of difference of powers — no, because that [difference of powers] is impossible given the identity or non-identity of the property-bearer. If it be said there is no fault because of the nature of producing both without intermixture — no. For its [quality of producing] non-fire is not self-dependent; rather, it depends on the nature of its generator. And since it is thus dependent, by what can the reality of fire [production] be prevented? For when that [effect] is to be produced, it is not [the case that the cause] does not have that nature. Therefore, because of the diversity of the effect, the cause also must be diverse. And it is not so by its own nature. Hence, the entry of diversity through auxiliary causes [is required].

children.text:
yad.i hi pūrvapūrvabhūtapariṇatiparamparāmātramevottarottaranibandhanam, na paralokārthī kaścidiṣṭāpūrtayoḥ pravarteta /
na hi niṣphale duḥkhaikaphale vā kaścideko 'pi prekṣāpūrvakārī ghaṭeta; prāgeva jagat /
[ku.1.126] lābhapūjākhyātyarthamiti cet- lābhādaya eva kinnibandhanāḥ? na hīyaṃ pravṛttiḥ svarūpata eva taddhetuḥ /
yato vānena labdhavyaṃ yovainaṃ pūjayiṣyati, sa kimartham? khyātyarthamanurāgārthaṃ ca /
jano dātari mānayitari ca rajyate /
"janānurāgaprabhavā hi sampadaḥ" /
iti cenna- nītinarmasaciveṣveva tadarthaṃ dānādivyavasthāpanāt /
traividyatapasvino dhūrtavakāḥ eveti cenna- teṣāṃ dṛṣṭasampadaṃ pratyanupayogāt /
[ku.1.127] sukhārthaṃ tathā karotīti cenna- nāstikairapi tathā karaṇaprasaṅgāt, sambhogavat /
lokavyavahārasiddhatvādaphalamapi kriyate, vedavyavahārasiddhatvātsandhyopāsanavaditi cet- gurumatametat, na gurormatam /
tato nedamanavasara eva vaktumucitam /
[ku.1.128] vṛddhairvipralabdhatvādbālānāmiti cenna- vṛddhānāmapi pravṛtteḥ /
na ca vipralambhakāḥ svātmānamapi vipralabhante /
te 'pi vṛddhatarairityevamanādiriti cet- na tarhi vipralipsuḥ kaścidatra, yataḥ pratāraṇaśaṅkā syāt /
idaṃ prathama eva kaścidanuṣṭhāyāpi dhūrtaḥ parān anuṣṭhāpayatīti cet- kimasau sarvalokottara eva; yaḥ sarvasvadakṣiṇayā sarvabandhuparityāgena sarvasukhavimukho brahmacaryeṇa tapasā śraddhayā vā kevalaparavañcana(29)kutūhalī yāvajjīvamātmānamavasādayati /
kathaṃ cainamekaṃ prekṣā (30)pūrvakāriṇo 'pyanuvidadhyuḥ? kena vā cinhenāyamīdṛśastvayā lokottaraprajñena pratāraka iti nirṇītaḥ? na hyetāvato duḥkharāśeḥ pratāraṇasukhaṃ garīyaḥ /
(31)yataḥ pākhaṇḍābhimateṣvapyevaṃ dṛśyata iti cenna- hetudarśanādarśanābhyāṃ viśeṣāt /
anādau caivambhūte 'nuṣṭhāne pratāyamāne prakārāntaramāśrityāpi bahuvittavyayāyāsopadeśamātreṇa pratāraṇā syāt; (32)natvanuṣṭhānāgocareṇa karmaṇā /
anyathā pramāṇavirodhamantareṇa pākhaṇḍitvaprasiddhirapi na syāt /
[ku.1.129] astu dānādhyayanādireva vicitro heturjagadvaicitryasyeti cenna- kṣaṇikatvāt /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Let giving, study, and the like alone be the various causes of the diversity of the world — no, because [things are] momentary.
Because what is required [as the cause] exists at a later time,
An action long destroyed is sufficient for [producing] a result, not without a special potency of <s>karma</s> (action).
The enjoyment of those who are undifferentiated [in their actions] is not [explained] even by the material elements that have been modified. || 9 ||

For if only the succession of transformations of earlier and earlier elements were the sole basis of later and later [effects], then no one seeking the other world would engage in <s>iṣṭāpūrta</s> (Vedic sacrifices and charitable works). For no one who acts deliberately would engage in what is fruitless or has only suffering as its result — much less the whole world. [Objection:] If [it is said that one acts] for the sake of gain, honor, and fame — then what is the basis of gain itself and the rest? For this activity is not in itself the cause of those. And the one from whom something is to be gained, or the one who will honor him — for what purpose [does he act]? For the sake of fame and for the sake of affection. People are attracted to one who gives and one who honors. 'For prosperity arises from the affection of people.' If [this is objected to] — no, because the arrangement of giving and so forth for that purpose is [found] only among ministers of statecraft and pleasure. [Objection:] If [it is said that] the Vedic scholars and ascetics are merely the words of charlatans — no, because [Vedic rites] are of no use with respect to the visible prosperity of those [charlatans]. [Objection:] If [it is said that] one acts thus for the sake of happiness — no, because then even the <s>nāstikas</s> (materialists) would also do the same, just as with enjoyment. [Objection:] If [it is said that] even though fruitless, it is done because it is established through worldly convention, just as <s>sandhyopāsana</s> (twilight worship) is done because it is established through Vedic convention — this is the opinion of the teacher [Kumārila], not the opinion of our teacher [Udayana]. Therefore this is not appropriate to state in this context. [Objection:] If [it is said that] the young are deceived by the elders — no, because the elders also engage [in these practices]. And deceivers do not deceive even themselves. [Objection:] If [it is said that] they too [were deceived] by still older ones, and thus it is beginningless — then there is no deceiver here, from whom the suspicion of fraud would arise. [Objection:] If [it is said that] at the very beginning, someone, having performed [the rites] himself, being a charlatan, makes others perform them — is he then superior to the entire world, who through the offering of all his possessions, through abandonment of all relatives, renouncing all pleasures, through <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), austerity, and faith, solely out of curiosity for deceiving others, afflicts himself for his entire life? And how would those who act deliberately follow this one person? And by what sign have you, with your extraordinary wisdom, determined that this one is a deceiver? For the pleasure of deception is not greater than such an immense heap of suffering. [Objection:] If [it is said that] the same is seen among heretics also — no, because there is a difference based on seeing and not seeing the reason. And if a practice of this kind, being beginningless, were being perpetuated, then even by resorting to another method, deception would occur merely by the instruction involving great expenditure of wealth and effort — but not by an action that is beyond the scope of actual practice. Otherwise, even without contradiction by a means of valid knowledge, the reputation of being a heretic would not be possible.

children.text:
tasmādastyatiśayaḥ kaścit /
īdṛśānyevaitāni svahetubalā'yātāni, yena niyatabhogasādhanānīti cet- tadidamamīṣāmatīndriyaṃ rūpaṃ sahakāribhedo vā? na tāvat aindriyakasyātīndriyaṃ rūpam, vyāghātāt /
dvitīye tvapūrvasiddhiḥ /
[ku.1.130] siddhyatu bhūtadharma eva gurutvādivadatīndriyaḥ /
avaśyaṃ tvayāpyetadaṅgīkaraṇīyam /
kathamanyathā mantrādibhiḥ pritibandhaḥ /
tathā hi- karatalānalasaṃyogāt yādṛśādevadāho dṛṣṭaḥ, tādṛśādeva mantrādipratibandhe sati dāho na jāyate; asati tu jāyate /
tatra na dṛṣṭavaiguṇyamupalabhāmahe /
nāpi dṛṣṭasādguṇye 'dṛṣṭavaiguṇyaṃ sambhāvanīyam; tasyaitāvanmātrārthatvāt /
anyathā, karmaṇyapi vibhāgaḥ kadācinna jāyeta /
na ca pratibandhakābhāvaviśiṣṭā sāmagrī kāraṇam; abhāvasyākāraṇatvāt /
tuccho hyasau /
pratibandhakottambhakaprayogakāle ca tena vināpi kāryotpatteḥ /
prākpradhvaṃsādivikalpena cāniyatahetukatvāpātāt /
akiñcitkarasya pratibandhakatvāyogāt; kiñcitkaratve cātīndriyaśakteḥ svīkārāt /

children.translated_text: And even when, in the application of <s>mantras</s> and the like, the mutual absence [of factors] obtains, the effect does not arise.

children.text: ato 'tīndrīyaṃ kiñciddāhānuguṇamanugrāhakamagnerunnīyate, yasyāpakurvatāṃ pratibandhakatvamupapadyate; yasminnavikale kāryaṃ jāyate (34)yasyaikajātīyatvādaniyatahetukatvaṃ nirasyata iti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, some supersensible [factor] favorable to burning is inferred as an auxiliary of fire, whose obstructing is accomplished by obstructors, in the absence of which the effect arises, and whose belonging to a single class removes the [charge of] indeterminate causation.
Here it is said: An entity as it actually is, like an effect, is considered to be a cause.
Obstruction is an incomplete aggregate; the cause of that [obstruction] is the obstructor. || 10 ||

Therefore there exists some special potency. [Objection:] If [it is said that] these very things, having arrived by the force of their own causes, are the fixed means of enjoyment — then is this a supersensible nature of these [things], or a difference in auxiliary causes? The first [option] is not [possible], because a supersensible nature of what is sensible is contradictory. But in the second [option], the establishment of <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit) is accomplished. [Response:] Let a supersensible property of an element, like gravity, be established. You too must necessarily accept this. For how else would there be obstruction by <s>mantras</s> (sacred formulas) and the like? For consider: from the contact of fire with the palm, just such a burn as is observed [normally] — when there is obstruction by <s>mantras</s> and the like, a burn does not arise; but when [the obstruction] is absent, it does arise. In that case, we do not perceive any deficiency in the visible [cause]. Nor should a deficiency in the unseen be supposed when there is an excellence in the seen, because [the unseen] has only that much scope. Otherwise, division in action would sometimes not arise. And the aggregate qualified by the absence of an obstructor is not the cause, because absence cannot be a cause — for it is insubstantial. And at the time of applying an obstructor or a counteracting agent, the effect arises even without it [i.e., the absence]. And through the option of prior-destruction and the like, there would be the consequence of an indeterminate cause. Because what accomplishes nothing cannot be an obstructor; and if it accomplishes something, then a supersensible power is accepted.

children.text:
n.a hyabhāvasyākāraṇatve pramāṇamasti /
na hi vidhirūpeṇāsau tuccha iti svarūpeṇāpi tathā; niṣedharūpābhāve vidherapi(reva) tucchatvaprasaṅgāt /
kāraṇatvasya bhāvatvena vyāptatvāttannivṛttau tadapi nivartata iti
 cenna- parivartaprasaṅgāt /
anvayavyatirekānuvidhānasya ca kāraṇatvaniścayahetorbhāvavadabhāve 'pi tulyatvāt /
abhāvasyāvarjanīyatayāsannidhiḥ na tu hetutveneti cet- tulyam /
pratiyoginamutsārayatastasyānyaprayuktaḥsannidhiriti cet- tulyam /
bhāvasyābhāvotsāraṇaṃ svarūpameveti cet- abhāvasyāpi bhāvotsāraṇaṃ svarūpānnātiricyate /
tasmāt yathā "bhāvasyaiva bhāvo janaka" iti niyamo 'nupapannaḥ, tathā "bhāva eva janaka" ityapi /
ko hyanayorviśeṣaḥ /
[ku.1.132] pratibandhakottambhakaprayogakāle tu vyabhicārastadā syāt; yadi yādṛśe sati kāryānudayaḥ, tādṛśa eva sati utpādaḥ syāt /
na tvevam; tadāpi pratipakṣasyābhāvāt /
asatpratipakṣo hi (35)pratibandhakābhimato mantraḥ pratipakṣaḥ /
sa ca tādṛśo nāstyeva /
yastvasti, nāsau pratipakṣaḥ /
tathāpi viśeṣye satyeva viśeṣaṇamātrābhāvastatra; sa cottambhakamantra evetyanyaiva sāmagrīti cet- na, viśiṣṭasyāpyabhāvāt /
na hi daṇḍini sati adaṇḍānāmanyeṣāṃ nābhāvaḥ, kintu daṇḍābhāvasyaiva kevalasyeti yuktam /
yathā hi kevaladaṇḍasadbhāve, ubhayasadbhāve, dvayābhāve vā kevalapuruṣābhāvaḥ sarvatrāviśiṣṭaḥ, tathā kevalottambhakasadbhāve, pratibandhakottambhakasadbhāve, dvayābhāve vā kevapratibandhakābhāvo 'viśiṣṭa ityavadhāryatām /
athaivambhūtasāmagrītrayameva kiṃ neṣyate? kāryasya tadvyabhicārāt; jātibhedakalpanāyāṃ ca pramāṇābhāvāt; yathoktenaivopapatteḥ /
bhāve vā kāmamasāvastu; kā no hāniḥ /
[ku.1.133] prākpradhvaṃsavikalpo 'pi nāniyatahetukatvāpādakaḥ, yasmin sati kāryaṃ na jāyate, tasminnasatyeva jāyata iti, atra saṃsargābhāvasyaiva prayojakatvāt /
yastu saṃsargābhāvatādātmyaniṣedhayorviśeṣamanākalayannitaretarābhāvena pratyavatiṣṭhate, sa pratibodhanīyaḥ /
tathāpyabhāveṣu jāterabhāvāt kathaṃ trayāṇāmupagrahaḥ syāt; anupagṛhītānāṃ ca kathaṃ kāraṇatvāvadhāraṇamiti cet- mā bhūjjātiḥ /
na hi tadupagṛgītānāmeva vyavahārāṅgatvam /
sarvatropādhimadvyavahāravilopaprasaṅgāt /
[ku.1.134] ete(ane)na pratibandhake satyapi tajjātīyānyasyābhāvasambhavāt kāryotpādaprasaṅgaḥ, anutpāde vā tato 'pyadhikaṃ kiñcidapekṣaṇīyamastīti nirastam /
yathā hi "tajjātīye sati kāryaṃ jāyate, arthāt asati na jāyate" iti sthite tadbhāve 'pi tajjātīyāntarābhāvānna bhavitavyaṃ kāryeṇeti (36)na tathaitadapi; anukūlavat pratikūle 'pi sati tajjātīyāntarābhāvānāmakiñcitkaratvāditi /
[ku.1.135] yattu "akiñcitkarasye'ti- tadapyasat /
sāmagrīvaikalyaṃ pratibandhyapadārtho mukhyaḥ /
sa cātra mantrādireva /
na tvasau pratibandhakaḥ /
tataḥ kiṃ tasyākiñcitkaratvena? tatprayoktārastu pratibandhāraḥ, te ca kiñcitkarā eveti kimasamañjasam /
ye tu vyutpādayanti; "kāryānutpāda eva pratibandha" iti- taiḥ (37)"pratibandhamakurvanta eva pratibandhakāḥ" ityuktaṃ bhavati /
tathā hi- kāryasyānutpādaḥ prāgabhāvo vā syāt, tasya kālāntaraprāptirvā /
na pūrvaḥ, tasyānutpādyatvāt /
na dvitīyaḥ, kālasya svarūpato 'bhedāt /
tadupādhestu mantramantareṇāpi svakāraṇādhīnatvāt /
prāgabhāvāvacchedakakālopādhistadapekṣa iti cenna- mantrātpūrvamapi tasya bhāvāt /
tasmāt sāmagrītatkāryayoḥ paurvāparyaniyamāttadabhāvayorapi pūrvāparabhāva upacaryate; vastutastu tulyakālatvameveti nāyaṃ panthāḥ /
[ku.1.136] na cedevaṃ śaktisvīkāre 'pi kaḥ pratīkāraḥ ? tathā hi pratibandhakena śaktirvā vināśyate, taddharmo vā, dharmāntaro vā janyate, na janyate vā kimapīti pakṣāḥ /
tatrākiñcitkarasya pratibandhakatvānupapatteḥ viparītadharmāntarajanane, tadabhāve satyeva kāryamityabhāvasya kāraṇatvasvīkāraḥ, prāgabhāvādivikalpāvakāśaśca /
tadvināśe taddharmavināśe vā punaruttambhakena tajjanane 'niyatahetukatvam; pūrvaṃ svarūpotpādakāt idānīmuttambhakādutpatteḥ /
na ca samānaśaktikatayā tulyajātīyatvānnaivamiti sāmpratam; vijātīyeṣu samānaśaktiniṣedhāt /
na ca pratibandhakaśaktimevottambhako viruṇaddhi, na tu bhāvaśaktimutpādayatīti sāmpratam; tadanutpādaprasaṅgāt /
kālaviśeṣāttadutpāde tadevāniyatahetukatvamiti /
[ku.1.137] syādetat- mā bhūtsahajaśaktiḥ; ādheyaśaktistu syāt /
dṛśyate hi prokṣaṇādinā vrīhyāderabhisaṃskāraḥ /
kathamanyathā kālāntare tādṛśānāmeva kāryaviśeṣopayogaḥ /
na ca mantrādīneva sahakāriṇaḥ prāpya te kāryakāriṇa iti sāmpratam- teṣu ciradhvasteṣvapi kāryotpādāt /
nāpi pradhvaṃsasahāyāste tathā; evaṃ hi yāgādipradhvaṃsā eva svargādīnutpādayantu; kṛtamapūrvakalpanayā /
teṣāmanantatvādanantaphalapravāhaḥ prasajyata iti cet- apūrvepi kalpite tāvāneva
 phalapravāha iti kutaḥ ? apūrvasvābhāvyāditi cet- tulyamihāpi /
tāvatāpi tatpradhvaṃso na vinaśyatīti viśeṣaḥ /
[ki.1.138] syādetat-"upalakṣaṇaṃ prokṣaṇādayaḥ; na tu viśeṣaṇam /
tathā cāvidyamānairapi tairupalakṣitā vrīhyādayastatra tatropayokṣyante, yathā guruṇā ṭīkā; kuruṇā kṣetram- iti cet- tadasat /
na hi svarūpavyāpārayorabhāve 'pyupalakṣaṇasya kāraṇatvaṃ kaścidicchati; atiprasaṅgāt /
vyavahāramātraṃ tu tajjñānasādhyam, na tu tatsādhyam /
tajjñānamapi svakāraṇādhīnam /
na tu tena niranvayadhvastena janyate /
(astu tāvat) astu vā tatrāpyatiśayakalpanā; kinnaśchinnam ? yadvā yāgāderapyupalakṣaṇatvamastu /
tadupalakṣitaḥ kālo yajvā vā svargādi sādhayiṣyati kṛtamapūrveṇa /
[ku.1.139] na ca devadattasya svaguṇākṛṣṭāḥ śarīrādayo bhogāya, tadbhogasādhanatvāt sragādivaditya(numānā)nvayivalādapūrvasiddhernāviśeṣa iti sāmpratam; icchāprayatnajñānairyathāyogaṃ siddhasādhanāt /
na ca tadrahitānāmapi bhoga iti yuktimat, yena tato 'pyadhikaṃ siddhyet /
nāpisvaguṇotpāditā iti sādhyārthaḥ, manasānaikāntikatvāt /
nāpi kāryatve satīti viśeṣaṇāyo hetuḥ; tathāpyupalakṣaṇaireva siddhasādhanāt /
asatāṃ teṣāṃ kathamutpādakatvamiti cet- tadetadabhimantraṇādiṣvapi tulyam /
[ku.1.140] tasmādbhāvabhūtamatiśayaṃ janayanta eva prokṣaṇādayaḥ kālāntarabhāvine phalāya kalpante /

children.translated_text: because they are employed for that purpose on the strength of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), just like sacrifice, agriculture, and medicine.

children.text: anyathā kṛṣyādayo durghaṭāḥ prasajyeran; bījādīnāmāparamāṇvantabhaṅgāt teṣu cāvāntarajāterabhāvānniyatajātīyakāryārambhānupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: Otherwise, agriculture and the like would be rendered impossible; because the seeds and other things undergo destruction down to the ultimate atoms, and since there is no intervening universal (<s>jāti</s>) among them, the origination of effects of a determinate class would be inexplicable.

Here it is stated— [ku.1.141] The <s>saṃskāra</s> (purificatory rite) is accepted as pertaining to the person alone, through sprinkling (<s>prokṣaṇa</s>), besprinkling (<s>abhyukṣaṇa</s>), and the like;
The <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities) of the ultimate atoms are their inherent qualities, such as those produced by heat (<s>pākaja</s>) and the like. //11//

Nor is there any <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) for the non-causality of <s>abhāva</s> (absence). For it is not the case that absence is insignificant in its positive form, and therefore also so in its own nature; since if absence in its negative form were insignificant, even positive existence would be open to the same charge of insignificance. Since <s>kāraṇatva</s> (causality) is pervaded by <s>bhāvatva</s> (positive existence), when the latter ceases the former also ceases—if one objects thus, we say no—because that would lead to a reversal of the argument. And since the conformity to co-presence and co-absence, which is the ground for ascertaining causality, applies equally to absence as to positive entities. If it be said that the presence of absence is due to its inevitability and not as a cause—the same applies equally. If it be said that the presence of absence is brought about by something else while it removes its counterpositive—the same applies equally. If it be said that the removal of absence is the very nature of a positive entity—then equally, the removal of positive entities does not differ from the very nature of absence. Therefore, just as the restriction that 'only a positive entity produces a positive entity' is untenable, so also is 'only a positive entity is a producer.' What indeed is the difference between these two? [ku.1.132] At the time of employing an obstruction-remover (<s>uttambhaka</s>), there would be deviation; if in the presence of a certain condition the effect does not arise, then in the presence of that very same condition it should arise. But it is not so; because even then the counteragent is absent. For the <s>mantra</s> (incantation) that is regarded as the obstruction is a counteragent having an existing counteragent. And such a one does not exist at all. That which does exist is not a counteragent. Even so, when the qualificand is present, there is merely the absence of the qualifier in that case; and the removal-mantra (<s>uttambhaka</s>) is just that—so it is a different aggregate of causes—if one argues thus, we say no, because even the qualified entity is absent. For it is not correct that when a man with a stick is present, there is no absence of other things without sticks, but only the absence of the stick alone. For just as the absence of the man alone is uniform whether there is the stick alone present, or both present, or both absent, so also the absence of the obstruction alone is uniform whether the remover alone is present, or both the obstruction and the remover are present, or both are absent—let this be carefully considered. Then why not accept just these three types of causal aggregates? Because the effect deviates from them; because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) for postulating a difference of universals; and because the matter is explained by what has already been stated. Or let it be a positive entity if you wish; what harm is there to us? [ku.1.133] The alternative of prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>) also does not establish that effects have indeterminate causes, for in the case where the effect does not arise when something is present and arises only when it is absent, the efficacy belongs to <s>saṃsargābhāva</s> (relational absence) alone. One who, failing to discern the distinction between relational absence and denial of identity, takes recourse to mutual absence (<s>itaretarābhāva</s>), needs to be instructed. Even so, since there is no universal (<s>jāti</s>) among absences, how can the three types be subsumed? And how can causality be ascertained for things not so subsumed?—if one objects thus, let there be no universal. For it is not the case that only things subsumed under a universal function as factors in practical usage. For that would lead to the dissolution of all usage involving limiting conditions (<s>upādhi</s>). [ku.1.134] By this same reasoning, the objection is refuted that even when the obstruction is present, since the absence of another entity of the same class is possible, the effect should arise; or that if it does not arise, something more than that must be required. For just as when it is established that 'the effect arises when something of that class is present, and by implication does not arise when it is absent,' even when that entity is present, the effect should not occur due to the absence of another member of the same class—this argument does not apply here either; because just as with favorable conditions, so also with unfavorable conditions, the absence of other members of the same class is inconsequential. [ku.1.135] As for the objection 'that which is inconsequential...'—that too is unsound. The deficiency in the causal aggregate is the primary thing to be obstructed. And that here is the <s>mantra</s> (incantation) and the like. But that is not an obstruction. What then is gained by its being inconsequential? Those who employ it are the obstructors, and they are indeed consequential—so what is inconsistent? Those who explain that 'the non-production of the effect itself is the obstruction'—by them it is effectively said that 'the obstructors did not even create the obstruction.' For thus: the non-production of the effect would either be <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior non-existence), or the attainment of a different time for it. Not the first, because prior non-existence cannot itself be produced. Not the second, because time is not different in its own nature. And since the limiting condition of time depends on its own causes even without the <s>mantra</s> (incantation). If it be said that the temporal limiting condition of prior non-existence depends on that—we say no, because that condition exists even before the <s>mantra</s>. Therefore, from the fixed sequence of the causal aggregate and its effect, a prior-posterior relation is figuratively attributed to their absences as well; but in reality there is only simultaneity—so this path is not viable. [ku.1.136] And if this is so, what remedy is there even if <s>śakti</s> (potency) is accepted? For either the obstruction destroys the potency, or destroys its property, or produces a different property, or produces nothing at all—these are the alternatives. Among these, since what is inconsequential cannot be an obstruction, if a contrary property is produced, then the effect occurs only when that is absent—thus one must accept the causality of absence, and there is scope for the alternatives of prior non-existence and the like. If the potency or its property is destroyed, then when the remover (<s>uttambhaka</s>) regenerates it, there is indeterminate causation; for previously the effect arose from what originally produced the nature, but now it arises from the remover. Nor is it correct to say that since they are of the same class due to having the same potency, there is no such problem; because the same potency is denied among things of different classes. Nor is it correct to say that the remover only blocks the potency of the obstruction and does not produce the potency of the positive entity; because that would lead to the non-production of the effect. If the effect arises due to a particular time, that itself constitutes indeterminate causation. [ku.1.137] It may be argued: let there be no innate potency; but let there be an imparted potency (<s>ādheyaśakti</s>). For we observe the consecration (<s>abhisaṃskāra</s>) of rice and the like through sprinkling (<s>prokṣaṇa</s>) and similar rites. How else could the same kind of things be useful for specific effects at a later time? Nor is it correct to say that they become effective only upon reaching the auxiliary causes such as <s>mantras</s> (incantations)—because the effect arises even when those have long since perished. Nor are they effective with the help of the destruction of those; for in that case, let the destructions of sacrifices and the like themselves produce heaven and so forth—rendering the postulation of <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit) unnecessary. If it be objected that because those destructions are infinite, an infinite stream of results would follow—the same applies even if <s>apūrva</s> is postulated: from where does the stream of results come? If it be said, from the very nature of <s>apūrva</s>—the same applies here as well. The distinction is that that destruction does not itself perish even by that much. [ku.1.138] It may be argued: 'Sprinkling and the like are merely indicatory marks (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), not qualifying attributes. And thus, even when they no longer exist, the rice and other things indicated by them will be employed in the respective rituals, just as a commentary by a teacher, or a field by a cultivator'—but this is incorrect. For no one accepts that an indicatory mark has causal efficacy when both its own form and its operation are absent; because that would lead to overextension. Mere practical usage, however, is accomplished by the knowledge of it, not by the thing itself. And that knowledge too depends on its own causes. It is not produced by something that has been completely destroyed without remainder. Or even if one postulates a special quality (<s>atiśaya</s>) there too, what is thereby settled? Alternatively, let sacrifice and the like also be mere indicatory marks. The time or the sacrificer indicated by them will accomplish heaven and the rest—rendering <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit) unnecessary. [ku.1.139] Nor is it correct to say that <s>Devadatta's</s> body and the like, attracted by his own qualities, serve for his enjoyment, and since they are means to that enjoyment like garlands and so forth, <s>apūrva</s> is established by inference without any difference—because the matter is accomplished as appropriate through <s>icchā</s> (desire), <s>prayatna</s> (effort), and <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge). Nor is it reasonable that even those devoid of these enjoy—so that something more than those could be established from that. Nor is 'produced by one's own qualities' the point to be proved, because <s>manas</s> (mind) renders it inconclusive. Nor is the reason qualified by 'being an effect'—because even then the matter is accomplished by indicatory marks alone. If it be asked how those things that are non-existent can have productive power—this same objection applies equally to consecration by <s>abhimantraṇa</s> (ritual incantation) and the like. [ku.1.140] Therefore, sprinkling (<s>prokṣaṇa</s>) and the like are suited for producing a result at a later time only by generating a real positive quality (<s>atiśaya</s>),

yathā hi devatāviśeṣoddeśena hutāśane havirāhutayaḥ samantrāḥ prayuktāḥ puruṣamabhisaṃskurvate, na vanhiṃ, nāpi devatāḥ; tathā vrīhyādyuddeśena prayujyamānaḥ prokṣaṇādiḥ puruṣameva saṃskurute, na tam /
tathā ca kārīrījanitasaṃskārādhārapuruṣasaṃyogājjalamucāṃ sañcaraṇajalakṣaraṇarūpā kriyā, tathā vrīhyādīnāṃ tattaduttarakriyāviśeṣāḥ /

yathācābhicārasaṃskāro yaṃ dehamuddiśya prayuktastadapekṣa eva tatsambaddhasyaiva duḥkhamupajanayati nānyasya; na vā tadanapekṣaḥ /

(39)tathā ca lākṣārasāvasekādayo (40)vyākhyātāḥ /

yathā hi kalamabījaṃ yavādeḥ, narabījaṃ vānarādeḥ, gokṣīraṃ mahiṣādeḥ jātyā vyāvartate; tathā tatparamāṇavo 'pi mūlabhūtāḥ pākajaireva vyāvartante /

[ku.1.146] tasmātpākajaviśeṣaiḥ saṃsthānaviśeṣaiśca viśiṣṭāḥ paramāṇavaḥ kāryaviśeṣamārabhante /
te ca tejo 'nilatoyasaṃsargaviśeṣaiḥ; te ca kriyayā; sā ca nodanābhighātagurutvavegadravatvādṛṣṭavadātmasaṃyogebhyo yathāyathamiti na kiñcidanupapannam /
nimittabhedāśca

tadyathā- hārītamāṃsaṃ haridrājalāvasiktaṃ (46)haridrāgnipluṣṭam upayogāt sadyo vyāpādayati /
"daśarātroṣitaṃ kāṃsye ghṛtaṃ cāpi viṣāyate" /
tāmrāpātre paryuṣitaṃ kṣīramapi tiktāyata ityādi /

[ku.1.147] yatra tarhi toye tejasi vāyau vā na pākajo viśeṣaḥ, tatra kathamudbhavānudbhavadravatvakaṭhinatvādayo viśeṣāḥ? kathaṃ vā (ca) pārthive pratimādau pratiṣṭhādinā saṃskṛte 'pi viśeṣābhāvāt pūjanādinā dharmo vyatikrame tvadharmaḥ apratiṣṭhite tu na kiñcit /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But where there is no cooking-produced difference in water, fire, or wind, how then [do we explain] the differences such as emergence and non-emergence, fluidity and hardness? And how is it that in an earthen image and the like, even when consecrated by installation and other rites, there is <s>dharma</s> (merit) through worship and the like, <s>adharma</s> (demerit) through transgression, but nothing [results] when it is not consecrated — despite the absence of any [physical] difference?

children.text: na ca tatra yajamānadharmeṇānyasya sāhāyakamācaraṇīyam; anyadharmasyānyaṃ pratyanupayogāt upayoge vā sādhāraṇyaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: Nor should one person be helped by the <s>dharma</s> (merit) of the sacrificer, for another's <s>dharma</s> is of no use to another; and if it were useful, the undesirable consequence of [merit] being common [to all] would follow.
Here it is said: Emergence, non-emergence, and the like [arise] from the conjunction of different determining conditions;
Or from the proximity of the deity, or from recognition. || 12 ||

For just as oblations of <s>havis</s> (clarified butter) offered into the fire with <s>mantras</s>, with reference to a particular deity, produce a transformation in the sacrificer, not in the fire, nor in the deities; so too the <s>prokṣaṇa</s> (sprinkling) and other rites performed with reference to rice and the like produce a transformation in the sacrificer alone, not in the rice itself. And thus, from the conjunction of the person — who is the substratum of the transformation produced by the <s>Kārīrī</s> (rain-producing sacrifice) — [with the clouds], there arises the activity in the form of the movement of rain-clouds and the falling of water, and likewise the various subsequent ritual actions with respect to the rice and the like. And just as in one case, from the deficiency of the agent, the object, or the instrument, there is no result, so too in the other case — because the Vedic character [of both cases] is equal. [Objection:] Then, just as with the <s>barhis</s> (sacrificial grass), rice and the like should have no further use. Or if they do have use, something else of the same class should also be employed, since there is no distinction. No [this does not follow]. For the ritual transformations are diverse. Some are useful for the effect only as auxiliaries of the designated object being acted upon. What can be done about this? For the Vedic injunction is insuperable. And just as the transformation produced by a <s>abhicāra</s> (sorcery) rite, performed with reference to a particular body, depends on that [body] alone and produces suffering only in the one connected to it, not in another — and is not independent of it — so too the transformations of consecration and the like are not in the least unuseful. [Objection:] How then is the rice and the like the object of transformation? — Through the very connection of the <s>prokṣaṇa</s> (sprinkling) and similar [rites] with [their] result. [Objection:] But whatever is done with reference to whatever produces some effect therein, just as the <s>putreṣṭi</s> (sacrifice for a son) and the <s>pitṛyajña</s> (sacrifice to ancestors) [produce effects in their respective objects]. And so, consecration and similar rites, being performed with reference to the rice and the like, [produce effects therein] — this is an inference. No, [we reply] — because it is inconclusive, due to the offering of <s>havis</s> and the like [being a counterexample]. For they do not produce anything in the fire and the like that corresponds to the future result. Or is it not observed that the operations of the senses, marks, and words, performed with reference to a cognizable object, produce something in the cognizer alone, not in the cognizable object? [Objection:] The same would follow for agriculture and medicine — no, because when the matter is explained by the differences of transformation produced by cooking, which are observable, there is no evidence for postulating something unobserved. And thus the applications of lac-extract, irrigation, and the like are explained [by observable means]. For this very reason, even when the particular seed undergoes destruction down to its ultimate atoms, and even when the atoms lack sub-universal distinctions, atoms that are differentiated by prior cooking-produced particularities alone initiate that particular effect. For just as <s>kalama</s> (a type of rice) seed is distinguished by its universal from barley and the like, and a human seed from a monkey and the like, and cow's milk from buffalo's and the like — so too their fundamental atoms are distinguished precisely by cooking-produced [qualities]. For it is impossible that cow's milk be fragrant, sweet, and cool, while its atoms be the contrary. Therefore the atoms are precisely of such a cooking-produced nature; and the initial special potency, or the final special potency, such as a sprout, is [produced] by atoms of precisely such a nature — so what need is there for postulating [additional] powers? Even at the beginning of a cosmic cycle, it is just so. At present, what is equipped with seeds and the like is brought about by us and others. But at that time, the distinguishing feature is that things that were separate come together through <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) alone. And it cannot be objected that the same should happen now as well, because if the actions of agriculture and the like were discontinued, the enjoyments produced by them would also be discontinued — and from the fear of disorder, it is inferred that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merits) serve as means of enjoyment precisely through the arrangement of visible actions.

children.text:
[ku.1.148] upanāyakādṛṣṭaviśeṣasahāyā hi paramāṇavo dravyaviśeṣamārabhante /
teṣāṃ viśeṣādudbhūtā(48)nudbhūtabhedāḥ prādurbhavanti /
tathā svabhāvadravā apyāpo nimittabhedapratibaddhadravatvāḥ kaṭhinaṃ karakādyārabhante ityādi svayamūhanīyam /
pratimādayastu tena tena vidhinā sannidhāpitarudropendramahendrādyabhimānidevatābhedāstatra tatrārādhanīyatāmāsādayanti; daṣṭamūrcchitaṃ rājaśarīramiva viṣāpanayanavidhinā'pāditacaitanyam /
sannidhānaṃ ca tatra teṣāmahaṅkāramamakārau, citrādāviva svasādṛśyadarśino rājña iti no darśanam /
anyeṣāṃ tu pūrvapūrvapūjitapratyabhijñānaviṣayasya pratiṣṭhitapratyabhijñānaviṣayasya ca tathātvamavaseyam /

children.translated_text: By this, [the efficacy of] consecrated water, leaves, and the like is also explained.

children.text: [ku.1.149] ghaṭādiṣu kā vārtā ? kuśalaiveti cenna- na hi sāmagrīdṛṣṭaṃ vighaṭayati; nāpyadṛṣṭam; jñāpakatvāt /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] What need is there of discussion regarding pots and the like? Skill alone [suffices]. No, [we reply] — for [skill] does not disrupt what is observed in the aggregate [of causes]; nor does <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) [disrupt it], since it is merely an indicator.

children.text: nāpyadṛṣṭamutpādayati; dharmajanane sarvadā vijayaprasaṅgāt; viparyaye sarvadā bhaṅgaprasaṅgāt- atrocyate-[ku.1.150] jayetaranimittasya vṛttilābhāya kevalam /
children.translated_text: Nor does <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) produce [something new]; for if it generated <s>dharma</s> (merit), there would always be the consequence of victory; and in the opposite case, there would always be the consequence of defeat. Here it is said:
The rules of examination are held [to exist] solely for the sake of obtaining the operation of the cause of victory or its opposite, after examining what is present. || 13 ||

For atoms, assisted by specific <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merits) brought by the performer, initiate specific substances. From the differences among those [atoms], the distinctions of emerged and non-emerged [forms] manifest. Similarly, even waters that are naturally fluid, when their fluidity is restricted by different determining conditions, initiate something hard like hail and the like — this should be worked out by oneself. As for images and the like, through various ritual procedures, [they become] the objects of deities such as <s>Rudra</s>, <s>Upendra</s>, <s>Mahendra</s>, and others who identify with them, and thereby attain the status of being worthy of worship in their respective [forms] — like the body of a king who has been bitten [by a snake] and rendered unconscious, which is restored to consciousness through the procedure of removing poison. And their presence there [is marked by] the sense of 'I' and 'mine,' just as a king recognizes his own likeness in a portrait — this is our view. But for others, the status of [the image as] being of that nature should be understood as the object of recognition of what was previously worshipped and previously consecrated.

yadyapi "dharmādyabhimānidevatāsannidhiratrāpi kriyate; tāśca karmavibhavānurūpaṃ liṅgamabhivyañjayantī'tyasmākaṃ siddhāntaḥ- tathāpi paravipratipatteranyathocyate /

na hi no darśane śaktipadārtha eva nāsti /
ko 'sau tarhi? kāraṇatvam /
