children.translated_text: Because the power of creating [a body] without [a prior] body and the supernatural powers (<s>vibhūtis</s>) like <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness) must necessarily be conceded [to some being].

children.text: astveka eveti cet- na tarhīśvaramantareṇānyatra samāśvāsa iti /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Let there be just one [such being]. — Then there is no confidence in anyone other than the Lord.
[Ku.2.288] He who, by the power of <s>māyā</s>, creates and dissolves [the universe] — [each] creation wondrous, unprecedented, extraordinary —
who plays with the world as if performing magic, producing garland after garland,

" (<s>Gītā</s> 4.7.8) thus. [Ku.2.278] What, moreover, is this acceptance by the multitude? It is the grasping, retaining, understanding, and practice [of a teaching] by those devoid of perception of [valid] reasons. For that would not occur here without a cause. [Ku.2.279] Nor is laziness and the like the cause, since [Vedic practice] is predominantly painful activity. Nor is it that, [having found] validity established elsewhere, one enters this [Vedic tradition] through lack of authority [in one's own tradition] and having no other recourse — because even those honored by other [traditions] do not enter here. Nor is it passion for food, drink, and the like — because [Vedic practice] is devoted to distinguishing and regulating these. Nor is it delusion from the force of habitual sophistry — because [Vedic] practice begins from childhood. Nor is it the association with possible deceptive heresies — because it operates through the succession of fathers and others. Nor is it the pursuit of mental tranquility through the conceit of yogic practice — because the beginner is all the more occupied with the ritualistic portion (<s>karmakāṇḍa</s>) alone. Nor is it for livelihood — because, by the reasoning stated above, there is no visible fruit. Nor is it trickery and fraud — because in the present case, that is impossible. [Ku.2.280] However, these reasons do apply to the acceptance of Buddhist and other [heterodox] traditions. For thus: greater ease of action there — [hence] the lazy; even the fallen gain entry — [hence] those with no other recourse; no restriction on food and the like — [hence] the passionate; acceptance at one's own will — [hence] habitual sophists; engagement without the succession of fathers — [hence] those associated with heresies; hearing [sayings] like 'knowing the difference between both, for whom is purity prescribed?' — [hence] those who conceit themselves as tranquil; the attainment of meals for seven hours and such — [hence] the unfit for livelihood; and stopping the sun, splitting stones, breaking branches, spirit possession, speaking of idols, alchemy — being deceived by such tricks, they accept [those traditions]. Thus it is conjectured. Therefore, those [heterodox traditions] are not accepted by the [genuine] multitude — this is the distinction. [Ku.2.281] It may be objected: If thus all activity is contradicted [at cosmic dissolution], nothing is produced, nothing destroyed — in a world like frozen space, whence arises creation again from what distinguishing factor? The <s>Sāṅkhyas</s>' [answer] 'from the transformation of <s>Prakṛti</s>' is attractive. The <s>Bhāskara</s> school's [answer] 'from the transformation of <s>Brahman</s>' is fitting. [The Buddhist answer] 'from the maturation of latent impressions' follows the <s>Saugata</s> doctrine. And [the answer] 'from a particular time' is untenable due to the absence of a distinguishing limiting adjunct. And [conditions that are] non-existent indicators cannot be distinguishers, since they are always of the same form. Nor [can it be] through knowledge, since being impermanent, it does not exist at that time; and if [knowledge is] permanent, there is no distinction either in terms of object or in terms of its own nature. — No — [Ku.2.282] Just as for living beings whose sleep is produced by the agitation and fatigue of the body, the continuity of the breath-stream continues, having as its sole purpose the gradual accomplishment of the completion of the life-span — so for the atoms that have acquired dispositions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) from the agitation of the great dissolution of the elements, the continuity of the series of actions, consisting of combinations called accumulation (<s>pracaya</s>), which is the exhalation of the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), continues with the sole purpose of marking time through gradations of slower and slowest [motion]. As to 'how long is this [period]?' — since there is no contradiction, it is accepted to be exactly as long as is well-known from scripture. Or the activities within another cosmic egg (<s>brahmāṇḍa</s>) serve as the limiting adjunct of time. In the time delimited by that, [there is] re-creation. Just as fruits are spread out on a gourd vine, so it is heard that thousands of cosmic eggs are strung upon the power of the Supreme Lord. [Ku.2.283] When such interruption [of creation] is possible, who is accepted by whom, such that validity would arise? And this matter is an indicator (<s>jñāpaka</s>), not a causal factor (<s>kāraka</s>). Since there is no causal factor, how could [the scripture], which is ceasing [at dissolution], establish an effect that is merely intended as an indicator? [Ku.2.284] It may be objected: There exist <s>Kapila</s> and others who have directly realized <s>dharma</s>, perfected through <s>karma-yoga</s>. They, seeing beings being roasted in the embers of <s>saṃsāra</s>, being supremely compassionate, will grace them with teaching of what is dear and beneficial; what need is there for a Supreme Lord who does not even know the count of insects? — No, because there is no confidence in anyone other than Him. For thus: even if we grant that the means of perceiving supersensible objects exists in human [teachers], that does not necessarily produce a genuine direct perception; whence would we have confidence? [Objection:] From agreement with other means of knowledge. — No, because [the teaching of] non-violence and the like as means to well-being lacks [such agreement]. [Objection:] But scripture exists [as authority]. — No, because that [scripture] too, having mere mental cultivation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) as its root, is a subject of non-confidence. [Objection:] One may proceed even on the basis of partial agreement. — No, because it is possible otherwise, like a dream narrative. Nor is there mental cultivation of what is not perceived. For thieves, snakes, and the like are cultivated [in the imagination] by the fearful only when [actually] perceived. [Ku.2.285] Nor is it perceived from any source that <s>karma</s> and <s>yoga</s> are means to well-being. Nor is the perception of their own nature useful anywhere, or achievable by mental cultivation. Nor is agreement-and-difference (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) possible here, since the fruit belongs to another body, and since the [fruit] is not experienced, there is an absence of that [fruit] when that [practice] is undertaken. Nor is it established simply from the continuity of both bodies in the form of agent and experiencer — because there is no such [continuity]. For no one perceives: 'I am experiencing the fruit of this previous action.' [Ku.2.286] Even mere conjecture that some may be so [i.e., experience fruits in other births] gives no confidence, since there is no means of knowledge for ascertainment. [Objection:] Confidence in <s>Kapila</s> and others comes from mutual agreement, like a teacher who fell asleep at midnight and awoke at dawn [continuing his teaching consistently]. — No, because there is no means of knowledge for continuity across births, as there is for continuity within a single birth. And even so, in the absence of continuity of particular qualifications such as Brahminhood with a particular qualified person, there would be no confidence of the form of practice. For there is no rule that from the Brahminhood of parents in a previous birth, there follows Brahminhood in the next — by which there would be establishment of the order of <s>varṇa</s> and other properties at the beginning of creation. Because no distinction of elements bound to particular unseen merit is perceived, as with the Lord. And because non-confidence in the perception of supersensible objects has been stated. [Ku.2.287] By this, the [claim of] establishing tradition through the arrangement of <s>varṇas</s> traveling between cosmic eggs is also rejected — because of the impossibility of the power of traveling [between cosmic eggs]. For even traveling to another continent is difficult. How then travel to another world? And how much more travel to another cosmic egg? [Objection:] From the attainment of powers like <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness) and the like, this too may be possible. — No, because here too there is no means of knowledge. Confidence is impossible from mere conjecture. [Objection:] The otherwise-inexplicable acceptance by the multitude is itself the means of knowledge here. — No, because when the matter is explained by a single postulation of this kind, there would be the fault of excess in further postulations.
to that god <s>Bhava</s>, whose glory of unobstructed, radiant meditation shines forth,
the sole ground of trust, the auspicious <s>Śiva</s> — bowing to Him,
may I be [His servant] even among the lowest.  [verse 4]
Thus ends the second chapter of the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s>.
<s>Śrī</s> (Auspiciousness).
Third chapter of the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s>.

children.text:
nanvetadapi katham,
tatra bādhaka(154)sadbhāvāt /
tathā hi- yadi syāt, upalabhyeta /
ayogyatvāt sannapi nopalabhyata iti cet- evaṃ tarhi śaśaśṛṅgamapyayogyatvānnopalabhyata iti syāt /
naitadevam, śṛṅgasya yogyatayaiva vyāptatvāditi cet- (155)cetanasyāpi yogyopādhimattayaiva vyāptatvāt tadbādhe so 'pi bādhita eveti tulyam /

children.translated_text: It is inferred even through the non-perception of the pervading [entity], its own object, and the like — [that it] does not exist.
For who would do anything without a purpose?
[Ku.3.302] [We] reply: Whence [comes] the perception of fitness in what is unfit? Whence, all the more, [comes] the obstruction?
Where is the unfit [hare's] horn sublated? Where is an inference without a basis?  [verse 5 of chapter 3]

[Objection:] But how is this [i.e., how can God be established]? Because there exists a sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka</s>) [against God's existence]. For thus: if [God] existed, He would be perceived. [Objection from the theist:] Even though existing, He is not perceived because of unfitness [of the perceiver]. — Then even a hare's horn, being unfit [for perception], might [be said to] exist but not be perceived. [Response:] That is not so, because the horn is pervaded by fitness itself [i.e., horns by nature are perceptible, and hare's horns don't exist]. — [Counter:] Similarly, a conscious being too is pervaded by having a fit limiting adjunct, so when that [adjunct] is sublated, that [perception of God] is also sublated. This is equal [in force].

children.text:
[ku.3.303] svātmaiva tāvat yogyānupalabdhyā pratiṣiddhuṃ na śakyate; kutastvayogyaḥ parātmā(paramātmā)? tathāhi- suṣuptyavasthāyāmātmānamanupalabhamānaḥ, nāstītyavadhārayet /
kasyāparādhenapunaḥ yogyo 'pyātmā tadānīṃ nopalabhyate? sāmagrīvaiguṇyāt /
jñānādikṣaṇikaguṇopadhāne hyātmā gṛhyata iti asya svabhāvaḥ /
jñānameva kuto na jāyata iti cintyate paścādvā kathamutpatsyata iti cet- manaso 'nindriyapratyāsannatayājananāt; tatpratyāsattau ca paścājjananāt /
[ku.3.304] manovaibhavavādināmidamasaṃmatam /
tathā hi /
mano vibhu sarvadā sparśarahitadravyatvāt, (157)(sarvadā) viśeṣaguṇaśūnyadravyatvāt nityatve satyanārambhakadravyatvāt jñānāsamavāyikāraṇasaṃyogādhāratvādityāde(158)riti cet-[ku.3.305] na sarveṣāmāpātataḥ svarūpāsiddhatvāt /
tathā hi- yadi rū(yadā hi rū)pādyupalabdhīnāṃ kriyātvena karaṇatayā mano 'numitiḥ, na tadā dravyatvasiddhiḥ; adravyasyāpi karaṇatvāt /
athāsāmeva sākṣātkāritayendriyatvena tadanumātavyam, tathāpi vyāpakasya nirupādhernendriyatvamityupādhirvaktavyaḥ /
tatra- yadi(tadyadi) karṇaśaṣkulīvat nipataśarīrāvayavasyopādhitvam, tadā tāvanmātre vṛttilābhaḥ taddoṣe ca vṛttinirodhaḥ śrotravat prasajyeta /
tataḥ śarīramātramupādhirabhidheyaḥ (ravaseyaḥ) /
tathā ca tadavacchedena vṛttilābhe, "śirasi me vedanā, pāde me sukha'mityādyavyāpyavṛttitvapratītivirodhaḥ; asamavāyikāraṇānurodhena vibhukāryāṇāṃ prādeśikatvaniyamāt /
śarīratadavayavādiparamāṇuparyantopādhikalpanāyāṃ kalpanāgauravaprasaṅgaḥ, (159)niyamānupapattiśceti- tato 'nyadevaikaṃ sūkṣmamupādhitvenātīndriyaṃ kalpanīyam /
tathā ca tasyaivendriyatve svābhāvike 'dhikakalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvāt dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādhaḥ /
[ku.3.306] atha jñānakrameṇendriyasahakāritayā tadanumānam; tataḥ sutarāṃ prāguktadoṣaḥ /
yadi ca manaso vaibhave 'pyadṛṣṭavaśāt krama upapādyeta, tadā manaso 'siddherāśrayāsiddhireva vaibhavahetūnāmiti /
[ku.3.307] atha yatrādṛṣṭasya dṛṣṭakāraṇopahāreṇopayogaḥ, tatra tatpūrṇatāyāṃ kāryamutpadyata eva anyathā antyatantusaṃyogebhyo 'pi kadācit, paṭo na jāyota; jāto 'pi vā kadācinnirguṇaḥ syāt; balavattā kulālena dṛḍhadaṇḍanunnamapi cakraṃ na bhrāmyeta /
yatra tu dṛṣṭānupahāreṇādṛṣṭavyāpāraḥ, tatra tadvaiguṇyāt kāryānudayaḥ; yathā paramāṇukarmaṇaḥ /
tadihāpi yadi viṣayendriyātmanāṃ samavadhānameva jñānahetuḥ, tadā tatsadbhāve sadaiva kāryaṃ syāt /
na hyetadatiriktamapyadṛṣṭasyopaharaṇīyamasti /
na ca sadaiva jñānodayaḥ /
tato 'tiriktamapekṣitavyam /
tacca yadyapisarvāṇyevendriyāṇi vyapnoti, tathāpi karaṇadharmatvena kriyākramaḥ saṅgacchate /
akalpite tu tasminnāyaṃ nyāyaḥ; pratipatturakaraṇatvāt; cakṣurādīnāmanekatvāt iti cet-[ku.3.308] nanvevamapi yugapadjñānāni mā bhūvan yugapadjñānaṃ tu kena vāryate /
bhavatyeva samūhālambanamekaṃ jñānamiti cenna- ekendriyagrahyeṣviva nānendriyagrāhyeṣvapi prasaṅgāt /
(160)teṣvapi bhavatyeveti cenna- vyāsaṅgakāle jñānakrameṇa vivādaviṣaye kramānumānāt /
[ku.3.309] bubhutsāviśeṣeṇa vyāsaṅge kriyākrama iti cet- mai(nai)vam nahyeṣa bubhutsāyā mahimā, yat abubhutsite viṣaye jñānasāmagryāṃ satyāmapi na jñānam /
api tu na tatra saṃskārātiśayādhāyakaḥ pratyayaḥ syāt /
yadi tvabubhutsite viṣaye sāmagrīmeva sā nirundhyāt, ghaṭāyonmīlitaṃ cakṣuḥ paṭaṃ naiva darśayet /
tasmād bubhutsāpīndriyāntarādākṛṣya
 bubhutsitārthagrāhiṇīndriye mano niveśayantī yugapadjñānānutpattāvupayujyate; na tu svarūpataḥ /
[ku.3.310] vibhuno 'pi manaso vyāpārakramāt krama iti cenna- tasya saṃyogātiriktasya karmarūpatve vaibhavavirodhāt, guṇarūpatve nityasya kramānupapatteḥ; anityasya ca nityaikaguṇasyāvibhudravyasaṃyogāsamavāyikāraṇakatvena tadantareṇānupapatteḥ /
tadapi kalpayiṣyata iti cet- tadeva tarhi manaḥsthāne niveśyatāṃ lāghavāya /
tasmādaṇveva mana iti /
[ku.3.311] tathā ca tasminnanindriyapratyāsanne nirupadhānatvādātmanaḥ suṣuptyavasthāyāmanupalambhaḥ /
etadeva manasaḥ śīlamiti kuto niścir(ṇī)tamiti cet- anvayavyatirekābhyām /
na kevalaṃ tasya, kiṃ tu sarveṣāmevendriyāṇām /
na hi viśeṣaguṇamanapekṣya cakṣurādyapidravye pravartate /
(161)svapnāvasthāyāṃ kathaṃ jñānamiti cet- tattatsaṃskārodbodhe viṣayasmaraṇena svapnavibhramāṇāmutpatteḥ /
udbodha eva kathamiti cet- mandataratamādinyāyena bāhyānāmeva śabdādīnāmupalambhāt /
antataḥ śarīrasyaivoṣmādeḥ pratipatteḥ /
yadā ca manastvacamapi parihṛtya purītati vartate, tadā suṣuptiḥ /
[ku.3.312] syādetat- parātmā tu kathaṃ parasyāyogyaḥ /
na hi sākṣātkārijñānaviṣayatāmevāyaṃ na prāpnoti; svayamapyadarśanaprasaṅgāt /
nāpi grahīturevāyamaparādhaḥ, tasyāpi hi jñānasamavāyikāraṇataiva (162) tadyogatā /
nāpi karaṇasya; sādhāraṇatvāt /
na hyāsaṃsāramekameva mana ekamevātmānaṃ gṛhṇātītyatra niyāmakamasti /
svabhāva iti cet- tarhi (163) muktau niḥsvabhāvattvaprasaṅgaḥ; tadekārthatāyā apāyāditi- na; bhojakādṛṣṭopagrahasya niyāmakatvāt /
yaddhi mano yaccharīraṃ yānīndriyāṇi yasyādṛṣṭenākṛṣṭāni, tāni tasyaiveti niyamaḥ /
taduktaṃ prāk- "pratyātmaniyamāt bhukte'riti /
etena parabuddhyādayo vyākhyātāḥ /
[ku.3.313] tadevaṃ yogyānupalabdhiḥ parātmādau nāsti /
taditarā tu na bādhiketi tavāpi saṃmatam /
ataḥ kimadhikṛtya pratibandiḥ /
na hi śaśaśṛṅgamayogyānupalabdhyā kaścinniṣedhati /
na ca prakṛte yogyānupalabdhiṃ kaścinmanyate /
athāyamāśayaḥ- ayogyaśaśaśṛṅgādāvanupalabdhirna bādhikā syāt- iti /
tataḥ kim /
tatsiddhyediti cet- evamastu, yadi pramāṇamasti /
paśutvādikamiti cet- parasādhane pratibandistarhi; na tadbādhane /
tatraiva bhaviṣyatīti cet- tat kiṃ tatra pratibandireva dūṣaṇam, atha kathañcittulyanyāyatayā yogyā eva parātmabuddhyādayaḥ te ca bādhitā evetyapahṛtaviṣayatvam? na prathamaḥ avyāpteḥ /
na hi paśutvādeḥ śaśaśṛṅgasādhakatvena kāryatvādeḥ kartṛmattvasādhakatvaṃ pyāptam, yena tasminnasati tat pratiṣiddhyeta /
na dvitīyaḥ; mitho 'nupalabhyamānatvasya vādiprativādisvīkārāt /
tathāpi paśutvādau ko doṣa iti cet- na jīnīmastāvat; tadvicārāvasare cintayiṣyāmaḥ /
[ku.3.314] syādetat- yatpramāṇagamyaṃ hi yat, tadabhāva eva tasyābhāvamāvedayati /
yathā rūpādiprati patterabhāvaścakṣurāderabhāvam /
kāyavāgvyāpāraikapramāṇakaśya parātmā; tadabhāva eva tasyābhāve pramāṇamaṅkurādiṣu- tanna- tadekapramāṇakatvāsiddheḥ /
anyathā suṣupto 'pi na syāt /
śvāsasantāno 'pi tatra pramāṇamiti cenna- niruddhapavano 'pi na syāt /
kāyasaṃsthānaviśeṣo 'pi tatra pramāṇamiti cenna- viṣamūrcchito 'pi na syāt /
śarīroṣmāpi tatra pramāṇamiti cenna- jalāvasiktaviṣamū(siktamū)rcchito 'pi na syāt /
tasmāt yadyat kāryamupalabhyate, tattadanuguṇaścetanastatra tatra siddhyati /
na ca kāryamātrasya kvacidvyāvṛttiriti /
na ca, tvadabhyupagatenaiva pramāṇena bhavitavyam, nānyeneti niyamo 'sti /
[ku.3.315] na ca prameyasya pramāṇena vyāptiḥ /
sā hi kārtsnyena vā syāt, ekadeśena vā syāt /
na prathamaḥ; pratyakṣādyanyatamā(ma) sadbhāve 'pi tatprameyāvasthiteḥ /
na dvitīyaḥ; puruṣaniyamena sarvapramāṇavyāvṛttāvapi prameyāvasthiteḥ /
aniyamena asiddheḥ; na hi sarvasya sarvadā sarvathātra pramāṇaṃ nāstīti niścayaḥ śakya iti /
[ku.3.316] kathaṃ tarhi cakṣurāderabhāvo niścayaḥ? vyāpakānulabdheḥ /
(164)caramasāmagrīniveśino hi kāryameva vyāpakam; tannivṛttau tathābhūtānyāpi nivṛttiḥ /
(165)yogyatāmātrasya kadācit kāryam, (166)tannivṛttau tathābhūtasyāpi nivṛttiḥ /
anyathā tatrāpi (167)sandehaḥ /
[ku.3.317] prakṛte 'pi vyāpakānupalabdhyā tatpratiṣedho 'stu-na, āśrayāsiddhatvāt /

children.translated_text: For neither <s>Īśvara</s> (God) nor His knowledge has been established anywhere.

[Objection:] If [it is said that God is] apprehended as an appearance (<s>ābhāsa</s>) — no, because of the impossibility of that [appearance] being a substratum, and because of the impossibility of it being something to be negated.
For the qualification of being a qualificand is positive, like having the absence of what is to be excluded;
The counter-positiveness of a real entity is the nature of being free from absence. || 2 ||

[ku.3.303] One's own self (<s>svātman</s>) cannot be negated by <s>yogyānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of what is fit to be apprehended); how then can the Supreme Self (<s>paramātman</s>), which is unfit [for ordinary perception], be so negated? For in the state of deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>), one who does not perceive the self would have to conclude "it does not exist." For what fault is the self, though fit [to be apprehended], not perceived then? Due to deficiency of the causal aggregate (<s>sāmagrī</s>). For the self is grasped only when momentary qualities such as cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) are present in it — that is its nature. "Why then does cognition itself not arise, or how will it arise later?" — Because the mind (<s>manas</s>), not being in proximity to the sense-organs, does not produce [cognition]; and when it comes into proximity, it produces [cognition] subsequently.
[ku.3.304] This is not accepted by the proponents of the all-pervasiveness of mind (<s>manovaibhavavādin</s>). For they argue: "The mind is all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>), being a substance devoid of touch at all times, being a substance devoid of particular qualities at all times, being an eternal non-originating substance, being the substratum of contact which is the non-inherent cause of cognition" — and so forth.
[ku.3.305] No, because all [these arguments] fail in their very form at first sight. For if the inference of the mind is from the fact that perceptions of color etc. are activities (<s>kriyā</s>) requiring an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), then substantiality (<s>dravyatva</s>) is not established, since even a non-substance can be an instrument. If those very [cognitions] are to be inferred as sense-organs (<s>indriya</s>) because they directly present [objects], even then all-pervasiveness, being without a limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>), does not entail sense-organ-ness — so an <s>upādhi</s> must be stated. If, like the ear-cavity, a bodily part in physical contact is the <s>upādhi</s>, then functioning would be limited to that extent, and obstruction of functioning upon its defect would follow, as with the ear. Therefore the entire body alone must be stated as the <s>upādhi</s>. And with functioning limited by it, there would be contradiction with the perception of non-comprehensive functioning such as "in my head there is pain, in my foot there is pleasure" — since products of an all-pervading [cause] are restricted to a particular location according to the non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>). If we postulate <s>upādhis</s> all the way down to the atoms of the body and its parts — there follows the fault of excessive postulation and the impossibility of accounting for regularity. Therefore something else, single, subtle, and imperceptible, must be postulated as the <s>upādhi</s>. And if that itself is naturally the sense-organ, then since there is no evidence for any additional postulation, there would be contradiction with the evidence establishing the subject [of inference].
[ku.3.306] If the inference is that mind cooperates with the sense-organs in the sequence of cognitions — then all the more the previously stated faults apply. And if even with the all-pervasiveness of mind, sequence is to be explained by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit), then since the mind itself is unestablished, there is the fault of unestablished locus (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>) for the arguments proving all-pervasiveness.
[ku.3.307] Now, where <s>adṛṣṭa</s> has its use through the contribution of visible causes, there when those are complete the effect arises necessarily — otherwise even from the final conjunction of threads, a cloth would sometimes not arise; or even if arisen, it would sometimes be quality-less; or a wheel, even pressed down by a strong potter with a firm stick, would not rotate. But where <s>adṛṣṭa</s> operates without the contribution of visible [causes], there due to its deficiency the effect does not arise — as with the movement of atoms. Similarly here: if the conjunction of object, sense-organ, and self is itself the cause of cognition, then when those are present, the effect should always be. For there is nothing beyond these that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> need contribute. But cognition does not always arise. Therefore something additional must be postulated. And even though it pervades all sense-organs, still as a property of an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), sequential activity is coherent. But if it is not postulated, this reasoning does not work — because the perceiver (<s>ātman</s>) is not an instrument, and because the sense-organs like the eye are multiple.
[ku.3.308] But even so, let there not be simultaneous cognitions — but by what is a single simultaneous cognition prevented? "There is indeed a single cognition grasping an aggregate [of objects]." — No, because the same would follow for objects graspable by different senses, just as for objects graspable by a single sense. "It does in those cases too." — No, because during concentrated attention, from the sequence of cognitions, sequence is inferred in the disputed case.
[ku.3.309] "The sequence of activity during concentration is due to a particular desire to know (<s>bubhutsā</s>)." — Not so; for it is not the power of desire that when there is no desire to know a particular object, even when the aggregate of causes for cognition is present, cognition [of that object] does not arise. Rather, there would not be a mental impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) producing further cognition regarding it. If, however, desire would block the very aggregate [of causes] regarding undesired objects, then an eye opened toward a pot would not see a cloth at all. Therefore desire too, drawing the mind away from other senses and fixing it upon the sense grasping the desired object, is useful in preventing simultaneous cognitions — but not intrinsically [as a cause of sequence].
[ku.3.310] "Even of an all-pervading mind, sequence follows from the sequence of its activity." — No, because if its activity, distinct from conjunction, is in the form of motion (<s>karma</s>), it contradicts all-pervasiveness; if in the form of a quality (<s>guṇa</s>), sequence is impossible for what is eternal. And if impermanent, being a quality of an eternal [substance having] only one quality, it would require as its non-inherent cause the conjunction of a non-all-pervading substance — without which it cannot occur. "That too will be postulated." — Then let that very thing be placed in the position of the mind, for the sake of parsimony (<s>lāghava</s>). Therefore the mind is atomic (<s>aṇu</s>) only.
[ku.3.311] And so, when the [atomic mind] is not in proximity to any sense-organ, due to the absence of a substrate, the self is not perceived in the state of deep sleep. "How is it established that this is the nature of the mind?" — By positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). Not of this [mind] alone, but of all sense-organs. For even the eye does not operate regarding a substance without reference to a particular quality. "How then is there cognition in the dream state?" — Because dream-illusions arise from recollection of objects when the relevant impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) are activated. "How does the activation [occur]?" — By the principle of degrees (more-or-less), from the apprehension of external sounds etc. At the very least, from the perception of heat etc. of the body itself. And when the mind, having abandoned even the skin, dwells in the excretory channel — that is deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>).
[ku.3.312] One might say: But how is the Supreme Self (<s>paramātman</s>) unfit for apprehension by another? For it is not that it cannot attain the status of being an object of direct perception (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) — since even oneself would then not be perceived. Nor is this the fault of the perceiver, for his capacity for such perception lies only in being the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) of cognition. Nor [the fault] of the instrument, since that is common [to all]. For there is no evidence establishing that one mind throughout all of <s>saṃsāra</s> grasps one self only. "It is its nature." — Then in liberation (<s>mukti</s>), there would be the absurdity of the loss of that nature; since the one-to-one relationship would cease. — No; because the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) of the experiencer (<s>bhoktṛ</s>) is the regulator. Whichever mind, body, and sense-organs are attracted by the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> of a particular [self], those belong to that self only — that is the rule. As stated before: "Due to per-self regulation, the experiencer [experiences]." By this, cognitions belonging to other selves etc. are explained.
[ku.3.313] Thus, <s>yogyānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of what is fit to be apprehended) does not apply to the Supreme Self etc. And non-<s>yogya</s> [non-apprehension of what is unfit] is not a refutation — you yourself agree. So on what grounds is there a counter-argument? No one negates a hare's horn by <s>yogyānupalabdhi</s>. And no one considers the present case to be <s>yogyānupalabdhi</s>. "But the intention is: non-apprehension regarding the unfit, like a hare's horn, should not constitute a refutation." — So what? "It would thereby be established [that God exists]." — Let it be so, if there is valid evidence (<s>pramāṇa</s>). "Like animality (<s>paśutva</s>) etc." — Then this is a counter-argument in establishing the positive; not in refuting [God's existence]. "It will be applicable there too." — Then is the counter-argument itself the refutation, or is it that somehow, by parity of reasoning, cognitions of the Supreme Self etc. are themselves fit, yet being refuted, the [argument] is rendered domain-less? Not the first, because of non-pervasion (<s>avyāpti</s>). For the capacity of animality etc. to prove a hare's horn does not entail the capacity of <s>kāryatva</s> (being-an-effect) to prove an agent — so that in its absence, the latter would be negated. Not the second; because mutual non-apprehension is accepted by both disputants. "What then is wrong with animality etc.?" — Let us not hurry; we will consider [this] when the occasion for its examination arises.
[ku.3.314] One might say: Whatever is knowable by a given means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), the absence of that very means serves as evidence for the absence [of that thing]. Just as the absence of color-perception [serves as evidence for] the absence of the eye etc. The Supreme Self is knowable only through bodily and verbal activities; the absence of those is the evidence for its absence in sprouts etc. — No, because it is not established that [bodily and verbal activities] are the only means [of knowing a self]. Otherwise, one in deep sleep would also not exist. "Breathing is also evidence." — Then one whose breath has stopped would also not exist. "A particular bodily configuration is also evidence." — Then one unconscious from poison would also not exist. "Bodily warmth is also evidence." — Then one doused with water while unconscious from poison would also not exist. Therefore whatever effect is observed, a conscious agent corresponding to it is established there. And there is no case where effects are entirely absent. Nor is there a rule that the evidence must be only of the kind you accept, and not any other.
[ku.3.315] And there is no pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) between a knowable entity and the means of knowledge [proving it]. For that pervasion would either be complete or partial. Not the first; because even when one particular means like perception is absent, the knowable entity may still exist [proven by another means]. Not the second; because even if all means of knowledge are absent for a particular person, the knowable entity still exists. [If it is] without restriction — unestablished; for no one can be certain that there is never any means at all, for anyone, at any time, in any manner.
[ku.3.316] How then is the absence of the eye etc. established? By non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>). For the effect is indeed the pervader of the aggregate of conditions operating at the final stage; in the absence of [the effect], the cause possessing those conditions is also absent. [Sometimes] mere fitness [for production can serve]: when a particular effect [sometimes results], in the absence of [the effect] the cause possessing that fitness is also negated. Otherwise there too there would be doubt.
[ku.3.317] "In the present case too, let the negation be through non-apprehension of the pervader." — No, because of the unestablished locus (<s>āśrayāsiddha</s>).

children.text:
na caitadābhāsapratipannasyāstīti kutastasya niṣedhādhikaraṇatvaṃ niṣedhyatā ce(ve)ti /
[ku.3.318] kathaṃ tarhi śaśaśṛṅgasya niṣedhaḥ? na kathañcit /
sa hyabhāvapratyaya eva /

children.translated_text: And this [absence] does not have an unreal counter-positive;
It is not an absence of ultimate reality, nor is there a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that has an unreal object.
Moreover: A defective aggregate of apprehension is the fitness [for negation] of a hare's horn and the like.
When that [aggregate] is present, there is no non-apprehension; and it does not exist when there is non-apprehension. || 3 ||

And since what is apprehended as an appearance does not have [real] existence, how then can it be the locus of negation or what is to be negated? [Ku 3.318] How then is the negation of a hare's horn [possible]? In no way [is it a real negation]. For that is merely an apprehension of absence.

children.text:
ken.a ca śaśaśaṅgaṃ pratiṣiddhyate, sarvathānupalabdhasya yogyatvāsiddheḥ /
taditarasāmagrīsākalyaṃ hi tat /
nanūktamābhāsopalabdhaṃ hi tat /
ata evāśakyaniṣedhamityuktam /
anupalambhakāle ābhāsopalambhasāmagryāḥ abhāvāt; tatkāle cānupalambhābhāvāditi /
kastarhi śaśaśṛṅgaṃ nāstītyasyārthaḥ? śaśe 'dhikaraṇe viṣāṇābhāvo 'stīti /
[ku.3.319] syādetat- yadyapīśvaro nāvagataḥ; yadyapi ca nābhāsasiddhena pramāṇavyavahāraḥ śakyasampādanaḥ, tathāpi, ātmanaḥ siddhāḥ, teṣāṃ sārvajñyaṃ niṣiddhyate, kṣityādikartṛtvaṃ ceti /
tathā hi- maditare na sarvajñāḥ cenatvādahamiva /
na ca te kṣityādikartāraḥ puruṣatvādahamiva /

children.translated_text: And likewise from [the property of] being a real entity and the like.
But this too has already been refuted earlier.
For: [Ku 3.320] [If] <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is well-known, [the argument] establishes what is desired; [if He is] beyond the range [of knowledge], the reason is unestablished.
There is no other establishment through a general [property]; even when a universal is [employed], that [fault] remains the same. || 4 ||

And by what is a hare's horn negated, since the fitness [for apprehension] of what is in no way apprehended is unestablished? For that [fitness] is the completeness of the aggregate other than that [object]. But it has been said that it [the hare's horn] is apprehended as an appearance. For that very reason it has been said that it cannot be negated. Because at the time of non-apprehension, the aggregate of apprehension-as-appearance is absent; and at the time of that [appearance], non-apprehension is absent. What then is the meaning of 'the hare's horn does not exist'? It means: in the hare as locus, the absence of a horn exists. [Ku 3.319] It may be objected: Even if <s>Īśvara</s> (God) has not been comprehended, and even if valid epistemic practice cannot be established through what is established as a mere appearance, nevertheless, selves are established, and their omniscience is to be negated, as well as their creatorship of earth and the like. For: 'Others than myself are not omniscient, because they are conscious beings, like myself. Nor are they the creators of earth and the like, because they are persons, like myself.'

children.text:
pramāṇa(ṇena)pratītānāṃ cetanānāṃ pakṣīkaraṇe siddhasādhanam /
tato 'nyeṣā(169)masiddhau hetorāśrayāsiddhatvam /

ātmatvamātreṇa so 'pi siddha iti cet- ko 'syārthaḥ? kimātmatvenopalakṣitā saiva vastugatyā sarvajñaviśvakartṛvyaktiḥ, atha tadanyā, ātmamātraṃ ātmatvamātra(170)meva vā pakṣaḥ; sarvatra pūrvadoṣānativṛtteḥ (ttiḥ?) athāyamāśayaḥ- ātmatvaṃ na sarvajñasarvakartṛvyaktisamavetaṃ jātitvāt gotvavat- iti- tadasat- niṣedhyāsiddherniṣedhasyāśakyatvāt /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If [it is said that] 'He too is established merely by [the property of] being a self' — what does this mean? Is the very individual who is omniscient and creator of all, as designated by the property of selfhood, [the subject]? Or is it something other than that? Or is the subject merely self, or merely the property of selfhood? In every case, the previous faults are not overcome. But if this is the intention — 'selfhood does not inhere in an individual who is omniscient and creator of all, because it is a universal, like cowness' — that is wrong, because since what is to be negated is unestablished, the negation cannot be carried out.

children.text: tathā cāprasiddhaviśeṣaṇaḥ pakṣa ityāśrayāsiddhiriti sa eva doṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus the subject has an unestablished qualifier, so the fault of the locus being unestablished [remains] — that is the very same defect.

children.text: tvadupagatāgamalokaprasiddhasyaiveśvarasyāsarvajñatvamakartṛtvaṃ ca sādhyata iti cenna- āgamādeḥ pramāṇatve bādhanādaniṣedhanam /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If [it is said that] the non-omniscience and non-creatorship of <s>Īśvara</s>, who is well-known in the scriptures and the world as you yourself accept, is to be proved — no, because if the scripture and the like are valid means of knowledge, [His omniscience] cannot be negated due to contradiction [with those sources].
But if [scripture] is a mere appearance, then that very fault of the locus being unestablished would arise, being untenable. || 5 ||

In making conscious beings known through <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) into the subject [of the inference], it is a case of establishing what is already established. And if others [beyond those known] are unestablished, the reason has the fault of having an unestablished locus.

children.text:
nigadavyākhyātametat (172) /
[ku.3.321] cārvākastvāha- kiṃ (173)yogyatāviśeṣā(ṣaṇā)graheṇa /
yannopalabhyate, tannāsti /
viparītamasti /
na ceśvarādayastathā, tato na santītyetadeva jyāyaḥ /

children.translated_text: [Objection:] If [it is said that] thus inference and other [means of knowledge] would be destroyed — this is not unwelcome [to the materialist].

children.text: tathā ca lokavyavahāroccheda iti cenna- sambhāvanāmātreṇa tatsiddheḥ /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If [it is said that] thus worldly practical dealings would be cut off — no, because that [practical dealing] is established merely through possibility.

children.text: saṃvādena ca prāmāṇyābhimānāt- iti- atrocyate-[ku.3.322] dṛṣṭyadṛṣṭyoḥ kva sandeho bhāvābhāvaviniścayāt /
children.translated_text: And because [one has] confidence in validity through concordance — to this it is said: [Ku 3.322] Where is there doubt between what is seen and what is unseen, given the ascertainment of existence and non-existence?
When the reason is contradicted by non-perception, even perception becomes difficult to obtain. || 6 ||

This is explained in the commentary. [Ku 3.321] The <s>Cārvāka</s> (materialist) however says: What need of apprehending a distinction of fitness? Whatever is not apprehended does not exist. The opposite exists. And <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and the like are not so [apprehended]; therefore they do not exist — this alone is better.

children.text:
sambhāvanā hi sandeha eva /
tasmācca vyavahārastasmin sati syāt /
sa eva tu kutaḥ? darśanadaśāyāṃ bhāvaniścayāt; adarśanadaśāyāmabhāvāvadhāraṇāt /
tathā ca gṛhādbahirga(nnirga)taścārvāko varāko na nivartate; pratyuta putradāradhanādyabhāvāvadhāraṇāt sorastāḍaṃ śokavikalo (174)vikrośet /
smaraṇānubhavānnaivamiti cenna- pratiyogismaraṇa evābhāvaparicchedāt /
parāvṛtto 'pi kathaṃ punarāsādayiṣyati? sattvāditi cet- anupalambhakāle 'pi tarhi santīti na tāvanmātreṇābhāvāvadhāraṇam /
tadaivotpannā iti cenna- anupalambhena hetūnāṃ bādhāt /
abādhe vā sa eva doṣaḥ /
[ku.3.323] ata eva pratyakṣamapi na syāt; taddhetūnāṃ cakṣurādīnāmanupalambhabādhitatvāt /
upalabhyanta eva; golakādi(175)rūpatvātteṣāmiti cenna- tadupalabdheḥ pūrvaṃ teṣāmanupalambhāt /
na ca yaugapadyaniyamaḥ; kāryakāraṇabhāvāditi /
[ku.3.324] etena- na paramāṇavaḥ santi; anupalabdheḥ /
na te nityā niravayavā vā, pārthivatvāt ghaṭādivat /
na pāthasīyaparamāṇurūpādayo nityāḥ rūpāditvāt dṛśyamānarūpādivat /
na rūpatvapārthivatvādi nityākāryātīndriyasamavāyi jātitvāt śṛṅgatvavat /
nendriyāṇi santi, yogyānupalabdheḥ /
ayogyāni ca śaśaśṛṅgapratibandinirasanīyānīti (176)evaṃ svargāpūrvadevatānirākaraṇaṃ nāstikānāṃ nisanīyam /
mīmāṃsakaśca toṣayitavyo bhīṣayitavyaśceti /
[ku.3.325] yadyevamanupalambhenādṛśyapratiṣedho neṣyate, anupalabhyopādhipratiṣedho 'pi naiṣṭavyaḥ /
tathā ca kathaṃ tathābhūtārthasiddhirapi; anumānabījapratibandhāsiddheḥ /
tadabhāve śabdāderapyabhāvaḥ; prāmāṇyāsiddheḥ /
seyamubhayataḥ pāśā rajjuḥ (177) /
[ku.3.326] atra kaścidāha- mā bhūdupādhividhūnanam, catuḥpañcarūpasampattimātreṇaiva pratibandhanirvāhāt /
tasyāśya sapakṣāsapakṣadarśanādarśanamātrapramāṇakatvāt /
yatra tu tadbhaṅgaḥ, tatra pramāṇabhaṅgo 'pyāvaśyakaḥ /
na hyasti sambhavo darśanādarśanayoraviplave (178)heturūpaviplavaiti /
[ku.3.327] aprayojako 'pi tarhi hetuḥ syāditi cet- bhūyodarśanāviplave ko 'yamaprayojako nāma? na tāvat sādhyaṃ pratyakāryamakāraṇaṃ vā; sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumānasvīkārāt /
nāpi sāmagryāṃ kāraṇaikadeśaḥ; pūrvavadabhyupagamāt /
nāpi vyabhicārī; tadanupalambhāt /
vyabhicāropalambhe vā sa eva doṣaḥ /
na ca śaṅkitavyabhicāraḥ; nirbījaśaṅkāyāḥ sarvatra sulabhatvāt /
nāpi vyāpyāntarasahavṛttiḥ; ekatrāpi sādhye 'nekasādhanopagamāt /
nāpyalpaviṣayaḥ; dhūmādestathābhāve 'pi
 (thābhūtasyāpi) hetutvāt /
nanu dhūmo (mo 'pi) vahnimātre 'prayojaka eva, tannivṛttāvapi tadanivṛtteḥ /
ārdrendhanavatvaṃ vahniviśeṣaṃ prati tu prayojakaḥ; tannivṛttau tasyaiva nivṛtteriti- etadapyayuktam- sāmānyaprayojakatāyāṃ viśeṣasādhakatvāyogāt; tadasiddhau tasyāsiddhiniyamāt; siddhau vā sāmānyaviśeṣabhāvānupapatteḥ /
nāpi kḷptasāmarthye 'nyasmin kalpanīyasāmarthyāprayojakaḥ; nāśe kāryatvasāvayavatvayorapi hetubhāvāditi /
[ku.3.328] tadetadapeśalam- kathaṃ hi viśeṣābhāvāt kaścidvyabhicarati kaścicca neti śkayamavagantum /
tato nirṇāyakābhāve sati sāhityadarśanameva śaṅkābījamiti kvāsau nirbījā /
evaṃ sati atiprasaktirapi cārvākanandinī (179)nopālambhāya /
[ku.3.329] svabhāvādeva kaścit kiñcidvyabhicarati, kaścicca neti svabhāva eva viśeṣa iti cet- kena cihnena punarasau nirṇeya iti nipuṇena bhāvanīyam; bhūyodarśanasya śataśaḥ pravṛttasyāpi bhaṅgadarśanāt /
yatra bhaṅgo na dṛśyate (180)tat tatheti cet- āpātato na dṛśyate iti sarvatra kālakrameṇāpi na drakṣyata iti ko niyanteti /
[ku.3.330] tasmādupādhitadvirahāveva vyabhicārāvyabhicāranivandhanam /
tadavadhāraṇaṃ cāśakyamiti /
nanu yaḥ sarvaiḥ pramāṇaiḥ sarvadāsmadādibhiryadvattayā nopalabhyate, nāsau tadvān; yathā bakaḥ śyamikayā /
nopalabhyate ca vahnau dhūma upādhimattayā- iti śkyamiti cenna- asyāpyanumānatayā tadapekṣāyāmanavasthānāt /
(181)sarvādṛṣṭeśca sandehāt; svādṛṣṭervyabhicārātaḥ; sarvadetyasiddheḥ /
[ku.3.331] tādātmyatadutpattibhyāṃ niyama ityanye /
tatra tādātmyaṃ vipakṣe bādhakāt bhavati /
tadutpattiśca paurvāparyeṇa pratyakṣānupalambhābhyām /

(182)na hyevaṃ sati śaṅkāpiśācī avakāśamāsādayati; āśaṅkyamānakāraṇabhāvasyāpi piśācāderetallakṣaṇāvirodhenaiva tattvanirvāhāditi- (183) naivamapi; ubhayagāmino 'vyabhicāranibandhanasyaikasyāvivecanāt; pratyekaṃ cāvyāpakatvāt /
children.translated_text: For when such [criteria] are in place, the phantom of doubt does not find an opening — since even the causal status of what is suspected as a cause, such as a ghost and the like, is sustained without contradicting this very definition — [Reply:] Not even so, because the ground of non-deviation, which applies to both [tādātmya and tadutpatti], cannot be discriminated as belonging to one alone; and because each individually is non-pervasive.

children.text: kutaśca kāryātmānau kāraṇamātmānaṃ ca na vyabhicārata iti /
children.translated_text: And why would the effect-nature and the cause-nature not deviate from the self [as substrate]?

children.text: [ku.3.332] atrocyate- śaṅkā cedanumāstyeva na cecchaṅkā tatastarām /
children.translated_text: [Ku.3.332] Here it is said: If there is doubt, then inference certainly exists; if there is no doubt, then all the more so [inference stands].
Doubt has <s>vyāghāta</s> (self-contradiction) as its limit; <s>tarka</s> (reductio reasoning) is held to have doubt as its limit. || 7 ||

For <s>sambhāvanā</s> (supposition) is indeed nothing but doubt. And therefore, practical activity would occur only when that [doubt] exists. But whence arises that [doubt] itself? In the state of seeing, there is certainty of existence; in the state of not-seeing, there is ascertainment of absence. And thus the wretched <s>Cārvāka</s>, having gone out from the house, does not turn back; rather, having ascertained the absence of sons, wife, wealth, and so forth, he would cry out, grief-stricken, beating his chest. [Objection:] This is not so, because absence is determined from the experience of remembering [the counterpositive] — [Reply:] No, because absence is delimited precisely through the remembering of the <s>pratiyogin</s> (counterpositive) alone. [Objection:] Even having turned away, how will he find them again? Because they exist — [Reply:] If so, then even at the time of non-apprehension they exist, and therefore absence is not ascertained by that alone. [Objection:] They were produced at that very moment — [Reply:] No, because the causes are contradicted by non-apprehension. Or if there is no contradiction, then the same defect [applies]. [Ku.3.323] For this very reason, even <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) would not be possible, since its causes — the eye and other [sense organs] — are contradicted by non-apprehension. [Objection:] They are indeed apprehended, because they have the nature of eyeballs and such — [Reply:] No, because prior to their apprehension there is non-apprehension of them. Nor is there a rule of simultaneity, because of the cause-effect relation. [Ku.3.324] By this [same reasoning]: atoms do not exist, because of non-apprehension. They are neither eternal nor partless, because of being earthly, like a pot and so forth. The <s>rūpa</s> (color) and other qualities of water-atoms are not eternal, because of being color and the like, like perceived color and so forth. <s>Rūpatva</s> (colorness), <s>pārthivatva</s> (earthiness), and the like are not eternal, nor effects, nor supersensuous, nor inherent <s>jātis</s> (universals), because of being universals, like hornness. The sense organs do not exist, because of qualified non-apprehension. And if they are unfit [for apprehension], they should be dismissed as obstructions like a hare's horn — thus the refutation of heaven, <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit), and deities by the <s>nāstikas</s> (nihilists) must be countered. And the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> must be both satisfied and intimidated. [Ku.3.325] If it is thus that the negation of the invisible through non-apprehension is not accepted, then the negation of <s>upādhis</s> (limiting conditions) through non-apprehension should also not be accepted. And in that case, how can the establishment of such an object [be achieved] either, since the establishment of the ground of <s>pratibandha</s> (invariable concomitance), the seed of <s>anumāna</s> (inference), is not accomplished? In the absence of that, even <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) and other [means of knowledge] would be absent, since their <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity) is not established. This is a rope that binds from both sides. [Ku.3.326] Here someone says: let there be no elimination of <s>upādhis</s> (limiting conditions), since <s>pratibandha</s> (invariable concomitance) is accomplished merely by the fulfillment of four or five conditions. For its [validity] is established merely by observation and non-observation in <s>sapakṣa</s> (homologous instances) and <s>vipakṣa</s> (heterologous instances). But where that breaks down, the breakdown of the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is also inevitable. For there is no possibility that the inferential form could be disrupted without a disruption in the pattern of observation and non-observation. [Ku.3.327] [Objection:] Then the <s>hetu</s> (logical reason) might be non-productive — [Reply:] What is this so-called non-productive [reason] when there is no disruption of observation in the majority of cases? It is not that [the reason] is a non-effect or non-cause with respect to the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum), since <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa anumāna</s> (inference based on general observation) is accepted. Nor is it merely one part of the causal complex, since it is accepted as before. Nor is it <s>vyabhicārin</s> (deviating), since such [deviation] is not apprehended. And if deviation were apprehended, the same defect [would apply]. Nor is it of suspected deviation, since groundless suspicion is easily available everywhere. Nor is it one co-occurring with another <s>vyāpya</s> (pervaded entity), since even for a single <s>sādhya</s>, multiple <s>sādhanas</s> (means of proof) are admitted. Nor is it of limited scope, since even smoke and the like, even when not of that nature, serve as <s>hetus</s> (logical reasons). [Objection:] But smoke too is non-productive with respect to fire in general, since fire does not cease when smoke ceases. Rather, the presence of wet fuel is productive with respect to a specific kind of fire, since that [specific fire] ceases when that [wet fuel] ceases — [Reply:] This too is incorrect, because when there is productivity with respect to the general, there cannot be the proving of a particular; since the non-establishment of the latter necessarily follows from the non-establishment of the former; or if it is established, the relation of general and particular would be untenable. Nor is it non-productive in the sense that when the capacity of one [cause] is already established, the capacity of another need not be postulated — since even for destruction, both effectness and compositeness serve as reasons. [Ku.3.328] This is inelegant — for how can it be understood that, due to the absence of a specific [condition], some [reasons] deviate and some do not? Therefore, in the absence of a determining factor, the mere observation of co-occurrence is itself the seed of doubt — so where is that groundless [suspicion]? This being so, the over-extension too, a darling of the <s>Cārvākas</s>, is not to be blamed. [Ku.3.329] [Objection:] By nature itself some [reasons] deviate from something and some do not — nature itself is the distinguishing factor — [Reply:] By what mark then is that to be determined? This must be carefully considered, since the observation of co-occurrence, even when occurring hundreds of times, has been seen to break down. [Objection:] Where no breakdown is seen, that is so — [Reply:] That it is not seen at first glance [does not entail that] it will never be seen in the course of time anywhere — who is the restrictor [that guarantees this]? [Ku.3.330] Therefore, it is the <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) and its absence alone that are the ground of deviation and non-deviation. And the ascertainment of that is impossible [without further means], it is said. [Objection:] That which is not apprehended by all <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), at all times, by persons such as ourselves, as possessing a certain property — that does not possess it; just as a crane [does not possess] blackness. And fire is not apprehended as possessing an <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) with respect to smoke — thus it can be determined. [Reply:] No, because this itself being an <s>anumāna</s> (inference), it depends on that [very thing it tries to establish], leading to infinite regress. And because there is doubt regarding the non-observation by all; and because one's own non-observation is subject to deviation; and because 'by all' is unestablished. [Ku.3.331] Others say: the invariable rule [is established] through <s>tādātmya</s> (essential identity) and <s>tadutpatti</s> (causal origination). Of these, <s>tādātmya</s> (essential identity) is established through a <s>bādhaka</s> (contradicting cognition) in the <s>vipakṣa</s> (dissimilar instance). And <s>tadutpatti</s> (causal origination) [is established] through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anupalambha</s> (non-apprehension) applied in sequence.

children.text:
[ku.3.333] kālāntare kadācidvyabhicariṣyatīti kālaṃ bhāvinamākalayya śaṅkyeta /
tadākalanaṃ ca nānumānamavadhīrya kasyacit /
mūhūrtayāmāhorātrapakṣamāsartvayanasaṃvatsarādayo hi bhāvino bhavanmuhūrtādyanumeyā eva, anavagateṣu smaraṇasyāpyanāśaṅkanīyatvāt /

[ku.3.334] svīkṛtamanumānam /

tataḥ śaṅkaiva phalataḥ svarūpataśca nivartanīyā /
tatra phalamasyāḥ vipakṣasyāpi jijñāsā tarkādāhanya nivartate; tato 'numānapravṛttau śaṅkāsvarūpamapīti sarvaṃ sustham /
[ku.3.338] na caitadanāgamam, nyāyāṅgatayā tarkaṃ vyutpādayataḥ sūtrakārasyābhimatatvāt /

children.translated_text: Otherwise, that exposition would be purposeless.
[Ku.3.339] This then is the summary: that [reason] for which there is no favorable <s>tarka</s> (reductio reasoning) is non-productive.

children.text: sa ca dvividhaḥ śaṅkitopādhirniścatopādhiśca; yatredamucyate- "yāvaccāvyatirekitvaṃ śatāṃśenāpi śaṅkyate /
children.translated_text: And that [non-productive reason] is of two kinds: one with a suspected <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) and one with an ascertained <s>upādhi</s>; regarding which it is said: "As long as non-deviation is doubted even to the extent of a hundredth part,
Whence then does the reason have the force of reaching the counter-positive [of the thesis]?

[Ku.3.333] [Objection:] One might suspect, anticipating a future time, that at some other time [the reason] will deviate. [Reply:] But that anticipation of time is not [possible] for anyone who dismisses <s>anumāna</s> (inference). For future moments, watches, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, half-years, years, and so on are themselves to be inferred through present moments and the like, since even memory is not to be suspected when [those future times] are not cognized. Or if there is no anticipation [of future time], on what basis could deviation be suspected? And thus, all the more is inference to be accepted. The same is to be said regarding other places as well. [Ku.3.334] [Objection:] Inference is accepted. We ask as a friend: how is the doubt to be removed? [Reply:] No [need for further answer], because <s>tarka</s> (reductio reasoning) operates as long as there is doubt. [Ku.3.335] For that [tarka], being present, by bringing about an undesired consequence either in the category of <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) or in the category of deviation dependent on it, severs the desire [to maintain the doubt]. And the cognizer, whose desire to maintain the <s>vipakṣa</s> (contrary thesis) has been severed, rests upon the <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark) whose co-occurrence has been apprehended through repeated observation; and from a cognizer who has so committed, the action is brought to completion through the instrument [of inference] — so what is untenable? [Ku.3.336] [Objection:] But <s>tarka</s> (reductio reasoning) too operates depending on <s>avinābhāva</s> (invariable concomitance). Therefore there must be an infinite regress. [Reply:] No, because doubt has <s>vyāghāta</s> (self-contradiction) as its limit. For only that is doubted where, if it were doubted, defects such as the contradiction of one's own activity would not arise — such is the convention of the world. For it is not even possible to doubt that the relation of cause and effect will not obtain. If that were so, doubt itself would not be possible, just as [the thought] 'everything will be false' [would be self-defeating]. [Ku.3.337] [Objection:] Then let it be stated: what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) for the negation of a supersensuous <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition)? [Reply:] Indeed, no supersensuous <s>upādhi</s> established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> exists, for the absence of which a <s>pramāṇa</s> need be sought. It is merely suspected that there is some other ground for the co-occurrence. Therefore, the doubt itself is to be removed — both in its result and in its essential nature. As for its result, which is the desire to investigate the <s>vipakṣa</s> (contrary case), that is struck down by <s>tarka</s> (reductio reasoning); and thereupon, when inference operates, the essential nature of the doubt too [is removed] — thus everything is well. [Ku.3.338] And this is not without scriptural authority, since the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras) [i.e., <s>Gautama</s>] intended <s>tarka</s> as a limb of <s>nyāya</s> (logical method) when he expounded it.
[Ku 3.340] An <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition) in that context is: that which pervades the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) while not being pervaded by the <s>sādhana</s> (probans).

children.text: taddharmabhūtā hi vyāptirjapākusumaraktateva sphaṭike, sādhanābhimate cakāstītyupādhirasāvucyata iti /
children.translated_text: For <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion), being a property of that [probans], shines in what is believed to be the probans — like the redness of a <s>japā</s> (hibiscus) flower in a crystal — and that is called the <s>upādhi</s> (limiting condition).
Thus they say: 'Others, who depend on the pervasions advanced by the opponent,
Even when those [pervasions] are observed, do not [thereby] accept the ascertainment of the non-pervading part.'

[ku.3.341] tadanena vipakṣadaṇḍabhūtena tarkeṇa sanāthe bhūyodarśane, kāryaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ vā tato 'nyadvā, samavāyi vā saṃyogi vānyathā vā bhāvo vābhāvo vā, saviśeṣaṇaṃ vā nirviśeṣaṇaṃ vā liṅgamiti niḥśaṅkamavadhāraṇīyam; anyathā tadābhāsa iti rahasyam /

children.translated_text: But this is not so in the case of contradiction; because pervasion itself is first disrupted — that is the distinction.

children.text: [ku.3.346] yattvaprayojakaḥ sandigdhānaikāntika ityanaikāntike 'ntarbhāvyate- tadasat- vyāptyasiddhyā hi nimittena vyabhicāraḥ śaṅkanīyo 'nyathā vā /
children.translated_text: [Ku 3.346] As for [the claim] that the non-probative [reason] is included under the inconclusive as a 'doubtfully inconclusive' — that is wrong. For deviation should be suspected either by reason of the non-establishment of pervasion or otherwise.

children.text: prathame asiddhireva dūṣaṇam; upajīvyatvāt; nānaikāntikam; upajīvakatvāt /
children.translated_text: In the first case, non-establishment itself is the fault, because it is what is depended upon; not inconclusiveness, because it depends [on the former].
Otherwise, the suspicion itself is the fault; for when [pervasion] is ascertained, there is no room for that [suspicion].

(Mīmāṃsā-ślokavārttika 14.1-5). [Ku 3.341] Thus, when induction (<s>bhūyodarśana</s>) is supported by reasoning that serves as a staff [to strike] the counter-positive, the inferential mark should be ascertained without doubt — whether it is an effect, a cause, or something else; whether it is related by inherence, conjunction, or otherwise; whether it is a positive entity or an absence; whether it is qualified or unqualified. Otherwise, it is a semblance [of a valid mark] — this is the essential teaching. [Ku 3.342] This is also the basis of [the relations of] essential identity and origination. For if effect-and-self were to transcend the cause, and self [were to transcend] the self, then the reality of those two [relations] would be contradicted. For this very reason, even the <s>Saugatās</s> (Buddhists), who admit the last cause within the aggregate, also infer the effect [from it]. Therefore, the definition of invariable concomitance is indeed the sublation of the counter-positive. [Ku 3.343] For example: in the son of a friend who is free from the transformation of food consisting of greens and the like, no undesirable [result occurs]; therefore that [food] is not its pervader. But it is the pervader of dark complexion, because its being a cause is ascertained. And it is the cause of that; and [to say] that it transcends that and yet exists — this is contradictory. The same should be worked out in other cases. [Ku 3.344] But where does the non-probative [reason] fit in? Nowhere, say some. For just as [the fault of] establishing what is already established is not [a case of] the subject being contradicted — because there is no removal of the subject; nor is it the [fault of the] property not belonging to the thesis when there is already a settled conclusion — because of the undesirable consequence of the destruction of what has passed in time; nor is it inconclusive and the like — because there is no deviation and the like — so too is this [non-probative reason]. But the <s>sūtra</s> (aphorism) is merely an indicator — that is wrong, because the division [of fallacies] has the purpose of determining the exact count, neither less nor more. [Ku 3.345] Where then do both [the non-probative and another] fall? Under 'unestablished' alone. For the cognition of the thesis-property of what is pervaded is 'establishment.' Its absence is 'non-establishment.' And this [non-establishment], arising from the non-cognition of any one of pervasion, thesis-property, or essential nature, is respectively called 'otherwise-established,' 'locus-unestablished,' or 'nature-unestablished.' The middle one [locus-unestablished] is also of two kinds: through non-cognition of the locus or the essential nature, or through non-cognition of the thesis-hood of its qualifier.
Third <s>Stavaka</s>: Examination of the non-sublatable nature of <s>Īśvara</s> (God) through <s>upamāna</s> (analogy).

children.text: [ku.3.347] upamānaṃ tu bādhakamanāśaṅkanīyameva, viṣayānatirekāditi kecit tathāhi- na tāvadasya viṣayaḥ sādṛśyavyapadeśyaṃ padārthāntarameva sambhāvanīyam; parasparavirodhe hi na prakārāntarasthitiḥ /
children.translated_text: [Ku 3.347] As for <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), some say it need not be suspected as a sublating [means of knowledge], because it does not extend beyond its subject matter. For consider: its subject matter cannot be conceived as a separate category designated by similarity; for when there is mutual contradiction, there is no existence of another mode.
Nor is there unity of mutually contradictory [entities], because of the contradiction in mere statement. || 8 ||

children.translated_text: But in the present case, that [further subdivision] is absent.

Therefore, this very cognition of similarity residing in this aggregate, assisted by the recollection of that aggregate, producing such a cognition, is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) called <s>upamāna</s> (analogy).

children.text: [ku.3.351] etadapi nāsti- sādharmyamiva vaidharmyaṃ mānamevaṃ prasajyate /
children.translated_text: [Ku 3.351] But even this does not hold: Just as similarity, so dissimilarity too would be a [separate] means of knowledge — this undesirable consequence follows.

children.text: arthāpattirasau vyaktamiti cet prakṛtaṃ na kim //9 //
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If [it is said that] that is clearly <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) — then why not [say the same of] the matter at hand? || 9 ||

For no mode other than existence and non-existence can be conceived, because they have the form of mutual affirmation and negation. For 'it is not an existent' — by negation alone is the affirmation of non-existence [achieved]. Then, setting that aside, how can one, with sincerity, again negate by one's own words: 'it is not a non-existent'? Similarly, 'it is not a non-existent' — by negation itself is the affirmation of existence [achieved]. Then, setting that aside, how can one who is not insane again negate by one's own words: 'it is not an existent'? For this very reason, the unity of such [contradictory] things is also impossible to comprehend, because negation and affirmation cannot coexist in one [thing]. Therefore, existence and non-existence alone constitute reality. [Ku 3.348] Even in the case of existence, there are only two [possibilities]: with qualities or without qualities.
