syādetat- prakāśamāne khalvarthe tadupāditsādirupajāyate; na tu suṣuptyavasthāyāmaprakāśamāne 'pyarthe ityanubhavasiddham /
tata icchāyāḥ kāraṇaṃ vilakṣaṇameva kiñcit parikalpanīyam, yasmin sati susvāpalakṣaṇamaudasīnyamarthaviṣayamātmano nivartate iti cet- hantaivaṃ susvāpanivṛttimanubhavaniddhāṃ pratijānānena jñānamevāparokṣyamiṣyante /
acetayanneva hi suṣupta ityucyate; acaitanyanivṛttireva hi caitanyaṃ jñānamiti /
tathā ca kālātyayāpadiṣṭo hetuḥ /
[ku.4.519] etena (3) kṣaṇikatvāditi nistam /
apica kimidaṃ kṣaṇikatvaṃ nāma? yadyāśutaravināśitvam, tadānaikāntikam /
athaikakṣaṇāvasthāyitvam, tadasiddhaṃ pramāṇābhāvāt /
nanu sthāyi vijñānaṃ yādṛśamarthakṣaṇaṃ gṛhṇadutpadyate, dvitīye 'pi kṣaṇe kiṃ tādṛśameva gṛṇhāti, anyādṛśaṃ vā, na vā kamapīti /
na prathamaḥ, tasya kṣaṇasyātītatvāt; pratyakṣajñānasya ca vartamānābhavatvāt /
na cātītameva vartamānatayollikhati(219), bhrāntatvaprasaṅgāt /
na dvitīyaḥ, viramyavyāpārāyogāt /
prathamato 'pi tathābhyupagame 'nāgatāvekṣaṇaprasaṅgāt /
na tṛtīyaḥ, jñānatvahāneriti mahāvratīyāḥ /
tadasat /
jñānaṃ gṛṇhātītyasyaivār'thasyānabhyupagamāt /
api tu tadeva grahaṇamityabhyupagamaḥ /
tathā ca jñānaṃ prathame yamarthamālambya jātam, dvitīye 'pi kṣaṇe tadālambanameva tannaveti praśnārthaḥ /
tatra tadālambanameva taditi paramārthaḥ /
nacaivaṃ bhrāntatvam, viparītānavagāhanāt /
tathāpi jñeyanivṛttau kathaṃ jñānānuvṛttiḥ? tadanuvṛttau vā kathaṃ jñeyanivṛttiriti cet- kimasminnanupapannam? na hi jñānamarthaścetyekaṃ tattvamekāyuṣkaṃ veti /
[ku.4.520] satyapi vā kṣaṇikatve kathamapratyakṣam? itthaṃ yathocyate-na svaprakāśam, vastutvāditaravastuvat /
na ca jñānāntaragrāhyam, jñānayaugapadyaniṣedhena samānakālasya tasyābhāvāt /
grāhakakāle grāhyasyātītatvena vartamānābhatvānupapatteḥ /
grāhyakāle ca grāhakasyānāgatatvāt- iti cet- nanvevaṃ jñātatāpi na pratyakṣā syāt, kṣaṇikatvāt /
katham? ittham- na svaprakāśā /
vastutvāt, na janakagrāhyā, anāgatatvāt /
viramyavyāpārāyogācca /
na samasamayajñānagrāhyā, jñānajanakendriyasambandhānanubhavāt (221) /
na ca taduttarajñānagrāhyā, tadānīmatītatvāt- iti /
kṣaṇikatvameva tasyāḥ kuta iti cet- tvaduktayuktereva /
tathāhi- yaṃ kṣaṇamāśritya jātā tataḥ paramapi tamevāśrayante anyaṃ vā, na vā kamapīti /
tatra na prathamaḥ, tasya tadānīmasattvāt /
na dvitīyaḥ, apratisaṅkramāt /
ekakṣaṇāvagāhini ca jñāne tadanyakṣaṇāśrayajñātatāphalatvena bhrāntatvaprasaṅgāt, rajatāvagāhini purovartivṛtti(222)jñātatāphala iva /
na cānyamapi kṣaṇaṃ jñānamavagāhate, tadānīṃ tasyāsattvāt /
na tṛtīyaḥ, niḥsvabhāvatāprasaṅgāt /
na hyasau tadānīṃ tadīyānyadīyā veti /
[ku.4.521] atītenāpi tenaiva kṣaṇenopalakṣitānuvartate iti cet- evaṃ tarhi vartamānārthatā prakāśasya (223) na syāt /
anyathā jñānasyāpi tathānuvṛtteḥ ko doṣaḥ? nahi vartamānārthaprakāśasambandhamantareṇa jñānasyānyā vartamānāvabhāsatā nāma /
arthanirapekṣaprakāśanānuvṛttimātreṇa tathātve bhūtabhāviviṣayasyāpi jñānasya tathābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
[ku.4.522] atha mā bhūdayaṃ doṣa iti sthūla eva vartamānaḥ prakāśenāśrīyate ityabhyupagamaḥ, tadā tajjñānasyāpi sa eva viṣaya iti tasyāpi na kṣaṇikatvamiti /
[ku.4.523] nanu (4) jñānamaindriyakaṃ cet, viṣayasañcāro na syāt,sañjātasambandhatvāt /
na ca jijñāsāniyamānniyamaḥ, tasyāḥ saṃśayapūrvakatvāt, tasya ca dharmijñānapūrvakatvāt, dharmiṇaśca sannidhimātreṇa jñāne jijñāsāpekṣaṇe vā ubhayathāpyanavasthānāditi- tanna- jñātatāpakṣe 'pi tulyatvāt /
tasyā api hi jñeyatve tatparamparājñānāpātāt; jijñāsāniyamasya ca tadvadanupapatteḥ /
nacendriyasambandhavicchedādvirāma iti yuktam- ātmaprākaṭyāvyāpanāt /
svabhāvata eva kācidasāvajijñāsitāpi jñāyate, na tu sarveti cet- tulyam /
prāgutpannajñātatāsmaraṇajanitajijñāsaḥ samunmīlitanayanaḥ sañjātajñānasamutpāditaprākaṭyaṃ jijñāsureva pratipadyate ityato nānavastheti cet- tulyametat /
[ku.4.524] nanu (5) jñānaṃ na savikalpakagrāhyam, tasya nirvikalpakapūrvakatvād; nirvikalpakagṛgītasya tāvatkālānavasthānāt; tasya tenaiva vināśāt /
nāpi kevalanirvikalpakavedyam, tasya savikalpakonneyatvena tadabhāve pramāṇābhāvāt /
na ca samavāyābhāvavannirvikalpakanirapekṣasavikalpakagocaratvaṃ
 jñānasyeti sāmpratam- tayorviśeṣaṇāṃśasya prāggrahaṇādanumānādivattadupapatteḥ; prakṛte tu jñānatvāderanupalabdheragṛhītaviśeṣaṇāyāśca buddherviśeṣyānupasaṅkramātkathamevaṃ syāt? na; utpannamātrasyaiva bāhyaviṣayajñānasyālocanāt /
tatastatpuraḥsaraṃ prathamata eva tajjātīyasya jñānāntarasya vikalpanāt /
indriyasannikarṣasya tadaiva viśeṣaṇagrahaṇalakṣaṇasahakārisampatteḥ /
vyaktyantarasamavetamapi hi sāmānyaṃ gṛhītaṃ tadevetyupayujyate (224) /
anyathānumānādivikalpānāmanutpādaprasaṅgaḥ; tadgatasya viśeṣaṇasyāgrahaṇādanyagatasya cānupayogātkiṃ liṅgagrahaṇasahakāri syāditi /
etena śabdādipratyakṣaṃ vyākhyātamiti /
[ku.4.525] syādetat- (6) viṣayanirūpyaṃ hi jñānamiṣyate /
na cātīndriyasya paramāṇvādermanasā vedanamasti /
na cāgṛhītasya viśeṣaṇatvam /
na ca nityaparokṣasyāparokṣaviśiṣṭabuddhiviṣayatvam, vyāghātāditi- na, bāhyendriyagrāhyasyāgrāhyasya vā pūrvajñānopanītasyaiva manasā vedanāt /
anyathātīndriyasmaraṇasyāpyanutpattiprasaṅgāt /
iyāṃstu viśeṣaḥ- tasmin sati tadbalādeva; asati tu tajjanitavāsanābalāt /
na caivaṃ sati smaraṇametat; agṛhītajñānagocaratvāt /
na ca viṣayāṃśe tattathā syāditi yuktam- avacchedakatayā prāgavasthāvadavabhāsanāt /
na ca pratyabhijñānamapi grahaṇasmaraṇākāram; virodhāt /
atha grahaṇasmaraṇayoḥ kiyatī sāmagrī? adhikor'thasannikarṣo grahaṇasya, saṃskāramātraṃ sannikarṣaḥ smaraṇasya /
atha grahaṇatve 'pi kuta etadaparokṣākāram? kāraṇāntaranirapekṣeṇa saṃskārādhika(225)sannikarṣavatendriyeṇa janitatvāt /
atha kaḥsannikarṣaḥ? jñānena saṃyuktasamavāyaḥ, tadarthena saṃyuktasamavetaviśeṣaṇatvamiti /
manaso nirapekṣasya bahirvyāpāre 'ndhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅga iti cet- jñānāvacchedakaṃ prati nāyaṃ doṣaḥ /
na ca jñānāpekṣayā bahirityasti /
nāpi tadviṣayāpekṣayā nirapekṣatvam, tasyaiva jñānasyāpekṣaṇāt /
[ku.4.526] athāpi jñānaṃ pratyakṣamityatra kiṃ pramāṇam? pratyakṣameva /
yadasūtrayat- "jñānavikalpānāṃ bhāvābhāvasaṃvedanādadhyātmam" (nyāya.5-1-31) iti /

children.translated_text: [Ku.4.527] [Objection:] God's knowledge is not valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), because being eternal, it produces no result.
Nor is it a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), because it is not a causal factor.

children.text: ata eva ca na tadaśrayaḥ pramāteti- ucyate- mitiḥ samyak paricchittistadvattā ca pramātṛtā /
children.translated_text: And for this very reason, its possessor is not a knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>). — [We] reply: Valid cognition (<s>miti</s>) is correct ascertainment; the possession of that is the status of a knower (<s>pramātṛtā</s>).
The exclusion of the absence of that [correct ascertainment] is validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) — in <s>Gautama</s>'s view.  [verse 5]

Do you not see that just as [one says] "the activity of making a pot, the activity of making a cloth," [so too one says] "the pot was made, the pot will be made"? Accept likewise that just as [one says] "cognition of a pot, cognition of a cloth," [so too] "the pot was known, will be known, is being known." "How can there be a property-property-bearer (<s>dharma-dharmin</s>) relation between two unconnected [things]?" — Just as [one says] "the destroyed pot." "How is this too [possible]?" — Surely you are ready to say that even by destruction something is done to the pot. "Destruction, whose determination depends on that [destroyed thing's] determination, belongs to it by its very nature — so what need of another relation?" — The same applies in the present case.
[ku.4.515] (4) By this, the [objection that] "how can the object be an action (<s>karma</s>), since effects have no substrate [in it]?" is refuted. Because that is coherent through the object being the locus of the instrument's operation, like a thing to be destroyed. And the property of being the natural determiner of the result is likewise [applicable].
[ku.4.516] (5) Now, since knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) is imperceptible, it must be inferred from an uncommon effect; in its absence, how can it be inferred? And being unperceived, how can it enter the domain of practical usage? — Therefore <s>jñātatā</s> ("known-ness") is postulated from the otherwise inexplicable nature of knowledge-based behavior. But this too is wrong — because of the fallacy of mutual dependence (<s>parasparāśraya</s>). For <s>jñātatā</s> would [itself] require knowledge to be inferred, and knowledge [once] known would make the otherwise-inexplicable behavior point to <s>jñātatā</s>.
[ku.4.517] Why moreover is knowledge imperceptible? (1) "Because it is not apprehended by the sense-organs." — No. In an inferential formulation, this is undifferentiated from the probandum (<s>sādhyāviśiṣṭa</s>). And if mere non-apprehension is cited, how — qualified by fitness [for perception] — would it indicate the absence of perceptual apprehension? But if qualified by that [fitness for perception], then how is knowledge imperceptible?
[ku.4.518] (2) "Because it is not the substrate of such <s>jñātatā</s>." — No, because of unestablished locus (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>). "The locus is established by the very otherwise-inexplicable behavior." — No, because that behavior is explained by knowledge as its cause. "Even when [the causal conditions of knowledge] — the contact of self and mind etc. — are present, there is no behavior regarding objects in deep sleep, so this is not so." — No, because those conditions alone are not the cause of behavior. Otherwise, even accepting knowledge, the same [problem] would apply. "From the otherwise inexplicable nature of memory (<s>smaraṇa</s>)." — No, because that too is unestablished. "At least there is some cause of behavior." — So what? This alone does not establish that it is knowledge, since that very thing is unestablished. "Still, a determined agent's activity must have as its cause some property of the agent." — Let it be desire (<s>icchā</s>), which is established by perception; but not knowledge. "How then does that [desire] arise in a determinate locus?" — No, because even accepting knowledge, the same applies. "From some cause." — Then let desire too be from that; what need of postulating knowledge? One might say: When an object is manifest, desire for it etc. arises; but not in the state of deep sleep when the object is not manifest — this is established by experience. Therefore some distinctive cause of desire must be postulated, in the presence of which the indifference characteristic of sound sleep regarding objects ceases for the self. — Well then! By one who acknowledges the cessation of deep sleep through experience, knowledge itself as directly experienced is conceded. For one is said to be in deep sleep when one is not cognizing; the cessation of non-cognition is cognition, i.e., knowledge. And thus the reason is vitiated by temporal displacement (<s>kālātyayāpadiṣṭa</s>).
[ku.4.519] By this, (3) [the argument] "because of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>)" is also disposed of. Moreover, what is this momentariness? If it means being destroyed very rapidly — then it is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). If it means lasting only one moment — that is unestablished, due to absence of evidence. Now [the Buddhist argues]: If lasting cognition, of whatever kind it was when it arose grasping a particular moment of an object — in the second moment too, does it grasp the same, something different, or nothing? Not the first, since that moment has passed; and since perceptual knowledge has only present objects. And it does not merely represent the past as present, since that would entail error. Not the second, because of the impossibility of an operation that has ceased. And if this is accepted even regarding the first [moment], it would follow that future objects would also be perceived. Not the third, since knowledge-ness would be lost. — Thus argue the "Great Vow" proponents [Buddhists]. But this is wrong. Because it is not accepted that knowledge "grasps" [something]; rather, it itself is the grasping. And so the question means: the object on which knowledge was based when arising in the first moment — in the second moment too, does it have that same object or not? The ultimate answer: it does have that same object. And this does not entail error, since there is no apprehension of the contrary. "Even so, how does knowledge persist when the knowable has ceased? Or if knowledge persists, how has the knowable ceased?" — What is impossible here? For it is not the case that knowledge and its object are one entity with a single lifespan.
[ku.4.520] Even granting momentariness, how would [knowledge] be imperceptible? This is argued: "It is not self-luminous (<s>svaprakāśa</s>), being a real entity, like other real entities. Nor is it graspable by another cognition, since simultaneous cognition is prohibited and there is no [cognition] at the same time. At the time of the grasper, the graspable has passed and cannot be present. At the time of the graspable, the grasper is future." — But then <s>jñātatā</s> (known-ness) too would not be perceptible, being momentary. How? Thus — it is not self-luminous, being a real entity. It is not graspable by its producer, being future. And because of the impossibility of an operation that has ceased. It is not graspable by a cognition at the same time, because one does not experience the sense-contact that produces [simultaneous] cognition. Nor is it graspable by a subsequent cognition, since by then it has passed. "How do you know that <s>jñātatā</s> is momentary?" — By your own reasoning. For: does the <s>jñātatā</s> that arose depending on a [particular] moment, in the next moment too depend on that same moment, or another, or none? Not the first, since that [moment] no longer exists then. Not the second, since there is no transference [of substratum]. And if cognition grasps only one moment, then having a <s>jñātatā</s> that is the effect of another moment's substratum would entail error — like a cognition-grasping-silver having a <s>jñātatā</s> that is the effect of what is present before [it]. Nor does cognition grasp another moment either, since [<s>jñātatā</s>] does not exist at that time. Not the third, since this would lead to essencelessness (<s>niḥsvabhāvatā</s>). For it would then belong neither to this nor to that.
[ku.4.521] "It persists as characterized by that very past moment." — Then there would be no present-object-ness of the manifestation. Otherwise, what is wrong with knowledge too persisting in the same way? For knowledge has no "present-appearance" other than its connection with the manifestation of a present object. If the [present] nature is [explained] by mere persistence of manifestation independent of the object, then even knowledge of past and future objects would also be [present] — which is absurd.
[ku.4.522] If, however, one accepts that even a gross present [object] is taken by manifestation [as its content], then that very thing is the object of that cognition, and so cognition too is not momentary.
[ku.4.523] (4) "If knowledge is perceptible, there should be no change of object, since the connection [with the sense-organ] has been established. Nor is restriction [of object] due to the restriction of desire-to-know (<s>jijñāsā</s>), since that presupposes doubt, which presupposes knowledge of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), and if the <s>dharmin</s> is known by mere proximity, or if desire is required — either way there is infinite regress." — No, because the same applies to the <s>jñātatā</s> view. For if that too is an object of knowledge, there would be an infinite series of cognitions about it; and the restriction through desire-to-know would be equally impossible. "Knowledge ceases when the sense-connection is broken." — That is not right, since it does not encompass the self's manifestation. "By nature, some things are known even without desire, but not all." — The same [objection] applies. "One who opens one's eyes, with desire arising from memory of previously produced <s>jñātatā</s>, perceives the manifestation produced by the arising cognition — therefore no infinite regress." — The same applies [to our position].
[ku.4.524] (5) "Knowledge is not graspable by determinate perception (<s>savikalpaka</s>), since that requires prior indeterminate perception (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>). What is grasped by indeterminate perception does not persist long enough [for the next stage]. And it is destroyed by that very [indeterminate perception]. Nor is it cognizable by indeterminate perception alone, since without determinate perception [to follow], there is no means of valid cognition." "And it is not the case that knowledge, like the absence of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), is an object of determinate perception independent of indeterminate perception." — This is not right. In those cases, the qualifier-aspect has been grasped earlier, so [determinate perception] is possible as with inference etc. But in the present case, since knowledge-ness etc. is not perceived, and a cognition with an ungrasped qualifier does not advance to the qualificand — how could this be? — No; because external-object-knowledge itself, immediately upon arising, serves as the apprehension (<s>ālocana</s>). From that, a determinate cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) of the same kind arises at the very first [moment]. Since sense-contact has the capacity for qualifier-grasping at that very time. For a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) grasped as inhering in another particular is employed as "that very same." Otherwise there would follow the non-arising of even inferential determinate cognitions — since the qualifier pertaining to that [particular thing] would not be grasped, and what pertains to another would not be applicable, so what would serve as an auxiliary to grasping the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>)? By this, the perceptibility of words (<s>śabda</s>) etc. is also explained.
[ku.4.525] (6) "Knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) is held to be determined by its object. And there is no mental cognition of supersensible entities like atoms etc. Nor can what is not grasped serve as a qualifier. Nor can what is eternally beyond perception be an object of a directly-experienced qualified cognition — due to contradiction." — No, because the mind cognizes what has been brought to it by prior knowledge, whether it is graspable by external senses or not. Otherwise, even supersensible memory could not arise. The distinction is this: when [the external object] is present, [knowledge arises] by its force directly; when absent, by the force of impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) produced by it. "In that case, it would be memory, not [direct] apprehension; since the object of knowledge has not been grasped [directly]." — Nor is it right to say that the object-aspect would be so [i.e., memorial]; because as a delimiting factor, it appears as in the previous state. "Nor is recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) of the form of both grasping and memory." — Because of contradiction. What then is the extent of the causal conditions of grasping versus memory? Grasping has additional object-proximity; memory has only impressions as its proximity. "Even if it is grasping, why is it in the form of direct experience (<s>aparokṣa</s>)?" — Because it is produced by a sense-organ that has proximity greater than mere impressions, without dependence on another cause. "What is that proximity?" — For knowledge: <s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s> (contact-cum-inherence); for its object: being a qualifier through what inheres in what is conjoined [with the sense]. "If the mind operates on external objects without dependence [on external senses], there should be no blind or deaf people." — This fault does not apply to the delimiter of cognition. And there is no "external" relative to cognition. Nor is there independence relative to its object, since that very cognition depends on [the object].
[ku.4.526] Furthermore, what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the proposition "knowledge is perceptible"? Perception itself. As was taught in the <s>sūtra</s>: "The presence and absence [of cognition] regarding internal cognitions and thoughts is [known] introspectively" (<s>Nyāya Sūtra</s> 5.1.31).

children.text:
samīcīn.o hyanubhavaḥ prameti vyavastathitam /
tathāca anityatvena viśeṣaṇamanarthakam, nityānubhavasiddhau tadvyavacchedabhyāniṣṭatvāt; asiddhau ca vyavacchedyābhāvāt /
na cedamanumānam, āśrayāsiddhibādhayoranyatarākrāntatvāt /
na tat pramākaraṇamiti tviṣyata eva,pramayā sambandhābhāvāt /
tadāśrayasya tu pramātṛtvametadeva yat tatsamavāyaḥ /
kārakatve satīti tu viśeṣaṇaṃ pūrvavannirarthakamanusandheyam /
yadyevam, "āptaprāmāṇyād" (nyāya.2-2-37) iti sūtravirodhaḥ /
tena hīśvarasya prāmāṇyaṃ pratipādyate, na tu pramātṛtvamiti cet- na- nimittasamāveśena vyavahārasamāveśāvirodhāt /
pramāsamavāyo hi pramātṛvyavahāranimittam; pramayā tvayāyogavyavacchedena sambandhaḥ pramāṇavyavahāranimittam /
tadubhayañceśvare /
atrāpi kāryayeti viśeṣaṇaṃ pūrvavadanarthakamūhanīyam /
[ku.4.528] syādetat- pramīyate 'neneti pramāṇam, pramiṇotīti pramātā iti kārakaśabdatvamanayoḥ /
tathāca kathamakārakamartha iti cet- na- etasya vyutpattimātranimittatvāt /
pravṛttinimittaṃ tu yathopadarśitameva; vyavasthāpanāt /
anyathā asmadādiṣu na pramātṛvyavahāraḥ syāt; sarvatra svātantryābhāvāt /
karaṇavyavahārastvanyatra yadyapyanyanimittako 'pi, tathāpīhoktanimittavivakṣayaiveti /
evantarhi pañcamapramāṇābhyupagame 'pasiddhāntaḥ /
na hi tat pratyakṣamanumānamāgamo vā, anindriyaliṅgaśabdakaraṇatvāt- na- sākṣātkāripramāvattayā pratyakṣāntarbhāvāt; indriyārthasannikarṣotpannatvasya ca laukikamātraviṣayatvāt /
[ku.4.529] syādetat- tathāpīśvarajñānaṃ na pramā, viparyayatvāt /
yadā khalvetadasmadādivibhramānālambate, tadaitasya viṣayamaspṛśato na jñānāvagāhanasambhava iti tadartho 'pyālambanamabhyupeyam /
tathāca tadapi viparyayaḥ, viparītārthālambanatvāt /
tadanavagāhane vā asmadādervibhramān aviduṣastadupaśamāyopadeśānāmasarvajñapūrvakatvamiti na- vibhramasyāprāmāṇye 'pi tadviṣayasya tattvamullikhato 'bhrāntatvāt /
anyathā bhrāntisamucchedaprasaṅgaḥ; pramāṇābhāvāt /
tathāpyāropitārthavacchinnajñānālambanatvena kathaṃ na bhrāntatvamiti cet- na- yad yatra nāsti tatra tasyāvagatiriti bhrāntyarthatvāt /

children.translated_text: [God's cognition,] having that [erroneous cognition] as its object and thus touching upon [reality] everywhere, is in accordance with truth.

children.text: nahi na tadrajatam, nāpi tatrāsat, nāpi tannāvagatamiti /
children.translated_text: For it is not that that [object] is not silver, nor that it was not there [as the substratum], nor that it was not cognized.
[Ku.4.530] For one who directly perceives, who is eternally connected [with all objects], whose state is independent of any other means,
in whom the sequence of all existing things is arranged — [His is] an experience of reality as it truly is.

For it is established that correct experience is valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>). And thus, qualifying it with 'non-eternality' is purposeless — because if the existence of eternal experience is established, its exclusion is undesirable; and if not established, there is nothing to exclude. Nor is this an [valid] inference, since it is afflicted by either the unestablished basis or contradiction. That [God's knowledge] is not an instrument of valid cognition — this is indeed accepted, due to the absence of a relation with [producing fresh] valid cognition. But the knower-hood of its possessor is precisely this: co-inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) with it. The qualification 'when there is causal agency' should be understood as purposeless, as before. [Objection:] If so, there is conflict with the <s>sūtra</s> 'from the authority of the trustworthy' (<s>Nyāya-Sūtra</s> 2.2.37). For that [sūtra] teaches God's authority (<s>prāmāṇya</s>), not His knower-hood. — No, because when the ground [for a designation] is present, there is no contradiction in the designation being present too. For co-inherence with valid cognition is the ground for the designation 'knower'; while the relation with valid cognition through the exclusion of its absence is the ground for the designation 'means of valid knowledge.' Both of these [apply] to God. Here too, the qualification 'productive [of results]' should be understood as purposeless, as before. [Ku.4.528] It may be objected: '<s>Pramāṇa</s>' means 'that by which one measures' and '<s>pramātṛ</s>' means 'one who measures' — these are words denoting causal agents. How then can a non-agent be so designated? — No, because [etymological derivation] serves only as the occasion for linguistic competence. The ground for actual usage is as indicated above, since it has been established. Otherwise, there would be no designation of 'knower' for us [ordinary beings] either, since independence is absent everywhere. The designation 'instrument,' though elsewhere based on other grounds, here is intended precisely with the ground stated. [Objection:] Then there would be the fault of accepting a fifth means of knowledge. For it [God's knowledge] is not perception, inference, or scripture, since its instrument is not a sense-organ, inferential mark, or word. — No, because it is included within perception as a kind of valid cognition that directly apprehends; and because 'being produced from sense-object contact' applies only to mundane [perception]. [Ku.4.529] It may be objected: Even so, God's knowledge is not valid cognition, because it is erroneous. For when this [divine knowledge] takes as its object our errors and the like, and since it is impossible for it to cognize [something] without touching its object — the object of that [error] too must be accepted as [its] object. And thus it too is erroneous, since it takes an erroneous object as its object. Or, if it does not cognize that [error], then the teachings aimed at removing the errors of ignorant beings like us would not presuppose an omniscient [being]. — No, because even though the error is not a valid cognition, [God's knowledge] is unerring since it correctly touches upon the reality of that error's object. Otherwise, there would follow the impossibility of ever correcting error, due to the absence of a means of knowledge [for that]. [Objection:] But still, how is it not erroneous, since it takes as its object a cognition delimited by a superimposed object? — No, because the meaning of 'error' is: the cognition of something where it is not, in [something] where it is not.
For one whose faulty vision — caused by even a trace [of defect] — has departed, whose husk of doubt has fallen away,
what [need] of others who are tainted by the opening of [mere] doubts? That <s>Śiva</s> is my means of valid knowledge.  [verse 6]
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s>.
<s>Śrī</s> (Auspiciousness).
Salutation to the blessed <s>Śrīnivāsa</s>, the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>.
Fifth chapter of the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s>.
[Objection:] If there were a valid proof for God, all this would indeed be so.

children.text: tadeva tu na paśyāma iti cet- nahyeṣa sthāṇoraparādhaḥ yadenamandho na paśyati /
children.translated_text: 'But we do not see that [proof].' — [We reply:] It is not the fault of the post that a blind man does not see it.
For thus: From effect, design (<s>āyojana</s>), sustenance, and the like; from words; from cognition; from scripture;
from sentences; and from the specific number [of atoms] — the omniscient, imperishable [God] is to be proved.  [verse 1]

children.text: [ku.5.602] kṣityādi kartṛpūrvakaṃ kāryatvāditi- na bādho 'syopajīvyatvāt pratibandho na durbalaiḥ /
children.translated_text: [Ku.5.602] 'The earth and the like have a maker, because they are effects' — [Objection:] this [inference] is contradicted. — No, because it [the inference] is the foundation [of other proofs], obstruction [of it] is not [achieved] by weaker [arguments].
There is no contradiction between [partial] proof and [partial] non-proof; nor is non-proof [of certain aspects] groundless.  [verse 2]

children.text:
[ku.5.603] tathāhi- atra ye śarīraprasaṅgamudghāṭayanti, kasteṣāmāśayaḥ? kimīśvaraṃ pakṣayitvā kartṛtvāccharīritvam; tataḥ (atha) śarīravyāvṛtterakartṛtvam; atha kṣityādikameva pakṣayitvā kāryatvāccharīrikartṛkatvam; yadvā śarīrājanyatvādakāryatvam; tata eva vākartṛkatvam; paravyāptistambhanārthaṃ viparītavyāptyupadarśanamātraṃ veti? tatra prathamadvitīyayorāśrayāsiddhibādhāpasiddhāntapratijñāvirodhāḥ /
tṛtīye tu vyāptau satyāṃ nedamaniṣṭam; asatyāntu na prasaṅgaḥ /
caturthe bādhānekāntau (229) /
pañcametvasamarthaviśeṣaṇatvam /
ṣaṣṭhe 'pināgṛhyamāṇaviśeṣayā vyāptyā bādhaḥ /
na cāgṛhyamāṇāviśeṣayā (230) vyāptyā gṛhyamāṇaviśeṣāyāḥ satpratipakṣatvam /
asti ca kāryatvavyāpteḥ pakṣadharmatāparigraho viśeṣaḥ /
kartāśarīrī, viparīto na karteti cānayostadvirahaḥ /
[ku.5.604] nanu yad buddhimaddhetukaṃ taccharīhetukamiti niyame yaccharīrahetukaṃ na bhavati tad buddhimaddhetukamapi na bhavatīti viryayaniyamopi syāt /
tathāca pakṣadharmatāpi labhyata iti cenna- gaganādeḥsapakṣabhāgasyāpi sambhavātkevalavyatirekitvānupapatteḥ /
anvaye tu viśeṣaṇāsāmarthyāt /
hetuvyāvṛttimātrameva hi tatra kartṛvyāvṛttivyāptam; na tu śarīrarūpahetuvyāvṛttirityuktam /
vyāptaśca pakṣadharma upayujyate, na tvanyo 'tiprasaṅgāt /
etena tadvyāpakarahitatvāditi sāmānyopasaṃhārasyāsiddhatvamuktaṃ veditavyam /
nahi yadvyāvṛttiryadabhāve 'nvayavyatirekābhyāmupasaṃhartumaśakyā, tattasya vyāpakaṃ nāmeti /
[ku.5.605] viśeṣavirodhastu viśeṣasiddhau sahopalambhena tadasiddhau mithodharmiparihārānupalambhena nirasto nāśaṅkāmapyadhirohatīti /
[ku.5.606] syādetat- asti tāvat kāryasyāvāntaraviśeṣaḥ yataḥśarīrikartṛkatvamanumīyate /
tathāca tatprayuktāmeva vyāptamupajīvetkāryatvasāmānyamiti syāt- na syāt- nahi viśeṣostīti sāmānyamaprayojakam /
tathāsati saurabhakaṭutvanīlimādiviśeṣe (231) sati na dhūmasāmānyamagniṅgamayet /
kiṃ nāma (232) sādhakasāmānye sādhyasāmānyamāśritya pravartamāne tadviśeṣaḥsādhyaviśeṣavyāptimāśrayet; natu viśeṣe sati sāmānyamakiñcitkaram, tasyāpi viśeṣāntarāpekṣayā(233)kiñcitkaratvaprasaṅgāt /
[ku.5.607] saurabhādiviśeṣaṃ vihāyāpi dhūme vanhirdṛṣṭaḥ, na tu viśeṣaṃ vihāya kārye karteticenna- kāryaviśeṣaḥ kāraṇaviśeṣe vyavatiṣṭhate; na tu kāryakāraṇasāmānyayoḥ pratibandhamanyathākuryāditi /
kiṃ na dṛṣṭaṃ kāryaṃ kāraṇamātre aṅkuro bīje tadviśeṣo dhānye tadviśeṣaḥśālau tadviśeṣaḥ kalame ityādi bahulaṃ loke? kva vā dṛṣṭamaṇudravyārabhyaṃ dravyam, nityarūpādyārabdhaṃ rūpādi? tathāpi sāmānyavyāpteravirodhātsiddhyatyeva /
avaśyañcaitadevamaṅgīkartavyam; anyathā kāryatvasyākasmikatvaprasaṅgāt /
[ku.5.608] syādetat- anvayayvatireki tāvadidaṃ kāryatvamiti paramārthaḥ /
tatrākāśādervipakṣāt kiṃ kartṛvyāvṛtteḥ kāryatvavyāvṛttiḥ āhosvitkāraṇamātravyāvṛtteriti sandihyate- tadasat- karturapi kāraṇatvāt /
kāraṇeṣu cānyatamavyatirekasyāpi kāryānutpattiṃ prati prayojakatvāt; anyathā kāraṇatvavyāghātāt, karaṇādiviśeṣavyatirekasandehaprasaṅgācca; kathaṃ hi niścīyate kimākāśāt kāraṇavyāvṛttyā
 kāryatvavyāvṛttiḥ uta karaṇavyāvṛttyā; evaṃ kimupādānavyāvṛttyā kimasamavāyivyāvṛttyā, kiṃ nimittavyāvṛttyeti? kāryatvāt karaṇamupādānamasamavāyi nimittaṃ vā buddhyādiṣu na siddhyet /
kartuḥ kāraṇatve siddhe sarvametaducitam; tadeva tvasiddhamiti cet- kiṃ paṭādau kuvindādirakāraṇameva kartā? prastute vodāsīna eva sādhayitumupakrāntaḥ? tasmāt yatkiñcidetadapīti /
[ku.5.609] nanu kartā kāraṇānāmadhiṣṭātā sākṣādvā śarītavat, sādhyaparamparayā vā daṇḍādivat? tatra na pūrvaḥ, paramāṇvādīnāṃ śarīratvaprasaṅgāt /
na dvatīyaḥ, dvārābhāvāt /
na hi kasyacitsākṣādadhiṣṭeyasyābhāve paramparayādhiṣṭānaṃ sambhavati /
tadayaṃ pramāṇārthaḥ- paramāṇvādayaḥna sākṣāccetanādhiṣṭheyāḥ śarīretaratvāt, yatpunaḥ sākṣādadhiṣṭheyam, na tadevaṃ yathāsmaccharīramiti; nāpi paramparayādhiṣṭheyāḥ, svavyāpāre śarīrānapekṣatvāt svaceṣṭāyāmasmaccharīravat, vyatirekeṇa vā daṇḍādi udāharaṇam /
evañca (evaṃ) kṣityādi na cetanādhiṣṭhitahetukaṃ śarīretarahetukatvādityatipīḍayā satpratipakṣatvam /
apica paṭādau kuvindādeḥ kiṃ kārakādhiṣṭhānārthamapekṣā, teṣāmacetanānāṃ svato 'pravṛtteḥ? āho kārakatvena? na pūrvaḥ, teṣāṃ parameśvareṇaivādhiṣṭhānāt /
na hyasya jñānamicchā prayatno vā vemādīnna vyāpnotīti sambhavati /
na cādhiṣṭhitānāmadhiṣṭhātrantarāpekṣā tadarthameva, tathāsatyanavasthānādevāviśeṣāt /
na dvitīyaḥ, adhiṣṭhātṛtvasyānaṅgatvaprasaṅge dṛṣṭāntasya sādhyavikalatvāpatteḥ /
na ca hetutvenaiva tasyāpekṣāstviti vācyam- evaṃ tarhi yat kāryaṃ tatsahetukamiti vyāptiḥ, na tu sakartṛkamiti /
tathāca tayai(tathai)va prayoge siddhasādhanāt /
kiñcānityaprayatnapūrvakatvaprayuktāṃ vyāptimupajīvat kāryatvaṃ na buddhimatpūrvakatvena svabhāvapratibaddham /
na hyanityaprayatno 'pi buddhyā śarīravat kāraṇatvenāpekṣyate, yena tannivṛttāvapyakāryā r(ya) buddhirna nivartata iti /
[ku.5.610] tadetat prāgeva nirastaprāyaṃ nottarāntaramapekṣate /
tathāhi- sākṣādadhiṣṭhātari sādhye paramāṇvādīnāṃ śarīratvaprasaṅga iti kimidaṃ śarīratvam, yat prasajyate? yadi sākṣātprayatnavadadhiṣṭheyatvam, tadiṣyata eva /
na ca tato 'nyat prasañjakamapi /
athendriyāśrayatvam?tanna, tadavacchinnajñānajananadvāreṇendriyāṇāmupayogāt /
anavacchinne prayatne nāyaṃ vidhiḥ, nityatvāt /
ata eva nārthāśrayatvam (234) /
nahi nityajñānaṃ bhogarūpamabhogarūpaṃ vā, yatnamapekṣate; tasya kāraṇaviśeṣatvāt /
na ca nityasarvajñasya bhogasambhāvanāpi, viśeṣādarśanābhāve mithyājñānānavakāśe doṣānutpattau dharmādharmayorasattvāt /
tasmāt, sākṣātprayatnānadhiṣṭheyatvāt svavyāpāre tadanapekṣatvācceti dvayaṃ sādhyāviśiṣṭam /
anindriyāśrayatvādabhogāyatanatvāt svavyāpāre tadanapekṣatvācceti trayamapyanyathāsiddham /
abhogāyatanatvādanindriyāśrayo 'pi, bhoktṛkarmānupagrahādabhogāyatanamapi, sparśavadvegavaddravyāntara(235)nudyatvātta(236)danapekṣamapi syāt; acetanatvāccetanādhiṣṭhatamapi syāditi ko virodhaḥ? tathācasākṣātprayatnādhiṣṭhitetarajanyatvāditi sādhyasamaḥ /
indriyāśrayetarajanyatvāt bhogāyatanetarajanyatvāditi dvayamapyanyathāsiddham /
kāryajñānādyavapekṣatvāccharīretarajanyamapi syāt; acetanahetukatvāccetanādhiṣṭhituka(237)mapīti ko virodhaḥ? aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇaścapakṣaḥ /
nahi cetanānadhiṣṭhatahetukatvaṃ kvacit pramāṇasiddham /
na ca cetanādhiṣṭhitahetukatvaniṣedhaḥ sādhyaḥ, hetorasādhāraṇyaprasaṅgāt /
gaganāderapi sapakṣādvyāvṛtteḥ /
[ku.5.611] yatpunaruktaṃ kuvindādeḥ paṭādau kathamapekṣeti, tatra kārakatayeti kaḥsandehaḥ? kintu kārakatvameva tasya jñānacikīrṣāprayatnavataḥ, na svarūpavataḥ /
tadevacādhiṣṭhātṛtvam /
yattvadhiṣṭhite kimadhiṣṭhāneneti- tatkiṃ kuvinda udvāryate, īśvaro vā, anavasthā vā'pādyate? na prathamaḥ, anvayavyatirekasiddhatvāt /
na dvatīyaḥ, paramāṇvadṛṣṭādhiṣṭhātṛtvasiddhau jñānādīnāṃ sarvaviṣayatve vemādyadhiṣṭhānasyāpi nyāyaprāptatvāt /
na tu tadadhiṣṭhānārthameveśvarasiddhiḥ /
na tṛtīyaḥ, tasmin pramāṇābhāvāt /
tathāpyekādhiṣṭhitamaparaḥ kimarthamadhitiṣṭhatīti praśne kimuttaramiti cet- hetupraśno 'yam, prayojanapraśno vā? nādyaḥ, īśvarādhiṣṭhānasya nityatvāt /
kuvindādyadhiṣṭhānasya svahetvadhīnatvāt /
na dvitīyaḥ, kāryaniṣpādanena bhogasiddheḥ spaṣṭatvāt /
ekādhiṣṭhānenaiva kāryaṃ syāditi cet- syādeva /
tathāpi na sambhede 'nyataravaiyarthyam /
parimāṇaṃ prati saṅkhyāparimāṇapracayavat pratyekaṃ
 sāmarthyopalabdhau sambhūyakāritvopapatteḥ /
asti tatra vaijātyamiti cet- ihāpi kiñcidbhaviṣyatīti /
na cākurvataḥ kulālādeḥ kāyasaṅkṣobhādisādhyo bhogaḥsiddhyediti tadarthamasya kartṛtvamīśvaro 'numanyate, tadarthamātratvādaiśvaryasyeti /
[ku.5.612] yatvanityaprayatnetyādi- bhavedapyevaṃ yadyanityaprayatnanivṛttāveva buddhirapi nivarteta; na tvetadasti; (238) udāsīnasya prayatnābhāve 'pi buddhisadbhāvāt /
hetubhūtā buddhirnivattate ithi cenna- udāsīnabuddherapi saṃskāraṃ prati hetutvāt /
kārakaviṣayā buddhirnivartate iti cenna- udāsīnasyāpi kārakaboddhṛtvāt /
na hi ghaṭādikamakurvantaścakrādikaṃ nekṣāmahe /
hetubhūtā kārakabuddhirnivartate iti cenna- (cakrā(239)dibuddherapi saṃskāraṃ prati hetutvāt /
kārakaphalahetubhūtā kārakabuddhirnivartata iti cenna-) ayatamānasyāpi duḥkhahetubhūtāyā api taddhetukaṇṭakasparśabuddherbhāvāt (240) /
cikīrṣāhetubhūto 'nubhavo nivartata iti cenna- kenacinnimittenākurvato 'pi cikīrṣātaddhetubuddhisambhavātat /
anapekṣakṛtihetucikīrṣākāraṇaṃ buddhirnivartate iti cet- na tarhi buddhimātram /
tathācānityaprayatnahetukatvaprayuktaṃ viśiṣṭaprayatnacikīrṣāhetubuddhimatpūrvakatvamiti tannivṛttau tadeva nivartatām, na tu buddhimatpūrvakatvamātram /
tatra tasyāprayojakatvāditi buddhimatpūrvakatva(miti)sādhyapakṣe parīhāraḥ /
sakartṛkamiti prayatnapradhānapakṣe śaṅkaiva nāsti; tasyaiva tatrānupādhitvāt /
[ku.5.613] etena- śarīrasambandhe buddhigatakāryatvavad buddhisambandhe prayatnagatakāryatvamupādhiriti- nirastam /
yo hi buddhyā śarīravaccharīranivṛttyā buddhinivṛttivadvā prayatnena buddhiṃ buddhinivṛttyā prayatnanivṛttiṃ (vā?) sādhayet, sa evaṃ kadācidupālabhyaḥ /
vayantvavagatahetubhāvaṃ kalitaśaktisakala(241)kārakaprayoktāraṃ kāryādevānumimānā naivamāskandanīyāḥ tatra (242) tasyānupādhitvāt /
[ku.5.614] na ca prayatna ātmalābhārthameva matimapekṣate, viṣayalābhārthamapyapekṣaṇāt /
tataḥ prayatnādbuddhiḥ tannivṛtteśca prayatnanivṛttiḥ siddhyeti vistṛtamanyatra /
kāryabuddhinivṛttyā tu kārya eva prayatno nivartate, na nityaḥ /
nitye ca prayatne nityaiva buddhiḥ pravartate, nānityā /
na hi tayā tasya viṣayalābhasambhavaḥ /

children.translated_text: Since in the absence of that [effort] prior to the body etc., if the body does not arise, it would never arise at all.
In summary: just as [the body] is not produced by [the body itself, i.e.,] not self-generated, so too it is not generated by non-eternal effort.
[Ku 5.615] The impurity of others' reasoning, being merely pseudo-reasoning (<s>tarkābhāsa</s>), is not a [valid] refutation.
But the reasoning favorable [to our thesis] here is an ornament; the dropping of the effect [argument is also an ornament]. (Verse 3)

[Ku 5.603] Consider: Those who raise the objection about [God having] a body — what is their intention? Is it that, taking <s>Īśvara</s> (God) as the subject, [one infers] from creatorship that He has a body? And then from the exclusion of a body, [that He is] not a creator? Or, taking earth and the like as the subject, [one infers] from being an effect that it has a creator with a body? Or from not being produced from a body, that it is not an effect? And from that alone, that it has no creator? Or is it merely the display of a contrary pervasion for the purpose of obstructing the opponent's pervasion? In the first and second [options], there are the faults of unestablished locus, contradiction, deviation from the established doctrine, and contradiction with the thesis. In the third, if the pervasion holds, this [conclusion] is not undesirable; but if it does not hold, the objection does not arise. In the fourth, there are the faults of contradiction and inconclusiveness. The fifth has an impotent qualifier. In the sixth also, there is contradiction by a pervasion whose distinction is not apprehended. And a pervasion whose distinction is not apprehended cannot be a counter-argument to one whose distinction is apprehended. And the distinction lies in the fact that being-an-effect is pervaded by [having a] creator, and this pervasion encompasses the thesis-property. 'A creator [must have] a body' and 'the opposite [i.e., the bodiless] is not a creator' — both of these lack that [pervasion]. [Ku 5.604] [Objection:] If the rule is 'whatever is caused by an intelligent being is caused by an embodied being,' then the contrapositive rule too would hold: 'whatever is not caused by an embodied being is not caused by an intelligent being either.' And thus the thesis-property would also be obtained. No, [we reply] — because since space and the like, which belong to the similar class, also exist, purely negative inference is not possible. In the positive [concomitance], because of the impotence of the qualifier. For only the exclusion of the cause as such is pervaded by the exclusion of the creator; but it has been stated that the exclusion of a cause in the form of a body [is not so pervaded]. And it is the pervaded thesis-property that is useful, not another, because of over-extension. By this, it should be understood that the non-establishment of the general induction from the exclusion of its pervader is stated. For that whose exclusion cannot be inductively established through positive and negative concomitance in the absence of another is not called its pervader. [Ku 5.605] And the contradiction of a particular is removed — when the particular is established, by co-perception; when it is not established, by the non-apprehension of the mutual avoidance of properties — and it does not even ascend to the level of a doubt. [Ku 5.606] It may be objected: There is indeed a sub-particular of being an effect from which being created by an embodied being is inferred. And so, the general property of being an effect would depend on the very pervasion occasioned by that [particular]. [Reply:] It would not be so — for it is not the case that because a particular exists, the general is non-probative. If that were so, then when there is a particular such as fragrance, pungency, or blueness, the general [property of being] smoke would not indicate fire. What indeed — when the probative general is operating in dependence on the provable general, the particular of the probative [property] would depend on the pervasion of the particular of the provable [property]; but it is not the case that when a particular exists, the general is ineffective, for then the general too would be ineffective in dependence on yet another particular. [Ku 5.607] [Objection:] Setting aside the particular such as fragrance, fire is observed from smoke; but setting aside the particular, a creator is not [observed] from an effect. No, [we reply] — a particular effect is determined in relation to a particular cause; but it does not alter the invariable connection between the generalities of cause and effect. Is it not observed that an effect [is produced from] a cause in general — a sprout from a seed, a particular [sprout] from grain, a particular [grain] from rice, a particular [rice] from <s>kalama</s> — abundantly in the world? And where has it been observed that a substance produced by atomic substances, or a quality produced by eternal qualities [arises without a general causal connection]? Nevertheless, since there is no contradiction with the general pervasion, it is indeed established. And this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, there would be the consequence that being-an-effect is without cause. [Ku 5.608] It may be objected: This being-an-effect has both positive and negative concomitance — that is the ultimate truth. In that case, from the dissimilar class such as space, does the exclusion of being-an-effect [follow] from the exclusion of a creator, or from the exclusion of a mere cause? — That is wrong — because even the creator is a cause. And among causes, the absence of even one has the probative force for the non-production of the effect; otherwise, the very nature of causality would be contradicted, and there would be the consequence of doubting the absence of specific causes such as instruments. For how can it be determined: 'Is the exclusion of being-an-effect from space due to the exclusion of a cause, or due to the exclusion of an instrument; is it due to the exclusion of a material cause, or due to the exclusion of a non-inherent cause, or due to the exclusion of an efficient cause?' From being-an-effect, the instrument, the material cause, the non-inherent cause, or the efficient cause — none of these would be established with respect to cognitions and the like. If the causality of the creator is established, all of this is appropriate; but if that alone is unestablished — then is a weaver not a cause at all with respect to cloth? Or has one begun to prove what is irrelevant in the matter at hand? Therefore, even this [objection] is [of] negligible [force]. [Ku 5.609] [Objection:] Is the creator a controller of causes directly, like [the soul controls] a body, or indirectly, like a stick and the like? In the first case, there would be the consequence that atoms and the like would be [God's] body. In the second, there is no means [of control]. For without something being directly controllable, indirect control is not possible. The meaning of this argument is: atoms and the like are not directly controllable by a conscious being, because they are other than a body — what is directly controllable is not such as our body. Nor are they indirectly controllable, because in their own operation they do not depend on a body, like our body in its own motion — or, by the negative mode, a stick and the like serve as an example. And thus, earth and the like are not caused by something controlled by a conscious being, because they are caused by something other than a body — this constitutes a counter-argument that causes considerable difficulty. Moreover, as for the weaver's role with respect to cloth — is the dependency because of the control of instruments, since those [instruments], being unconscious, do not operate by themselves? Or is it as a cause? Not the first, because those [instruments] are controlled by <s>Parameśvara</s> (the Supreme Lord) Himself. For it is not possible that His knowledge, desire, and effort do not extend to the loom and the like. And there is no need for a second controller for what is already controlled, since otherwise there would be an infinite regress without any distinction. Not the second either, because if controllership were irrelevant, the example would lack the provable [property]. Nor can it be said that the dependency is merely as a cause — for then the pervasion would be 'whatever is an effect has a cause,' not 'has a creator.' And in a proof formulated with that [pervasion], there would be the fault of establishing what is already established. Moreover, being-an-effect, which depends on a pervasion occasioned by being caused by a non-eternal effort, is not intrinsically connected with being preceded by intelligence. For a non-eternal effort too is not depended upon by intelligence as a cause, like a body, so that even when it [effort] ceases, intelligence, which is not an effect [of effort alone], would not cease. [Ku 5.610] All this has been mostly refuted earlier and does not require a further response. For consider: when proving a direct controller, [the objection about] the consequence of atoms being a body — what is this 'body-ness' that allegedly follows? If it means being directly controllable by effort, that is precisely what we maintain. And there is nothing else to be objected to from that. If it means being the substratum of sense-faculties — no, because the sense-faculties are useful through the medium of generating cognition delimited by that [body]. In the case of non-delimited effort, this rule does not apply, because of its eternality. For this very reason, it is not the substratum of objects. For eternal knowledge, whether it has the form of enjoyment or not, does not depend on effort, since that [effort] is a specific cause. And for one who is eternally omniscient, there is no possibility of enjoyment, since in the absence of non-perception of distinctions, with no room for erroneous cognition, with no arising of defects, <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) would not exist. Therefore, the two [faults] — 'not being directly controllable by effort' and 'not depending on that in their own operation' — are not different from the provable. And the three — 'not being the substratum of sense-faculties,' 'not being the locus of enjoyment,' and 'not depending on that in their own operation' — are all otherwise-established. From not being the locus of enjoyment, it may also not be the substratum of sense-faculties; from not assisting an enjoyer, it may also not be the locus of enjoyment; from being propelled by another substance possessing contact and velocity, it may also be independent of that [body] — and from being unconscious, it may also be not controlled by a conscious being — what contradiction is there? And thus, 'being produced by something other than what is directly controlled by effort' is equal to the provable. And 'being produced by something other than the substratum of sense-faculties' and 'being produced by something other than the locus of enjoyment' — both are otherwise-established. 'Because it does not depend on knowledge of the effect and the like, it may also be produced by something other than a body'; 'because its cause is unconscious, it may also be controlled by a conscious being' — what contradiction is there? And the subject has an unestablished qualifier. For the property of having a cause that is not controlled by a conscious being is nowhere established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And the negation of having a cause controlled by a conscious being is not provable, because of the consequence that the reason would be uncommon — since even from the dissimilar class of space, it [the reason] would be excluded. [Ku 5.611] As for what was said about the weaver's role with respect to cloth — what doubt is there that it is as a cause? But his very causality consists of his being possessed of knowledge, desire, and effort — not of his mere form. And that itself is controllership. As for 'what is the need of control when [the instruments] are already controlled' — is the weaver being excluded, or <s>Īśvara</s> (God), or is an infinite regress being generated? Not the first, because [the weaver's role] is established through positive and negative concomitance. Not the second, because when the controllership of atoms and <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) by <s>Īśvara</s> is established, and when His knowledge and the like extend to all objects, the control of the loom and the like is also obtained through proper reasoning. But the establishment of <s>Īśvara</s> is not merely for the purpose of controlling those [instruments]. Not the third, because there is no evidence for it. Even so, [in response to] the question 'why would another control what is already controlled by one?' — is this a question about the cause or the purpose? Not the first, because the control by <s>Īśvara</s> is eternal, and the control by the weaver and the like depends on its own causes. Not the second, because the purpose — the accomplishment of enjoyment through the completion of the effect — is evident. [Objection:] If control by one alone would suffice for the effect — it would indeed. But even so, in a combination, there is no uselessness of either, just as in the case of number, measure, and mass with respect to quantity — when the capacity of each is apprehended, cooperative causation is established. [Objection:] If there is heterogeneity there — something [similar] will also be present here. And it should not be thought that since a potter who is not making [pots] does not attain the enjoyment accomplished through bodily exertion and the like, therefore his creatorship is inferred for the sake of that [enjoyment], and that lordship exists merely for that purpose. [Ku 5.612] As for [the objection] 'because of being caused by non-eternal effort' — it might be so if intelligence also ceased with the cessation of non-eternal effort; but this is not so, because intelligence exists even in the absence of effort for one who is disinterested. [Objection:] If [it is said that] intelligence that is a cause ceases — no, because even the intelligence of the disinterested is a cause with respect to impressions. [Objection:] If [it is said that] intelligence directed toward instruments ceases — no, because even the disinterested knows instruments. For it is not the case that one who is not making pots and the like does not look at the wheel and the like. [Objection:] If [it is said that] intelligence that is a cause of the instruments ceases — no, because the intelligence of the wheel and the like too is a cause with respect to impressions. [Objection:] If [it is said that] intelligence of instruments that is a cause of the fruit of the instruments ceases — no, because even for one who is not striving, the cognition of the thorn-prick, which is a cause of suffering, is present. [Objection:] If [it is said that] the experience that is a cause of the desire-to-do ceases — no, because even when one is not acting for some reason, the desire-to-do and the intelligence that is its cause can exist. [Objection:] If [it is said that] the intelligence that is the cause of the desire-to-do that is the cause of the effort that does not depend [on anything further] ceases — then it is not mere intelligence [that is in question]. And thus, the property of being preceded by one possessing intelligence — which is [qualified as] distinguished-effort-desire-to-do-cause-intelligence-preceded — caused by being caused by non-eternal effort — when that [entire complex] ceases, let that very [complex] cease, not the mere property of being preceded by an intelligent being. In the thesis where the provable is [mere] being-preceded-by-intelligence, this is the solution — [the objection] is non-probative with respect to that. And in the thesis where the provable is 'having a creator,' where effort is primary, there is no objection at all, since that [effort] is not a limiting condition there. [Ku 5.613] By this, [the objection] 'just as being-an-effect in connection with intelligence is a limiting condition for connection with a body, so being-an-effect in connection with effort is a limiting condition for connection with intelligence' — is refuted. For whoever would prove [the connection with] a body through intelligence, like a body [proves the connection], or the cessation of intelligence through the cessation of a body — or [would prove that] through effort, intelligence [is connected], or through the cessation of intelligence, the cessation of effort — only such a person could sometimes be thus objected to. But we, who infer from the effect alone a creator whose causal nature is known and who directs all causes with fully ascertained powers, are not to be assailed in this way, since that [effort] is not a limiting condition there. [Ku 5.614] And effort does not depend on intelligence merely for the sake of attaining the self, but also for the sake of attaining the object. Therefore, from effort [comes] intelligence, and from the cessation of that [effort], the cessation of effort is established — this is discussed at length elsewhere. But through the cessation of intelligence directed toward the effect, only the effort directed toward that effect ceases, not the eternal [effort]. And when effort is eternal, intelligence too operates eternally, not non-eternally. For there is no possibility of attaining the object through that [non-eternal intelligence] for [a being whose effort is eternal].

kāraka(244)vyāpāravigam.e hi kāryānutpattiprasaṅgaḥ, cetanācetanavyāpārayorhetuphalabhāvāvadhāraṇāt, kāraṇāntarābhāva iva kartrabhāve kāryānutpattiprasaṅgaḥ, karturapikāraṇatvāt /

na tvevam /
na caivaṃ cetanavyabhicāro 'pi śakyābhidhāna ityalaṃ bālapralāpānāṃ samādhānaiḥ /
[ku.5.617] tadutpatterasiddhāvapi tattadupādhividhūnanena svābhāvikatvasthitau- yadi kartāramatipatya kāryaṃ syāt, svabhāvamevātipatediti kāryavilopaprasaṅga iti /

children.translated_text: Now, if He [God] is always and everywhere without distinction, there would be the consequence of the effect always arising — this is the fault in the thesis of a non-dependent God; in the thesis of a dependent [God], it may be set aside — [but] this is like a child's playing with a lamp-bud setting the city on fire — no, because there would be the consequence of the non-causality of the stable universe itself.
The answer has already been given previously to the Buddhist who says 'Yes [there is no stable universe].'
[Ku 5.618] 'One who investigates the teaching of the sages and the instruction of <s>dharma</s>, not contradicting the <s>Veda</s> and <s>Śāstra</s>, by reasoning —
he knows <s>dharma</s>, not another.' (<s>Manu</s> 12.106)

[Ku 5.615 cont.] For when the operation of an agent (<s>kāraka</s>) is absent, there is the consequence of the non-production of the effect, because the cause-effect relation between the operations of conscious and unconscious [entities] has been ascertained. Just as in the absence of another cause, so too in the absence of an agent, there is the consequence of non-production of the effect, because the agent too is a cause.
[Ku 5.616] But [the opponent] says: the determination of the production of that [effect] from perception and non-perception applies only to visible [causes], not to invisible ones. Because perception and non-perception are competent to establish and negate only that much — like smoke and fire, or like swaying and wind. For one does not say 'smoke is an effect of fire, therefore of gastric [fire] too'; nor 'branch-swaying [is an effect] of wind, therefore of still [air] too.' Rather, only of terrestrial [fire] and tangible [wind]. Likewise here too, it is proper to understand only an embodied [being] as the cause, and not another — this is wrong. For perception and non-perception, being concerned with visible [entities], are the means for determining the production of that [effect]; but visibility itself is not what is to be sought [in the conclusion]; rather, [what is sought is] the two universals that belong to what is visible. For when those [universals] are grasped, in determining the production of that [effect], everything of that universal — whether visible or invisible — is determined as possessing that production. Just as for you [the Buddhist], the successively higher causal status of touch, color, taste, and smell [is determined]; and for us, the establishment of supersensory inherence etc.

If this were not so, then even for the cited examples of fire and wind — which possess light and form — how would there be establishment of the production of those [effects] for the lightless and formless [varieties of fire and wind]? If the establishment would be common to gastric [fire] and still [air] as well — it would indeed be so, if the effect without a body etc., like [the effect] without terrestrial fire that has touch and momentum, or without tangible wind — [if] smoke and swaying would arise from mere fire or mere wind [regardless of type]. But it is not so. Nor can deviation from conscious [causes] be articulated in this way. Enough of attending to childish prattle.
[Ku 5.617] Even when the production of that [effect] from that [cause] is not established, by eliminating each adventitious condition, the thesis of naturalness stands: if the effect were to transcend the agent, it would transcend its own nature — and there would be the consequence of the dropping of the effect. All this has been demonstrated more elaborately in the <s>Ātmatattvaviveka</s>, so it is not repeated here. And when the invariable relation is thus established, there is no room for petty objections from the [entities that are] invariably related. Because [opponents] are forced to accept the establishment of the invariable relation; and if that is not established, [their own] establishment is impossible for that very reason.

atr.a prathamena sarvajñatvam, cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭerupalakṣaṇāt /

caturthena vyāpakatvam, padā vyāpterupalakṣaṇāt /

children.translated_text: And the <s>Smṛti</s> [says]: 'I am the origin of all; from me everything proceeds' (<s>Gītā</s> 10.8) — and so forth.
By this, the scriptures that teach about <s>Brahmā</s> and others should be understood [as referring to the supreme God].
[Ku 5.619] And even from the argument by deployment: if [atoms had] independence, insentience would be lost; the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) does not destroy the seen.
In the absence of a cause, the absence of the effect; and the particular [belongs to one who] possesses particularity. (Verse 4)

Here, by the first [expression], omniscience [is indicated], because the eye indicates vision. By the second, being the speaker of all [truths], because the mouth indicates speech. By the third, being the universal auxiliary, because the arm indicates auxiliary function. By the fourth, all-pervasiveness, because the foot indicates pervasion. By the fifth, being the principal cause characterized by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>; for those two, conveying the conduct of the world, are [called] 'arms.' By the sixth, having as his objects to be governed the atoms and the primary [causes]; for they, being of a mobile nature, are metaphorically called 'wings' (<s>patatra</s>), since they 'fall' (<s>patanti</s>). 'Sandhamati' [means] 'generating together' — the prefix is connected with a gap; thus the meaning is 'conjoining and producing.' '<s>Dyāvā</s>' indicates the seven upper worlds; '<s>Bhūmi</s>' [indicates those] below; '<s>Eka</s>' [means] 'without beginning.'

children.translated_text: Otherwise, all general pervasions would be destroyed — this has been stated.
By this, the counter-thesis of [God's] bodilessness etc. is also set aside.

children.text: [ku.5.622] atrāpyāgamasaṃvādaḥ- "yadā sa devo jāgarti tadedaṃ ceṣṭate jagat /
children.translated_text: [Ku 5.622] Here too there is agreement with scripture: 'When that God is awake, this world acts;

children.text: yadā svapiti śāntātmā tadā sarvaṃ nimīlati" //
children.translated_text: when he, the peaceful-souled, sleeps, then everything closes.'

For atoms etc., not directed by a conscious [agent], move about, being insentient — like an axe etc. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of non-production of the effect without a cause; because it is ascertained that the activity of an insentient [entity] is an effect of being governed by a conscious [agent].
[Ku 5.620] This meaning rests on a specific [kind of] activity, not on mere activity as such. If it be said that bodily movement requires governance by a conscious being — then what indeed is this 'bodily movement'? If the intended meaning is that activity whose non-inherent cause is the conjunction of a self possessing effort, or that which has mere effort as its cause — that is wrong, because that very [effort] is not an adventitious condition there. If [it be said that] the true nature [of bodily movement] is having as its fruit the attainment and avoidance of what is beneficial and harmful — that is wrong, because it does not cover eating poison, hanging oneself, etc. If [the fruit is] the attainment and avoidance of what is desired and undesired — is it for the agent, or for another? In either case, there is no distinction, since it is common to the activity of atoms etc. And because the operation of a conscious [agent] is required even for deluded endeavor that does not [actually] correspond [to the intended result]. If [bodily movement is defined as] activity inherent in a body — no, because even the activity of a dead body would be consequentially preceded by a conscious [agent]. If [it is stipulated:] 'of a living [body]' — no, because even the twitching of the eye etc. would consequently be admitted as governed by a conscious [agent]. If [the condition is:] 'when no other substance with touch intervenes' — no, because the absurd consequence would arise that even fire and wind are admitted as such. If [the condition is:] 'of a body when no other substance with touch is applied' — no, because a body is characterized only by [its] bodily movement [itself, leading to circularity].
[Ku 5.621] If [it be said that] the universal-and-particular 'bodily-movement-ness' is that from which one infers 'this activity is preceded by effort' — no, because mere activity alone suffices for that inference. If [it be said that] 'because it is preceded by the cognition of an experiencer' — then it rests precisely on that. And by this much alone, the pervasion of mere activity by the governance of a conscious being possessing mere effort is not set aside. Because the particular's being a cause of a particular does not contradict the general pervasion.
'The ignorant creature, powerless over his own happiness and suffering,

children.text: īśvaraprerito gacchet svargaṃ vā śvabhrameva vā" //
children.translated_text: impelled by <s>Īśvara</s>, goes to heaven or to the dog's pit [hell].'
'Under my supervision, <s>prakṛti</s> gives birth to the moving and the unmoving;
I heat, I rain, I withhold and I release.' (<s>Gītā</s> 9.10)

children.translated_text: [Ku 5.625] And also from dissolution (<s>saṃharaṇa</s>).

children.text: brahmāṇḍādi dvyaṇukaparyantaṃ jagat prayatnavadvināśyaṃ vināśyatvāt pāṭyamānapaṭavat /
children.translated_text: The entire world, from the cosmic egg (<s>brahmāṇḍa</s>) down to the dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>), is destructible by one possessing effort, because it is destructible — like a cloth being torn.
Here too there is scriptural authority: 'He, pervading all beings with His forms,
ever whirls [them] like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.'

(<s>Gītā</s> 9.19) and so on. Here, waking and sleeping are the obtaining and non-obtaining of auxiliary conditions. In [the argument for] <s>Īśvara</s>'s (God's) impulsion, ignorance and lack of effort have been shown as reasons, [and these are] common to atoms and the like as well. And heaven and hell are indicative of the desired and undesired [results] respectively. This very [point of] universal governance is elaborated further below, with 'by me' and so forth. Not only am I the governor in impulsion, but also in restraint. For whoever has power over something is capable of both impelling and sustaining it, just as the more recent [illustration of] the impulsion and sustaining of the body and vital breath has been shown, with 'I heat' and so on. [Ku 5.623] And also from sustenance (<s>dhṛti</s>). For the entire world, from the earth to the cosmic egg (<s>brahmāṇḍa</s>), directly or indirectly governed by the effort of a sustainer, does not fall despite possessing gravity — like a bird's body in the sky, and like substances conjoined with it. By this, the scriptures (<s>āgama</s>) teaching the world-protectors (<s>lokapāla</s>) such as <s>Indra</s>, <s>Agni</s>, <s>Yama</s>, and others are also explained. And the usage of complete identity with everything is grounded in [God's] pervading all things — 'This self alone is all this'; just as one magician [appears as] 'a horse, a boar, a tiger, a monkey, a <s>kinnara</s>, a mendicant, an ascetic, a brahmin,' and so on. [Objection:] If it be said that this is already established from <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) alone, since that accounts for it — [we reply:] Even if that [adṛṣṭa] exists, [God's effort is still required] because, through the co-variation of presence and absence with effort, [effort] is also the cause of the persistence [of the world]. And because one part of the cause is not a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>) with respect to another cause. Or if it were a limiting condition, there would be the undesirable consequence that all [causes] are non-causes. [Objection:] If it be said that this [argument] applies only to the persistence of the body, not to the persistence of other things — that is not so, because it does not extend to the persistence of the vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>) and the sense organs; and because [the objection] has been set aside by the earlier reasoning. [Ku 5.624] Here too there is scriptural authority: 'Under the command of this Imperishable, O <s>Gārgī</s>, heaven and earth stand sustained' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad</s> 3.8.9). The 'command' is the effort that serves as the enforcing power. 'But the supreme Person is other [than these], designated as the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>), who, entering the three worlds, sustains [them] — the imperishable Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>)' (<s>Gītā</s> 15.17) — thus the <s>smṛti</s> (tradition). Here, 'supreme' means being free from transmigration (<s>saṃsāra</s>), omniscience, and so on. 'Highest' means being the object of universal worship. 'Three worlds' is indicative of all [worlds]. 'Entering' is the conjunction of one possessing knowledge, will, and effort. 'Sustaining' means supporting. 'Imperishable' means devoid of adventitious particular qualities. 'Lordship' means the unobstructedness of His will. By this, the scriptures concerning <s>Kūrma</s> (the tortoise [avatāra]) and the like are also explained.
'All beings, O son of <s>Kuntī</s>, return to My <s>prakṛti</s> (material nature)
at the end of the <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic cycle); at the beginning of the <s>kalpa</s>, I send them forth again.'
(<s>Gītā</s> 9.7) and so on.
By this, the scriptures that teach the <s>Raudra</s> (destructive) aspect [of God] are also explained.
[Ku 5.626] And also from convention (<s>pada</s>): Being effects and being without limiting conditions (<s>upādhi</s>) — thus for sustenance and destruction;
by severance, for convention (<s>pada</s>) too, and for cognition — as before. //5//

children.text:
padaśabdenātr.a padyate gamyate vyavahārāṅgamartho 'neneti vṛddhavyavahāra evocyate /
ato 'pīśvarasiddhiḥ /
tathāhi - yadetat paṭādinirmāṇanaipuṇyaṃ kuvindādīnām, vāgvyavahāraśca vyaktavācām, lipitatkramavyavahāraśca bālānām, sa sarvaḥsvatantrapuruṣaviśrāntaḥ vyavahāratvāt nipuṇataraśilpinirmitāpūrvaghaṭaghaṭanānaipuṇyavat, caitramaitrādipadavat, patrākṣaravat, pāṇinīyavarṇanirdeśakramavacceti /
[ku.5.627] ādimān vyavahāra evam, ayantvanīdiranyathāpi bhaviṣyatīticenna- tadasiddheḥ /
ādimattāmeva sādhayitumayamārambhaḥ /
na caivaṃ saṃsārasyānāditvabhaṅgaprasaṅgaḥ, tathāpi tasyāvirodhāt /
na hi- caitrādivyavahāro 'yamādimāniti bhavasyāpyanāditā nāsti, tadanāditve vā na caitrādipadavyavahāropyādimāniti /
astvarvāgdarśī kaścidevātra mūlamiti cenna- tenāśakyatvāt /
kalpādāvādarśābhāsasyāpyasiddheḥ /

children.translated_text: Objection: The senior person who teaches the convention has been ascertained [to be an embodied being]; but <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is not like that.

children.text: tatkathamevaṃ syāt- na- śarīrānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyini kārye tasyāpitadvattvāt /
children.translated_text: How then could it be so? — [We reply:] No, because He too possesses that [body], since the effect [i.e. convention] conforms to the co-variation of presence and absence with the body.

children.text: gṛṇhāti hi īśvaropi kāryavaśāccharīramantarāntarā; darśayati ca vibhūtimiti /
children.translated_text: For <s>Īśvara</s> too assumes a body from time to time as required by His effects; and He manifests [His] glory (<s>vibhūti</s>).

children.text: atrāpyāgamaḥ- pitāhamasya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ //
children.translated_text: Here too there is scriptural authority: 'I am the father of this universe, the mother, the sustainer, the grandfather.'

By the word <s>pada</s> here is meant conventional usage (<s>vṛddhavyavahāra</s>), that by which the object that is an element of practical activity is reached or known. From this too <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is established. For thus: The skill in producing cloth and the like possessed by weavers and others, the verbal usage of articulate speakers, and the literacy and sequential usage of children — all these rest upon an independent person, because they are conventional practices, like the skill in fashioning a novel pot produced by a more skilled artisan, like the words '<s>Caitra</s>', '<s>Maitra</s>', and so on, like letters on a leaf, and like the order of phoneme-specification in <s>Pāṇini</s>'s [grammar]. [Ku 5.627] Thus conventional usage has a beginning. [Objection:] But this [particular usage] could exist otherwise [i.e. without a beginning] — that is not established. This very undertaking is to establish that it has a beginning. Nor is there the undesirable consequence that the beginninglessness of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence) would be broken; because even so, there is no contradiction with that [beginninglessness]. For it is not the case that [from] 'this usage of <s>Caitra</s> and others has a beginning' [it follows that] your [saṃsāra's] beginninglessness does not exist; or that if that [saṃsāra] is beginningless, then the conventional usage of the words '<s>Caitra</s>' and the like does not have a beginning. [Objection:] If it be said that let there be some earlier teacher [who initiated the convention] as the root here — that is not possible through him [a finite being], because of his incapacity. Because even a mirror-image [teacher] at the beginning of the <s>kalpa</s> is unestablished. And creation and dissolution have [already] been proved.

children.text: (gī.9-17) tathā- yadi hyayaṃ na varteyaṃ (ya?) jātu karmaṇyatandritaḥ /
children.translated_text: (<s>Gītā</s> 9.17) Likewise: 'For if I were not ever engaged in action unwearied,
human beings, O <s>Pārtha</s>, would follow My path in every way.'
