children.translated_text: For when the conformity of that [impression] to agreement and difference [with memory] is established, the mental impression is postulated through its otherwise-inexplicability — but not otherwise. Similarly here too.

children.text: na cedevam, tavāpi brahmabhiduraśaravimokasamasamayahatasya hantṛtvaṃ na syāt /
children.translated_text: And if this were not so, for you too, the slayer-hood of one who kills [a Brahmin] with a <s>Brahma</s>-piercing arrow released at the same moment would not hold.
And the father-hood of one sleeping in his own house would [apply to the killing].
By this, [the objection that] 'neither [works]' is refuted.

For [what is meant by] <s>karma</s> (action)? Is it the result (<s>phala</s>), or the unseen potency (<s>apūrva</s>) that is its cause, or the ritual act (<s>kriyā</s>) that is its cause? Not the first, because the desire for the result would be a non-cause for activity; and because of overextension — as has been stated. Not the second, because of the impossibility of linguistic competence. For the ground of the application of the injunctive suffix (<s>liṅ</s>) is either novelty (<s>apūrvatva</s>), or being-an-effect (<s>kāryatva</s>), or both. Not the first: if the novelty that is the ground for word-application is known through another means of knowledge, then novelty is contradicted [since it is already known]. If not known, there is no linguistic competence. Because if the relation [between the word and its meaning] is not known, the relation cannot be cognized. And if [it is said to be] known from that very [injunctive suffix], there would be the fault of mutual dependence. Nor is it proper [to say] that just as the word 'earth' applies to earth presented as possessing smell, similarly the injunctive suffix applies to <s>apūrva</s> presented as an effect through the ground of novelty [presented] not too remotely — because in that case, since both [novelty and being-an-effect] are apprehended, through the priority of ontological parsimony, it is possible [to explain the application] by resting on being-an-effect alone as the syntactic connection. But there is no cognition of novelty here. [Ku.5.664] It may be objected: The injunctive suffix is applied having being-an-effect as an indicator. And what is indicated by that — whether sacrifice, effort, or something else accessible to means of knowledge other than words — is not capable of being a means to heaven as a qualification of the qualified person. And one who desires cannot be enjoined regarding an undesired result. Therefore, something else, something non-mundane, is indicated by this [suffix], which is the domain of the injunctive and other [verbal] applications — what is impossible [about this]? — No, because indication is either recollection or inference. Both are impossible without a known relation. For being-an-effect does not indicate novelty in the way that a disposition [indicates an object], or a mind [indicates thoughts], or unseen merit [indicates results] — since [such indication] requires knowledge [of the relation]. Therefore, just as an elephant [indicates] its footprint, or smoke [indicates] a fire-banner, it would indicate [only] through knowledge of that relation, not otherwise. And thus the 'establishment through reasoning' (<s>nyāyasampādana</s>) is [like] crying in the wilderness. For not even by a thousand reasonings can one grasp a connection that is unknown, nor does a word whose connection is unknown function. By this, the [claim that] 'linguistic competence is in the effect of the action due to non-apprehension of difference' is refuted — for non-apprehension of an unknown difference is not a factor in practical usage, due to overextension. Moreover, if novelty is postulated as the ground for application, the mundane injunctive suffix would become purposeless. Because there would be nothing to indicate [as novel] there [in the mundane sphere]. If [one says] that there being-an-effect alone is the ground for application — then let it be so in the present case too, since it is already postulated and possible. [Ku.5.665] [Objection:] Let that very [being-an-effect] be the ground for application, and let the obtaining of a particular <s>apūrva</s> instance be through the method of reasoning. — No, because there would follow the non-obtaining of the eternal prohibitions and <s>apūrva</s>. And in this position, the procedure 'what is ascertained in one case [holds] in another likewise' is impossible, because being-an-effect alone has been ascertained as the ground for application, not novelty. And the method of reasoning is impossible there. For a particular instance is obtained in conformity with the result. But that is not heard [in scripture] there. Nor can what is unheard be postulated. Because there is no seed [for it]. For that would be postulated either through the otherwise-inexplicability of the injunction, or through the otherwise-inexplicability of the cognition of being-an-effect — as in the world. Not the first, because in your view, that [injunction] has the form of what is to be obtained [i.e., the injunction itself is the goal]. Since even when the result of heaven is heard, [you say] there is enrichment of what is to be proved. Not the second, because when there is cognition of that [being-an-effect] through the force of words, that [reasoning method] is not needed. For in the world, that cognition depends on [knowing something to be] a means to a desired [end]; but not in the <s>Veda</s> — by [your own] admission. Otherwise, the [property of] being a means to the desired would first have to be learned from the <s>Veda</s>, since no other means of knowledge [can establish it]; then 'it is an effect' — and so the injunction would be inferential, not verbal. [Objection:] Let the result be inferential: 'whatever is to be done is a means to the desired' — through this pervasion. — That too is not proper, because of deviation with pleasure. [Objection:] When it is different [from pleasure]. — [There is] deviation with the absence of suffering. [Objection:] Setting aside the result. — Then what exactly has been said? [Objection:] What is desired by nature. — Then anything different from that would be undesired, and [saying] 'that is to be done' would be a contradiction. [Objection:] It is the means to that [desired end]. — 'When it is a means to that' — this qualification is no different from what is to be proved. [Objection:] 'This is not desired by nature, yet it is to be done; therefore it must be a means to the desired — hence [the injunction is] for the sake of the means.' — No, because 'this is not desired by nature' is unestablished. Because [to-be-doneness] is pervaded by volition directed at no other purpose. Otherwise, that [to-be-doneness] is unestablished. Hence from the contradiction, one or the other [premise] must be abandoned. [Ku.5.666] [Objection:] Let there be non-obtaining of the eternal prohibitions and <s>apūrva</s> — what is lost for us? — What is lost? Even in the context of desire-based qualifications, that [<s>apūrva</s>] is not obtained. For the injunctive suffix does not state that the effect is a means to heaven. Nor is it obtained through the otherwise-inexplicability of the co-occurrence with the phrase 'desiring heaven' — because it is explained merely by delimiting the qualified person, like Brahminhood and the like. Nor is this a [valid] inference: 'for whoever has a desire, whatever is to be done on account of that desire is a means to that desired [end]' — because to-be-doneness intrinsically [i.e., independently of] another desire is unestablished. Because by that very desire, to-be-doneness is easily non-conclusive. And because conditional to-be-doneness cannot be cognized without cognizing [it to be] a means to the desired. What is the point of this detailed investigation? At least this much is cognized from words: that one who desires one thing should do another thing. [Objection:] This alone suffices for inference. — But what is to be expressed must be syntactically connected, and what is fit is connected. 'One desiring one thing should do another' is unfit for [syntactic] connection — so how would it be expressed? [Objection:] From that very [syntactic requirement], the proof of its being a means [follows]. — Then, since to-be-doneness, being-a-means-to-the-desired, and the same-meaning [of these] are expressed through inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), there is no room for inference. And in the <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> view, the proof of being-a-means is not [established either], because syntactic fitness is explained merely by delimiting the qualified person. [Ku.5.667] And being-an-effect is not possible for <s>apūrva</s>. For if that [being-an-effect] is pervasion by volition — [it applies] only to rice and the like, since they are [already] established. If it is being a result of volition — [it applies] to the sacrifice itself, since [the result] arises from it alone directly. If it is being the intended object of volition — [it applies] to heaven itself, since it is naturally beautiful. But not to <s>apūrva</s>, since it is the opposite. [Objection:] [The desiredness of <s>apūrva</s> is] conditional, like breastfeeding and the like. — That too [applies] to the sacrifice itself. Since when heaven is established as what is to be achieved, the sacrifice alone is connected as the means. [Objection:] Because of the temporal gap [between sacrifice and heaven], this does not work. — However it works, let it be postulated in accordance with scripture. [Objection:] Through an intermediary function it might somehow work. But there is no function-functionary relationship between things at different times. And causation is proper through a function. And the restriction to the prior time without interruption is the truth. Otherwise there is overextension. — No, because mere prior-existence-restriction is [sufficient for] causation. Because only a subsidiary effect conforming to the [final] effect is the function. Because in agriculture, medicine, and the like, such practice is abundant. [Objection:] That [usage] is figurative. — No, because there is no contradiction in the primary meaning. [Objection:] Then let the father, long deceased, have agency through making the son his intermediary function, when a Brahmin is killed by the son. And thus worldly affairs would be disrupted. — No, because even when the son exists, sometimes that [killing] does not occur through him; and even when he does not exist, sometimes it occurs through [another] cause — therefore [the son] being unreliable, [he] is unfit to be a function. For only that which, having generated [the effect], invariably precedes the [effect] with respect to that [effect] is the function of that [cause] with respect to that [effect] — and nothing else. Just as a mental impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is [the intermediary function] of experience with respect to memory.

children.text:
[ku.5.668] astu tarhi kriyādharma eva kāryatvaṃ vidhiḥ /
sarvohi kartavyametaditi pratyeti /
tataḥ kuryāmiti saṅkalpya pravartate iti cet- na- kartavyaṃ mayeti kṛtyadhyavasāyārtho vā syāt, kartavyaṃ mayetyucitārtho vā syāta? tatra prathamaḥsaṅkalpānna bhidyate /
vyavahitakāryasaṅkalpo hi kartavyo mayeti, sannihitakāryasaṅkalpastu kuryāmiti /
sa ca na liṅārthaḥ; sattāmātreṇa pravartanādityuktam /
tadetat kartavyatāyāṃ jātāyāṃ pravartate iti vastusthitau bhrāntairjñātāyāmiti gṛhītam /
aucityantu kriyādharmaḥ prāgabhāvavattvam, tasmin sati śakyatvaṃ vā, tasmin sati
 kartāraṃ pratyupakārakatvaṃ vā? prathame kutaścidapi na nivarteta /
dvitīye duḥkhe 'pi tathāvidhe pravarteta /

children.translated_text: But the third [option] will be discussed [below].

children.text: [ku.5.669] astu tarhi karaṇadharmaḥ- na- karaṇaṃ hi śabdaḥ, taddharmo 'bhidhā vā syāt; tadartho bhāvanādiḥ (268) vā, taddharma iṣṭasādhanatā vā /
children.translated_text: [Ku 5.669] Then let it be a property of the instrument. No — for the instrument is the word [itself]; [and] its property would either be denotation, or its meaning such as <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive operation), or its property would be being-a-means-to-the-desired.
Not the first: Since it [denotation] is not a [real] entity and since there is no engagement [from it], denotation is not more important [than other properties].
Because the sublating [argument] is the same [in all cases], even elimination [of alternatives] is difficult to achieve. || 13 ||

[Ku 5.668] Then let the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) be precisely the property of the action, namely 'ought-to-be-done-ness.' For everyone cognizes 'this ought to be done,' and then, resolving 'I shall do [it],' engages [in action]. No, [we reply] — 'it ought to be done by me' — would this mean the resolve to do the duty, or would it mean the propriety [of doing it]? In the first case, it does not differ from the resolve [itself]. For the resolve regarding a distant effect is 'it ought to be done by me,' and the resolve regarding a proximate effect is 'I shall do [it].' And that [resolve] is not the meaning of the injunctive suffix; because it has been stated that engagement [comes] from mere existence [of the resolve]. This is grasped by those who are confused about the state of affairs — when the 'ought-to-be-done-ness' has arisen, one engages. But as for propriety — is it a property of the action, namely having prior non-existence? Or, given that, is it capability? Or, given that, is it being beneficial to the agent? In the first case, one would never desist from anything [that has prior non-existence]. In the second, one would engage even in what is painful of that kind.

children.text:
saṅgatipratisandhānādhikāyā.ṃ tasyāṃ pramāṇābhāvāt /
anyasamavetasyāpūrvavadanyavyāpāratvenāpyupapatteḥ /
viṣayatayāpi (viṣayatāyāmapi) ca svavyāpāraṃ pratiliṅgavaddhetubhāvāvirodhāta /
adhikattve 'pi tato 'pravṛtteḥ /
bālānāṃ tadabhāve 'pi tadbhāvāt /
śabdāntareṇa tacchrāviṇāmapyapravṛtteḥ /
na ca vilakṣaṇaiva sā liṅo viṣayaḥ /
tadvailakṣyaṇyaṃ pratītiṃ (pratipattim) prati cet, arthaviśeṣo 'pi syāt /
pravṛttimātraṃ prati cet, abhidhāsamavetaṃ taditi kutaḥ? tatsannidhānāditi cennaḥ aniyamāt /
anyasya sarvasya niṣedhāditi cenna- pravṛttihetuttvaniṣedhasya tulyatvāt /
tatsannidhiniṣeṣasya cāśakyatvāt /
śabdaikavedyatve cāvyutpatteḥ /
"pravṛttyanyathānupapattisiddhe vyutpatti'rityapi vārtam- nahi pravṛttihetuḥ kaścidastīti pravartate /
[ku.5.670] iṣṭasādhanatā tu syāt /
sarvo hi mayā kriyamāṇametanmama samīhitaṃ sādhayiṣyatīti pratisandhatte, tata icchati kuryāmiti, tataḥ karotīti sarvānubhavasiddham /
tadayaṃ vyutpitsuryajjñānāt prayatnajananīmicchāmavāptavān, tajjñānameva liṅśrāviṇaḥ pravṛttikāraṇamanuminoti /
tataśca kartavyataikārthasamavāyinī iṣṭasādhanatāliṅārtha ityavadhārayati /
na ca vācyam evañcet varaṃ kartavyataivāstu, avaśyābhyupagamanīyatvāt; kṛtamiṣṭasādhanatayeti- yathā hi neṣṭasādhanatāmātraṃ pratītya pravartate, asādhyeṣu vyabhicārāt- tathā prayatnaviṣayasamavāyinīmiṣṭasādhanatāmadhigamyādhikārī pravartate ityanubhavaḥ /
tatra viṣayo dhātunā, bhāvanā'khyātamātreṇa,śeṣantu tadviśeṣeṇa liṅā ityevamiṣṭābhyupāyatāyāmadhigatāyāmanvayabalāt (269) tadviṣayasyeṣṭasādhanatvāvagatiriti kartavyataikārthasamavāyinīṣṭābhyupāyatāta liṅāḥ pravṛttinimittamityuktam /
[ku.5.671] karaṇasyeṣṭasādhanatābhidhāne jyotiṣṭomeneti tṛtīyayā na bhavitavyamiti tu deśyamavaiyākaraṇasyāvadhīraṇīyameva /
tatsaṅkhyābhidhānaṃ hi tadabhidhānamākhyātena /
na ca tat prakṛte /
na ca yāgeṣṭasādhanatābhidhānaṃ liṅā; kintvanvayabalāttalābha ityuktam /
[ku.5.672] yattu siddhā(ddho)padeśādapi pratīyate iṣṭasādhanatā; na cātaḥ saṅkalpātmā pravṛttirastīti deśyam- tatra samutkaṭaphalābhilāṣasya samarthasya tatsādhanatāvahame 'pi na (270) pravṛttiriti kaḥ pratīyāt /
sarvapakṣasamānañcaitat samānaparīhārañceti kiṃ tena /
[ku.5.673] atrābhidhīyate- astu prayatnaviṣayasamavāyinīṣṭasādhanatā pravṛttihetuḥ; tathāpi nāsau liṅārthaḥ sandehāt /
children.translated_text: [Ku 5.673] Here it is stated: Let being-a-means-to-the-desired, which inheres in the object of effort, be the cause of engagement; even so, that is not the meaning of the injunctive suffix, because of doubt.

children.text: sā hi kiṃ sākṣādeva liṅā'vagamyate, stanapānādāvanumānādiva bālena; kiṃ vā tatpratipāditāt kutaścidarthādanumīyate,ceṣṭāviśeṣānumitādivābhiprayaviśeṣāt samayābhijñeneti sandihyate /
children.translated_text: For is that [being-a-means-to-the-desired] cognized directly from the injunctive [suffix], as an infant [infers] from breast-feeding through inference? Or is it inferred from some meaning conveyed by that [suffix], as one who knows conventions [infers] a particular intention from a particular gesture? — this is doubtful.

children.text: evañca sati sā nābhidhīyate ityeva nirṇayaḥ- hetutvādanumānācca madhyamādau viyogataḥ /
children.translated_text: And in that case, the conclusion is precisely that it [being-a-means-to-the-desired] is not denoted [by the suffix]: because of its being a cause, because of inference, because of [its] separation from the middle [person] and the like,
Because of [the suffix's] established capacity elsewhere, and because of the impossibility of prohibition [on any other account]. || 14 ||

Because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (evidence) for that [denotation] being more [than what is established through] the consideration of syntactic connection. Because what inheres in something else could also be accounted for as the operation of something else, like <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit). And because, even as an object [of denotation], there is no contradiction with its being a cause, like an inferential mark, with respect to its own operation. Because even if it [denotation] were additional, there would be no engagement from it. Because children, even in its absence, have that [engagement]. Because even those who hear it from another word do not engage. And it cannot be said that

[ku.5.674] tathāhi- agnikāmo dāruṇī mathnīyāditi śrutvā kuta ityukte vaktāro vadanti, yatastanmanthanādagnirarasya sidhyatīti /
(taratimṛtyuṃ?) tarati brahmahatyāṃ yo 'śvamedhena yajate ityādāviṣṭābhyupāyatāyāmevāvagatāyāmanumimate tāntrikāḥ yat, "aśvamedhena yajeta mṛtyubrahmahatyātaraṇakāma" ityādividhim; nindayā ca niṣedham; tadyathā- "andhaṃ tamaḥ praviśanti ye ke cātmahano janāḥ" ityataḥ nātmānaṃ hanyāditi /
kuryyāḥ kuryyāmityatra vidhivihitaiva liṅ neṣṭābhyupāyatāmāha; kintu vaktṛsaṅkalpam /
nahīṣṭābhyupāyo mamāyamiti kuryāmitipadārthaḥ, kintutatpratipatteranantaraṃ yo 'sya saṅkalpaḥ kuryāmiti, sa eva /
sarvatra cānyatra vakturevecchābhidhīyate liṅetyavadhṛtam /
tathāhyājñādhyeṣaṇānujñāsampraśnaprārthanāśaṃsā liṅinānyaccakāsti /
yāṃ vakturicchāmananuvidadhānastatkṣobhādbibheti, sā ājñā /
yā tu śrotuḥ pūjāsaṃmānavyañjikā, sā adhyeṣaṇā /
vāraṇābhāvavyañjikā anujñā /
abhidhānaprayojanā sampraśnaḥ /
lobhecchā prārthanā /
śubhāśaṃsanamāśīriti /
[ku.5.675] na ca vidhivikalpeṣu niṣedha upapadyate /
tathāhi- yadābhidhā vidhiḥ, tadā, na hanyāt- hananabhāvanā nābhidhīyata iti vākyārtho vyāghātānnirastaḥ /
yadā kālatrayāparāmṛṣṭā bhāvanā, tadā neti sambandhe 'tyantābhāvo mithyā /
yadā kāryam, tadā, na hanyāt- na hananaṃ kāryamityanubhavaviruddham; kriyata eva yataḥ /
na hananena kāryam-
 hananakāraṇakaṃ kāryaṃ nāstītyartha ityapi nāsti /
duḥkhanivṛttisukhāptyoranyatarasya tatra sadbhāvāt /
[ku.5.676] hananakāraṇakamadṛṣṭaṃ (mapūrvam) nāstītyartha iti tu nirātaṅkaṃ dṛṣṭārthinaṃ pravartayedeveti sādhu śāstrārthaḥ /
ahananenāpūrvaṃ bhāvayediti tvaśakyaṃ kāraṇasyānāditvena kāryasyāpi tathābhāvaprasaṅgāt, bhāvanāyāśca tadaviṣayatvāt /
ahananasaṅkalpeneti yāvajjīvamavicchinnitatsaṅkalpaḥsyāt /
sakṛtkṛtvaivavā nivṛttiḥ; paścāddhanyādevāvirodhāt /
sampādito hyanena niyogārthaḥ /
"yāvadyāvaddhananasaṅkalpavān tāvattāvadviparītasaṅkalpenāpūrvaṃ bhāvayediti vākyārthaḥ, tathābhūtasyādhikāritvā'dityapi vārtam- tadaśruteḥ /
prasaktaṃ hi pratiṣidhyate,nāprasaktamiti cet- na vai kiñcidiha pratiṣidhyate; tadabhāvaḥ pratipādyate iti niṣedhārthaḥ; ahananasaṅkalpakaraṇakamapūrvaṃ (271) vākyārthaḥ /
kiñca na hanyāditi ahananenāpūrvasya kartavyatāpratyayo jāto vedāt; jātaśca hananakriyāyāṃ rāgāt /
niṣphalācca kāryādapekṣitaphalaṅgarīya iti nyāyena hanyādevetyaho vedavyākhyākauśalamāstikyābhimānino mīmāṃsakadurdurūṭasya (272) /
[ku.5.677] iṣṭasādhanatāpakṣe 'pi, na hanyāt- na hananabhāvanā iṣṭābhyupāya iti vākyārthaḥ /
tathācāniṣṭasādhantvaṃ kuto labhyate /
na hīṣṭasādhanaṃ yanna bhavati tadavaśyamaniṣṭasādhanaṃ dṛṣṭam, upekṣaṇīyasyāpi bhāvāt /
"yat rāgādiprasaktaṃ pratiṣidhyate tadavaśyamaniṣṭasādhanaṃ dṛṣṭam, yathāsaviṣamannaṃ na bhuñjīthā iti /
tena vede 'pyanumāsyate" ityapi na sādhīyaḥ- pratiṣedhārthasyaiva cintyamānatvāt /
na hi kartavyatvasyeṣṭasādhanatvasya bhāvanāyā vābhāvaḥ pratipādayituṃ śakyate; laukikānāṃ laukikapramāṇasiddhatvāt /
tathāpi pratipādyate tāvaditi cenna- pāṣaṇḍāgamaniṣedhenānekāntāt /
nāsau pramāṇamiti cenna- arthaviparyayapratipādanāviśeṣe 'syāpi tathābhāvāt /
tātparyyataḥ prāmāṇyamiti cenna- vidhiniṣedhayorananyaparatvāt; na vidhau paraḥ śabdārtha iti vacanāt /
tathāpi niṣedhe tathā bhaviṣyatīti cenna- avinābhāvataduddeśapravṛttyorabhāvāt /

children.translated_text: Nor does the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) in this [prohibitive expression] function as expressing opposition, as in '<s>asura</s>' or '<s>avidyā</s>'.
Because it is connected with a verbal action; and because it is not a compound.
Therefore: [Ku 5.678] An injunction is the speaker's intention regarding engagement [in action] etc., expressed by the optative (<s>liṅ</s>) etc.
It is to be denoted [by the verbal form]; but the relation of being a means to the desired [end] for the agent is to be inferred. (Verse 15)

[Ku 5.674] For thus: having heard 'One desiring fire should churn fire-sticks,' when [it is asked] 'why?', the speakers say: 'Because fire is obtained from churning those.' In [texts like] 'He crosses over brahmin-killing who sacrifices with the <s>Aśvamedha</s>' — when the relation of being a means to the desired [end] has been understood, the <s>Tāntrikas</s> (Mīmāṃsakas) infer a positive injunction: 'One who desires to cross over death and brahmin-killing should sacrifice with the <s>Aśvamedha</s>'; and from blame [they infer] a prohibition; for example, from 'They enter blind darkness who are killers of the self' [they infer] 'One should not kill the self.' In [expressions like] 'you should do, I should do,' the optative (<s>liṅ</s>) as enjoined in an injunction does not express the relation of being a means to the desired [end]; rather, [it expresses] the speaker's intention. For the meaning of 'I should do' is not 'this is a means to my desired [end]'; rather, it is precisely the intention that follows immediately upon the understanding of that [means-end relation] — 'I should do.' And it is determined that everywhere else too, the optative expresses only the speaker's wish. For thus: command, request, permission, question, entreaty, and blessing shine forth from the optative. That [speaker's wish] which, when not complied with, causes the hearer to fear [the speaker's] anger — that is a command (<s>ājñā</s>). That which manifests honor and respect for the hearer — that is a request (<s>adhyeṣaṇā</s>). That which manifests the absence of obstruction — permission (<s>anujñā</s>). That whose purpose is [mere] articulation — a question (<s>sampraśna</s>). A wish born of desire — entreaty (<s>prārthanā</s>). A wish for auspiciousness — blessing (<s>āśīḥ</s>).
[Ku 5.675] And prohibition cannot be accounted for in the alternatives of injunction. For thus: when injunction is denotation [of <s>bhāvanā</s>], then 'one should not kill' — 'the <s>bhāvanā</s> of killing is not denoted' — this sentence-meaning is contradictory and hence rejected. When [injunction is] <s>bhāvanā</s> untouched by any of the three times — then in the connection with 'not,' absolute absence is false [since <s>bhāvanā</s> is timeless]. When [injunction is the] ought-to-be-done (<s>kārya</s>), then 'one should not kill' — 'killing is not to be done' — this contradicts experience, since it is in fact done. '[Nothing] is to be achieved by killing' — the meaning that 'there is no effect caused by killing' — this too is false, since one of the two — cessation of suffering or attainment of pleasure — exists there.
[Ku 5.676] But the meaning 'there is no unseen merit (<s>apūrva</s>) caused by killing' — this fearlessly motivates one who desires visible [results] — this is a good interpretation of the <s>śāstra</s>. But 'by not-killing one should produce <s>apūrva</s>' is untenable, because if the cause is beginningless, the effect too would consequentially be so; and because <s>bhāvanā</s> does not have that [non-action] as its object. If [the meaning is] 'by the intention of not-killing' — then one would have an unbroken intention of that throughout life. Or if cessation [of the intention] occurs after doing it once, afterwards one would indeed kill, without contradiction; for the purpose of the injunction has been fulfilled by this. The [interpretation] that 'the sentence-meaning is: as long as one has the intention to kill, so long should one produce <s>apūrva</s> by the opposite intention, since one of such character is qualified [for the injunction]' — this too is futile, because it is not stated [in the text]. If it be said: what is applicable is prohibited, not what is inapplicable — well, nothing at all is being prohibited here; the absence of that [<s>apūrva</s>] is being taught — that is the meaning of the prohibition: the sentence-meaning is '<s>apūrva</s> produced by the intention of not-killing.' Moreover, from 'one should not kill,' the understanding of obligation (<s>kartavyatā</s>) regarding non-killing is produced by the <s>Veda</s>; and it is also produced regarding the act of killing through attachment. And by the principle that from a fruitless obligation one should accept the one with the desired fruit, 'one should indeed kill' — oh, what skill in Vedic interpretation possessed by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> frog-in-the-well who prides himself on orthodoxy!
[Ku 5.677] Even on the thesis that [injunction means] being a means to the desired [end]: 'one should not kill' — 'the <s>bhāvanā</s> of killing is not a means to the desired [end]' — this is the sentence-meaning. And then, from where is the [meaning of] being a means to the undesired obtained? For it is not observed that whatever is not a means to the desired is necessarily a means to the undesired, since there also exist things that are [merely] to be disregarded. The [argument] that 'what is prohibited when applicable due to attachment etc. is observed to be a means to the undesired, like poisoned food [in the prohibition] "one should not eat poisoned food"; therefore, in the <s>Veda</s> too it can be inferred' — this is not better, because the very meaning of prohibition is being deliberated. For the absence of obligation, or of being a means to the desired, or of <s>bhāvanā</s>, cannot be taught [by the Veda]; because these are established for worldly people by worldly means of knowledge. If it be said: even so, it is taught — no, because there is inconclusiveness, since heterodox scriptures also prohibit [various things]. If it be said: 'that [heterodox scripture] is not a valid means of knowledge' — no, because there is no distinction in teaching the opposite of the intended meaning, since this [Veda] too would be the same. If it be said: validity is through the purport — no, because injunctions and prohibitions have no other purport [beyond themselves]; as stated: 'in an injunction, the word-meaning has no other [referent].' If it be said: even so, in a prohibition it will be so — no, because of the absence of invariable concomitance and motivation directed toward that [other referent].

children.text:
tatr.a svayaṅkartṛkakriyecchābhidhānaṃ kuryāmiti /
sambodhyakartṛkakriyecchābhidhānaṃ kuryā iti /
śeṣakartṛkakriyecchābhidhānaṃ kurvīteti /
tathācāgnikāmo dāruṇī mathnīyādityasya laukikavākyasyayamarthaḥsampadyate, agnikāmasya dārumathane pravṛttirmameṣṭeti /
tataḥ śrotānuminoti, nūnaṃ kārumathanayatno 'gnerupāya iti /
yadviṣayo hi prayatno yasyāpteneṣyate, sa tasyāpekṣitahetu; tathā tenāvagataśca; yathā (273) mamai (yai?) va putrāderbhojanaviṣayaḥ iti vyāpteḥ /
viṣaṃ na bhakṣayedityasya tu viṣabhakṣaṇagocarā pravṛttirmama neṣṭetyarthaḥ /
tato 'pi śrotānuminoti, nūnaṃ viṣabhakṣaṇabhāvanā aniṣṭasādhanam; yadviṣayo hi prayatnaḥ karturabhimatasādhakopyāptena neṣyate, sa tato 'dhikatarānarthahetuḥ, tathā tenāvagataśca; yathā mamai(yai?)va putrādeḥ krīḍā- kardamaviṣabhakṣaṇādiviṣaya iti vyāpteḥ /
[ku.5.679] laukika eva vākye 'yaṃ prakāraḥ kadācidbuddhimadhirohati, na tu vedikeṣu, teṣu puruṣasya nirastatvāditi cenna- nirāsahetorabhāvāt /
tadastitve 'pi pramāṇaṃ nāstīti cet- mā bhūdanyat; vidhireva tāvat garbha iva puṃyoge pramāṇaṃ śruti kumāryāḥ; kimatra kriyatām? liṅo vā laukikārthātikrame, " ya eva laukikāsta eva vaidikāsta eva caiṣāmarthā" iti viplaveta /
tathāca jabagaḍadaśādivadanarthakatvaprasaṅga iti bhava susthaḥ /
syādetat /
tathāpi vaktṝṇāmupādhyāyānāmevābhiprāyo vede vidhirastu /
kṛtaṃ svatantreṇa vaktrā parameśvareṇeti cet- na- teṣāmanuvaktṛtayābhyāsābhiprāyamātreṇa pravṛtteḥ śukādivat tathāvidhābhiprāyābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: If it be said: 'what need of an independent speaker — the Supreme Lord [is the speaker]' — no, because those [teachers], being merely reciters, engage [in recitation] only with the intention of practice, like parrots, and lack any intention of that kind [i.e., injunctive intention].

children.text: bhāve vā na rājaśāsanānuvādino 'bhiprāya ājñā,kiṃ nāma rājña eveti laukiko 'nubhavaḥ /
children.translated_text: Or even if [they had such intention], it is not the case that the intention of one who recites a royal decree is the command; rather, [the command is] of the king himself — this is the worldly experience.

children.text: [ku.5.680] śruteḥ khalvapi- kṛtsna eva hi vedo 'yaṃ parameśvaragocaraḥ /
children.translated_text: [Ku 5.680] And from scripture itself: this entire <s>Veda</s> indeed has the Supreme Lord as its referent.
Its purport in injunction, like [that regarding] heaven etc., is precisely through the door of its own [primary] meaning. (Verse 16)

There, the expression of the wish for an action whose agent is oneself is 'I should do' (<s>kuryām</s>). The expression of the wish for an action whose agent is the one addressed is 'you should do' (<s>kuryāḥ</s>). The expression of the wish for an action whose agent is someone else is 'he should do' (<s>kurvīta</s>). And thus the meaning of the worldly sentence 'One desiring fire should churn fire-sticks' is realized as: 'The engagement of one desiring fire in churning wood is desired by me [the speaker].' From this, the hearer infers: 'Surely the effort of churning wood is a means to fire.' For whatever is the object of effort that is desired by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) for someone — that is the required cause for that person; and it is understood by him to be so — by the pervasion: as when [something is desired by me] for my own son etc. regarding food. And the meaning of 'One should not eat poison' is: 'Engagement directed toward eating poison is not desired by me.' From this too, the hearer infers: 'Surely the <s>bhāvanā</s> [directed toward] eating poison is a means to the undesired; for whatever is the object of effort that, even though [the agent] thinks it conducive [to his goal], is not desired by a trustworthy person — that is a cause of even greater misfortune; and it is understood by him to be so' — by the pervasion: as when [even something desired by] my own son etc. regarding play, mud-eating, poison-eating, etc. [is not desired by me].
[Ku 5.679] This procedure sometimes comes to mind in worldly sentences, but not in Vedic ones, because in those, the [human] person has been eliminated — [if this is the objection,] no, because of the absence of a reason for elimination. If it be said that even if that [person] exists, there is no proof — let there be no other [proof]; the injunction itself is the proof [of the speaker], just as conception of the unmarried girl is the proof of [her] union with a man; what can be done about it? Or [to say] that the optative transcends its worldly meaning — 'those which are worldly [meanings of optative] are the same as the Vedic, and those are their meanings' — this [principle] would be violated. And thus the absurd consequence of meaninglessness would arise, like in <s>jabagaḍadaśa</s> [a meaningless sequence of syllables]. So be at ease. It may be objected: even so, let the injunction in the <s>Veda</s> be [an expression of] the intention of the speakers, the teachers.

children.text:
n.a santyeva hi vedabhāgāḥ; yatra parameśvaro na gīyate /
tathāhi- sraṣṭṛtvena puruṣasūkteṣu, vibhūtyā rudreṣu, śabdabrahmatvena maṇḍalabrāhmaṇeṣu, pravañcaṃ puraskṛtya niṣprapañcatayopaniṣatsu, yajñapuruṣatvena mantravidhiṣu, dehāvirbhāvairupākhyāneṣu, upāsyatvena ca sarvatreti /
siddhārthatayā na te pramāṇamiti cenna- taddhetu(toḥ)kāraṇadoṣaśaṅkānirāsasya bhāvyabhūtārthasādhāraṇatvāt /
[ku.5.681] anyatrāmīṣāṃ tātparyamiti cet- svārthapratipādanadvārā,śabdamātratayā (274) vā? prathame svārthe 'pi pramāṇyameṣitavyam,
 tasyārthasyānanyapramāṇakatvāt /
ata eva tatra tasya smārakatvamityapi mithyā /
tatpratipādakatve 'pi na tatra tātparyamiti cet- svārthāparityāge (gena?) jyotiḥśāstravadanyatrāpi tātparye ko doṣaḥ? anyathā svarganarakavrātyaśrotriyādisvarūpapratipādakānāmaprāmāṇye bahu viplaveta /
tatrābādhanāttatheti cet- tulyam /
na tādṛśo '(gar)thaḥ kvacit dṛṣṭa iti cet- svargādayo 'pi tathā /
tanmithyātvetadarthināmapravṛttau vidhānānarthakyaprasaṅga iti cet- ihāpi tadupāsanāvidhānānarthakyaprasaṅgaḥ /
tanmithyātve hi sālokyasāyujyādiphalamithyātve kaḥ prekṣāvāṃstamupāsīteti tulyamiti /
[ku.5.682] vākyādapi /
saṃsargabheda(viśeṣa)pratipādakatvaṃ hyatra vākyatvamabhipretam /
tathāca yatpadakadambakaṃ yatsaṃsargabhedapratipādakam, tat tadanapekṣasaṃsargajñānapūrvakaṃ yathā laukikam; tathā ca vaidikamiti prayogaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus: whatever cluster of words conveys a specific connection, that [cluster] presupposes a cognition of that connection independent of [the sentence itself], like worldly [sentences]; and so too Vedic [sentences] — this is the formal argument.
And the counter-proof in the opponent's position has [already] been stated.
[Ku 5.683] And also from the specific number [of Vedic recensions]: The numbers [expressed in] 'I shall be,' 'I was,' 'I shall become,' and the like pertain to the speaker.
Even the designations of the [Vedic] branches (<s>śākhā</s>) [cannot be accounted for] without an original speaker (<s>ādyapravacana</s>). //17//

For there are indeed no portions of the <s>Veda</s> where the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) is not celebrated. For thus: as Creator in the <s>Puruṣasūktas</s>, through [His] glory (<s>vibhūti</s>) in the <s>Rudra</s> hymns, as the Sound-<s>Brahman</s> (<s>Śabdabrahman</s>) in the <s>Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇas</s>, as transcending the phenomenal world while presupposing the phenomenal in the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, as the Sacrifice-Person (<s>Yajñapuruṣa</s>) in the mantras and injunctions, through bodily manifestations in the narratives (<s>upākhyāna</s>), and as the object of worship everywhere. [Objection:] If it be said that these are not authoritative because their content is already established [by other means] — that is not so, because the removal of the suspicion of defects in the causes of that [established content] is common to both objects that are yet to be accomplished and objects that are [already] existent. [Ku 5.681] [Objection:] If it be said that the purport (<s>tātparya</s>) of these [passages] lies elsewhere — is it through the communication of their own meaning, or as mere words? In the first case, the validity [of these passages] regarding their own meaning must be sought, because that meaning has no other <s>pramāṇa</s> [to establish it]. For this very reason, [the claim] that [scripture] is merely a reminder (<s>smāraka</s>) there is also false. [Objection:] If it be said that even if [these passages] do communicate that [God's existence], their purport does not lie there — what fault is there if, without abandoning their own meaning, they also have purport elsewhere, like astronomical treatises (<s>jyotiḥśāstra</s>)? Otherwise, if the passages that describe the nature of heaven, hell, <s>vrātya</s>, <s>śrotriya</s>, and the like were not authoritative, much would be disrupted. [Objection:] If it be said that there is no contradiction there — the same [applies here]. [Objection:] If it be said that no such object is ever observed — heaven and the like are also like that. [Objection:] If it be said that if that [God] were false, there would be the purposelessness of the injunctions for those who seek that [result] — here too there would be the purposelessness of the injunctions for worshipping Him. For if that [God] were false, and the fruits of residing in His world (<s>sālokya</s>), merging with Him (<s>sāyujya</s>), etc. were false, what discerning person would worship Him? — so the [argument] is the same. [Ku 5.682] And also from sentences (<s>vākya</s>). For what is intended here as 'sentence-hood' is the capacity to convey a specific connection (<s>saṃsarga</s>).

children.text:
kāryatayā hi prāk saṅkhyoktā, samprati tu pratipādyatayocyate /
tathāhi- uttamapuruṣābhihitā saṅkhyā vaktāramanvetīti suprasiddham /
asti ca tatprayogaḥ prāyaśo vede /
tatastadabhihitayā tayāpi sa evānugantavyaḥ /
anyathānanvayaprasaṅgāt /
athavā samākhyāviśeṣaḥ saṅkhyāviśeṣa ucyate /
kāṭhakaṃ kālāpakamityādayo hi samākhyāviśeṣāḥ śākhāviśeṣāṇāmanusmaryante /
te ca na pravacanamātranibandhanāḥ, pravaktṝṇāmanantatvāt /
nāpi prakṛṣṭavacananimittāḥ; upādhyāyebhyo 'pi prakarṣe pratyutānyathākaraṇadoṣāt /
tatpāṭhānukaraṇe ca prakarṣābhāvāt /
kati cānādau saṃsāre prakṛṣṭāḥ pravaktāra iti ko niyāmaka iti /
nāpyādyasya vaktuḥ samākhyeti yuktam; bhavadbhistadanabhyupagamāt /
abhyupagame vā sa evāsmākaṃ vedakāra iti,vṛthā vipratipattiḥ /
[ku.5.684] syādetat /
brāhmaṇatve satyavāntarajātibhedā eva kaṭhatvādayaḥ /
tadadhyeyā tadanuṣṭheyārthā ca śākhā tatsamākhyayā vpapadiśyate iti kimanupapannam- na- kṣatriyāderapi tatraivādhikārāt /
na ca yo brāhmaṇasya viśeṣaḥ, sa kṣatriyādau sambhavati /

children.translated_text: Nor is there a separate <s>Veda</s> for <s>kṣatriyas</s> and others.

children.text: na ca kaṭhāḥ kāṭhakamevādhīyate, tadarthamevānutiṣṭhantīti niyamaḥ; śākhāsañcārasyāpi prāyaśo darśanāt /
children.translated_text: Nor is there a rule that <s>Kaṭhas</s> study only the <s>Kāṭhaka</s> [branch] and practice only its contents; because the migration between branches (<s>śākhāsañcāra</s>) is also generally observed.

children.text: prāgevaṃ (vāyaṃ) niyama āsīt; idānīmayaṃ viplavate iti cet- viplava eva tarhi sarvadā, kaṭhādyavāntarajātiviplavādityagatireveyam /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If it be said that formerly this rule existed, and now it is disrupted — then [we reply:] there would be disruption at all times, due to the disruption of the sub-castes such as <s>Kaṭha</s> and the like — so there is truly no way out of this [difficulty].
Therefore, this connection of the specific designation [of Vedic branches] is caused by the utterance of the original speaker alone — this is precisely what is to be proved.

For previously the [specific] number was cited as an effect; now it is cited as something to be explained. For thus: it is well-known that a number expressed in the first person [of the verb] pertains to the speaker. And such usage is found abundantly in the <s>Veda</s>. Therefore, by that [first-person number] too, the same [speaker, i.e., God] must be understood [as the referent]. Because otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of non-connection [between the number and any speaker]. Alternatively, the specific designation (<s>samākhyā</s>) is what is called the specific number. For the specific designations such as <s>Kāṭhaka</s>, <s>Kālāpaka</s>, and the like are recalled for the specific branches (<s>śākhā</s>). And these are not based on mere recitation (<s>pravacana</s>), because the reciters are infinite [in number]. Nor are they caused by excellent recitation; because even in the case of teachers, where there is excellence, there would rather be the fault of alteration. And because in the mere reproduction of a recitation, there is no excellence. And in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, how many excellent reciters are there — what is the determining factor? Nor is it proper [to say] that the designation belongs to the first speaker; because that [first speaker] is not accepted by you. Or if accepted, he is for us the very author of the <s>Veda</s> — so the dispute is pointless. [Ku 5.684] [Objection:] It might be this: given brahmin-hood, the sub-caste distinctions such as being a <s>Kaṭha</s>, etc., are themselves [the basis]; and the branch that is to be studied by them and whose content is to be practiced by them is designated by their name — what is problematic about this? — [We reply:] No, because even <s>kṣatriyas</s> and others are also entitled to [study] those very [branches]. And the distinguishing feature of a brahmin does not obtain in a <s>kṣatriya</s> and others.
<s>Śrīḥ</s> (Auspiciousness).

children.text:
[ku.5.685] sa evaṃ bhagavān śruto 'numitaśca kaiścit sākṣādapi dṛścate prameyatvādergha(tvāt gha)ṭavat /
nanu tatsāmagrīrahitaḥ kathaṃ draṣṭavyaḥ? sā hi bahirindriyagarbhamanogarbhā vā tatra na sambhavati; cakṣurāderniyataviṣayatvāt; manaso bahirasvātantryāt /
taduktam, "hetvabhāve phalābhāvā'dityādi- na- kāryaikavyaṅgyāyāḥsāmagryā niṣeddhumaśakyatvāt /
[ku.5.686] apica dṛśyate tāvadbahirindriyoparame 'pi asannihitadeśakālārthasākṣātkāraḥ /
na ca smṛtirevāsau paṭīyasī, "smarāmi" "smṛtam" veti svapnānusandhānābhāvāt; "paśyāmi," "dṛṣṭa" mityanuvyavasāyāt /
nacāropitaṃ tatrānubhavatvam, abādhanāt /
ananubhūtasyāpi svaśiracchedanāderavabhāsanācca /
smṛtiviparyāso 'sāviti cet- yadi smṛtiviṣaye viparyāsa ityarthaḥ, tadānumanyāmahe /
atha smṛtāvevānubhavatvaviparyāsaḥ iti; tadā prāgeva nirastaḥ /
na ca sambhavatyapi /
na hyanyenākāreṇādhyavasito 'nyena jñānāvacchedakatayādhyavasīyate /
tathāca sa ghaṭa ityutpannāyāṃ smṛtau bhrāmyatastaṃ ghaṭamanubhavāmīti syāt, na tvimaṃ ghaṭamiti /
na hyayaṃ ghaṭa iti smṛterākāraḥ /
tasmādanubhava evāsau svīkartavyaḥ /
[ku.5.687] asti ca svapnānubhavasyāpi kasyacit satyatvam, saṃvādāt /
tacca kākatālīyamapi na nirnimittam; sarvasvapnajñānānāmapi tathātvaprasaṅgāt /
hetuścātra dharma eva /
sa ca karmajavat yogajo 'pi yogavidheravaseyaḥ; karmayogavidhyostulyayogakṣematvāt /
tasmāt yogināmanubhavo dharmajatvāt pramā, sākṣātkāritvāt pratyakṣaphalam; dharmānanugṛhītabhāvanāmātraprabhavastu na prameti vibhāga iti /
atastatsāmagrīviraho 'siddhaḥ /
[ku.5.688] tathāpi vipakṣe kiṃ bādhakamiti cet- "dve brahmaṇī veditavye" ityādi yogavidhivaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ, aśakyānuṣṭhānopāyopadeśakatvāt /
na cāsākṣātkārijñānavidhānametat; arthajñānāvadhinādhyayanavidhinaiva tasya gatārthatvāditi /
etena paramāṇvādayo vyākhyātā iti /
[ku.5.689] tadenamevambhūtamadhikṛtya śrūyate- "na draṣṭurdṛṣṭerviparilopo vidyate" iti, "ekamevādvitīya'miti, "paśyatyacakṣuḥ sa śṛṇotyakarṇa" iti, "dve brahmaṇī veditavye parañcāparameva ce'ti, "yajñena yajñamayajanta
 devā" iti, (yajño (275) vai devā iti) "yajño vai viṣṇu'ratyādi /
smaryate ca- (gī.) "sarvadharmān parityajya māmekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja" iti, "madarthaṃ karma kaunteya muktasaṅgaḥsamācara" iti, "yajñārthāt karmaṇo 'nyatra loko 'yaṃ karmabandhana" iti, "yajñāyācarataḥ karma samagraṃ pravilīyate" ityādi /
anuśiṣyate ca sāṅkhyapravacane īśvarapraṇidhānam /
tamimaṃ jyotiṣṭomādibhiriṣṭaiḥ, prāsādādinā pūrtena,śītātapasahanādinā tapasā, ahiṃsādibhiryamaiḥ, śaucasantoṣādibhirniyamaiḥ, āsana(276)prāṇāyāmādinā yogena maharṣayo 'pi vividiṣanti /
tasmin jñāte sarvamidaṃ jñātaṃ bhavatītyevaṃ vijñāya śrutvaikatānastatparo bhavet /
yattedaṃ gīyate- "manmanā bhava madbhakto madyājī māṃ namaskuru /
māmevaiṣyasi yuktvaivamātmānaṃ matparāyaṇaḥ" /

children.translated_text: 'The enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all worlds,

children.text: suhṛdaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ jñātvā māṃ śāntimṛcchati" iti /
children.translated_text: the friend of all beings — knowing Me, one attains peace' (<s>Gītā</s> 5.29).
[Ku 5.690] Thus, with the abundant waters of the confluence of <s>śruti</s> (scripture) and <s>nīti</s> (reasoning), having been thoroughly cleansed,
those in whose hearts You find no abode — they are of stony essence.

[Ku 5.685] That Blessed Lord, thus heard [through scripture] and inferred [through reasoning], is also seen directly by some — because He is a knowable object (<s>prameya</s>), like a pot. [Objection:] But how can one who lacks the requisite causal conditions see Him? For those [conditions], whether involving the external sense organs or the mind, are not possible there — because the eyes and the like have restricted objects, and because the mind lacks independence with respect to external [objects]. As it has been said: 'In the absence of the cause, the absence of the result' and so on. — [We reply:] No, because the causal aggregate that is revealed solely by the effect cannot be denied. [Ku 5.686] Moreover, it is observed that even when the external sense organs have ceased [to function], there is direct realization of objects in distant places and times. Nor is that merely a vivid memory, because in the retrospection of dreams, [expressions like] 'I remember' or 'it was remembered' are absent; rather, [the retrospection takes the form] 'I saw,' 'it was seen.' Nor is the experience-status superimposed there, because there is no sublation. And because even what has never been experienced — such as one's own beheading — appears [in dreams]. [Objection:] If it be said that this is an error in memory — if the meaning is 'an error regarding the object of memory,' then we concede that. But if [the meaning is] 'an error consisting in the superimposition of experience-status upon memory itself,' then that has already been refuted above. Nor is it even possible. For what is apprehended under one aspect is not apprehended under another as the delimitor of the cognition. And thus, when the memory 'that is a pot' arises, one who is confused might [think] 'I am experiencing that pot' — but not 'I am experiencing this pot.' For 'this is a pot' is not the aspect of a memory. Therefore, that [dream cognition] must be accepted as genuine experience. [Ku 5.687] And some dream experiences are also true, because of [subsequent] corroboration. And that [corroboration], even if coincidental, is not without a cause; because otherwise all dream cognitions would be like that. And the cause here is <s>dharma</s> (merit) alone. And that [dharma], like merit born of [ritual] action (<s>karma</s>), is also to be understood as born of <s>yoga</s>, from the injunction of <s>yoga</s>; because the injunctions of <s>karma</s> and <s>yoga</s> are equally efficacious. Therefore, the experience of <s>yogins</s>, being born of <s>dharma</s>, is valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>); being a direct realization, it has the status of perceptual knowledge. But [cognition] arising from mere cultivation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) not supported by <s>dharma</s> is not valid — this is the distinction. Thus, the absence of the requisite causal conditions [for perceiving God] is not established. [Ku 5.688] [Objection:] Even so, what is the counter-proof in the opponent's position? — [We reply:] There would be the purposelessness of the <s>yoga</s>-injunctions such as 'Two <s>Brahmans</s> are to be known' and the like, because they would be teaching a means for an impossible accomplishment. Nor is this an injunction for [merely] non-direct knowledge; because that is already accomplished by the injunction of study, which culminates in the comprehension of the meaning. By this, [the arguments about] atoms and the like are also explained. [Ku 5.689] Regarding this very [God] of such nature, it is heard [in <s>śruti</s>]: 'There is no cessation of the vision of the seer,' and 'One alone, without a second,' and 'He sees without eyes, He hears without ears,' and 'Two <s>Brahmans</s> are to be known — the higher and the lower,' and 'By sacrifice the gods sacrificed the sacrifice,' and 'Sacrifice is <s>Viṣṇu</s>,' and so on. And it is remembered [in <s>smṛti</s>]: 'Abandoning all <s>dharmas</s>, take refuge in Me alone' (<s>Gītā</s> 18.66), and 'Perform action for My sake, O son of <s>Kuntī</s>, free from attachment' (<s>Gītā</s> 12.10), and 'Except for action for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action' (<s>Gītā</s> 3.9), and 'All action performed for the sake of sacrifice is completely dissolved,' and so on. And in the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> system, devotion to God (<s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s>) is taught. This very [God], through sacrifices such as the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and the like performed as <s>iṣṭi</s> (oblations), through meritorious works (<s>pūrta</s>) such as building temples and the like, through austerity (<s>tapas</s>) such as enduring heat and cold, through restraints (<s>yama</s>) such as non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>) and the like, through observances (<s>niyama</s>) such as purity (<s>śauca</s>) and contentment (<s>santoṣa</s>) and the like, and through <s>yoga</s> such as posture (<s>āsana</s>), breath-control (<s>prāṇāyāma</s>), and the like — even the great sages seek to know Him. When He is known, all this becomes known — thus understanding, having heard, one should become single-mindedly devoted to Him. As it is sung: 'Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, bow to Me; thus integrating the self, with Me as your supreme goal, you shall come to Me.'
But even those thinkers who propound doctrines contrary to what has been set forth,

children.text: kāle kāruṇika! tvayaiva kṛpayā te bhāvanīyā (278) narāḥ //18 //
children.translated_text: in due time, O Compassionate One, they too are to be cultivated by You through Your grace alone. //18//

children.text: asmākaṃ tu nisargasundara! cirācceto nimagnaṃ tvayī tyaddhā'nandanidhe! tathāpi taralaṃ nādyāpi santṛpyate (279) //
children.translated_text: O You who are naturally beautiful! My mind has long been immersed in You, O treasure of bliss (<s>ānandanidhi</s>)! And yet, being restless, it is still not satisfied even now.

children.text: tannātha! tvaritaṃ vidhehi karuṇāṃ yena tvadekāgratām /
children.translated_text: Therefore, O Lord (<s>Nātha</s>)! Quickly bestow compassion, so that when the mind attains one-pointedness in You,

children.text: yāte cetasi nāpnuvāma śataśo yāmyāḥ punaryātanāḥ //19 //
children.translated_text: We may not suffer hundreds of <s>Yama</s>'s torments again and again. || 19 ||
Thus this <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s> (Handful of Logic-Flowers), of resplendent beauty — may it please both the right and the left [i.e., both parties in debate],

children.text: no vā tataḥ kimamareśagurorgurustu prīto 'stvanena padapīṭhasamarpitenar (paṇena?280) //20 //
children.translated_text: Or if not, what of that? But may the teacher of the Lord of the gods — the Guru [<s>Śiva</s>] — be pleased by this [offering] placed at [His] footstool. || 20 ||
Thus is completed the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s> treatise composed by the illustrious <s>Udayana</s>, bearing the title <s>Nyāyācārya</s> (Master of Logic).
<s>Oṃ tat sat</s>.
May it be an offering to <s>Brahman</s>.
May there be auspiciousness.
May there be prosperity.
[Scribal mark.]
